Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” For there are those who praise and defend evil things, and so the fault is doubled and does not remain solitary. Against which it is said: “Hast thou sinned? do so no more.” To sin, that is, to defend evil, as Adam did, who, sought out for penance, added an excuse to his fault: “The woman, whom thou gavest me,” etc., as if: you were the occasion of sin, who gave the woman. But he pursues fault well who desires no prosperity of the world. Whence it is said: “Let them curse it who curse the day”; that is: they strike the night well by penance who trample on the light of prosperity, who do not have the day of delight. Or the day is the enemy’s suggestion; and they truly punish it as done who in his very smooth suggestion detect the snares of the deceiver, who rouse Leviathan the more against themselves. For others, whom he possesses securely, he sleeps; but for these he wakes for every battle. But because when the vices are conquered some very small thing remains which cannot be conquered, lest the victor be lifted up, he adds: “Let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night”; because even if they shine with virtues they drag remnants of the night, even resisting, so that from it they may shine better; whence, unwilling, they are humbly darkened. Hence the Chanaanite, not slain, becomes tributary to the tribe of Ephraim in the land of promise; because when we enter heavenly things with hope, vices remain among the best things, which yet serve us for the use of humility, lest he be proud who cannot conquer even small things. Whence again: “These are the nations which the Lord left, that by them he might instruct Israel,” that is, vices in which virtue is always exercised; and while it fears to be conquered the pride of virtue is held down, and in small things it learns that it does not by itself conquer greater. Or “let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night,” because the night, that is, consent to fault, handed down from Adam to us, so troubles the eye that even those who shine in the world like stars cannot see the eternal light as it is. And this is: “let it expect light and not see it”; because with however much ardour they leap up, yet in this flesh they will not see the light as it is, because of the blindness of condemnation in which we are born.
25_marg687: Allegorically. The year is grace from above, in which is the manifold life of the virtues, like days in the year. Or the year is the multitude of the redeemed, which is completed by the gathering of all the good, as the year by its days; which in Isaias is called “the acceptable year of the Lord.” The days are the several elect; the months, the many churches which make one catholic Church. But the night is not counted among these, that is, the devil; because he beholds the coming of Christ, but does not believe in it unto pardon with the elect. Whence “nowhere doth he take hold of the angels.” Or the days are the angelic spirits remaining in the light; the months their orders and dignities, such as the thrones and the rest; but the devil is brought back neither to the light nor to their order, but is shut out from that homeland for ever. Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary,” because it is separated from that throng; or he loses man, whom he had made his companion, and, when the elect are redeemed by grace, he is handed over alone with his body to hell.
25_marg688: Not worthy of praise: man, when laid low, worshipped idols, in which he praised the demons as the darkness of the night; but now that the idols are rejected it is not worthy of praise.
25_marg689: Let them curse it who, etc. In the old translation: “Let him curse it who curseth the day, who is ready to take the great whale.” The devil, who now lies hidden as night, at the end will be seen as day, when he will be lifted up above all that is called God or worshipped. But now he destroys his malice who at the end will destroy his power by his coming; who in the waters (namely of baptism) extinguishes the great whale, that is, his strength. Or “let them curse it,” that is, the night, the elect angels, announcing its darkness by condemning it, “who curse the day,” that is, who show that its feigned brightness, by which it presumed to become equal to God, is to be despised; “who are ready to raise up,” that is, to let loose, so that he may act with all his strength against the Church; for now he is held bound in the abyss and pressed down; and he who proudly lifted himself above the others has sunk, laid low, under their rule, so that now, bound by their ministry, he lies hidden, and at the end, loosed, he will wage open war.
25_marg690: Leviathan: that is, ‘their addition’, that is, of men, in whom after suggestion he does not cease to add evils. Or ‘reproach’, because when he promised to add godhead to Adam he also took away what he had. He is called by the prophet the crooked serpent, because he is soft, pouring in snares as through the smooth coils of words; and a bar, because he is hard through malice and strikes to death. When roused he will act openly; meanwhile, secretly. “With the mist of that night let the stars be darkened,” that is, the hypocrites, who shine by their works to the eyes of men. These are they whom the tail of the dragon, that is, the final persecution of Antichrist, draws; these are darkened, because the enemy’s malice so prevails over them that they are wrapped in open evils, being outwardly what they are within.
25_marg691: Let it expect light: this is according to his members, that is, the wicked who have faith and either do wicked things or good things with no right heart; and secure, because in their own and many people’s opinion they are holy, they await the day of the Lord, not in vain indeed. Of them the prophet says: “Woe to them that desire the day of the Lord.” The light, then, that is, Christ, who says: “I am the light of the world.” The dawn rising is the Church, which forsakes the former darkness and comes into the light of justice. Its rising is the beginning of eternal brightness. So in the judgment there is still dawn, in the kingdom day, whose rising in the light of the Lord’s coming the wicked will not see, because, pressed by darkness, they will not know with how great a light it rises. Whence: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” Or in the present they do not see the rising of the dawn who, when they see works, do not weigh the intention, imitating what they may be praised for outwardly, not what may raise them within to the light. Or this is a prophecy of Judea, which awaited Christ by prophesying, but did not know him when he came.
25_marg692: Nor the rising of the dawning of the day. Morally. The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, by which the saints will rise with the flesh to see the eternal light. But however much the elect shine here, they cannot penetrate what that glory of the new birth will be to them. This night did not shut but opened the doors of the womb, because it unlocked the desires of concupiscence to human conception unto sin. And when these doors, that is, the desires of fleshly concupiscence, are unlocked, we are dragged to countless evils of corruption. Whence, weighed down, we groan; because justice requires that what we did willingly we should bear unwillingly.
25_marg693: Because it shut not up: this is of the head itself. Paradise is the womb from which the human race came forth, growing by its offspring, conceived there in Adam its origin. The serpent opened its doors, because he burst into the bars of the mind, fortified by warnings from above, and dissolved God’s commandment in it. So Job, in his punishment, thinks again on the fault, and grieves at what the night, that is, the enemy’s dark suggestion, brought into the minds of men, and that man consented to him. He says that he did not shut who opened, and did not take away who brought on; because he would, as it were, take away if he kept still, and would shut if he ceased from bursting in; for the wicked one would, as it were, have been giving us gain if he had not brought losses, as we say robbers give life to their captives if they do not take it away.
25_marg694: Why did I not die in the womb? It is not to be believed that so great a man wishes he had perished as an untimely birth; but these words are to be weighed inwardly. Sin is done in the heart in four ways, and completed in deed in four. In the heart there is suggestion, by the enemy, as the serpent persuaded in paradise; then delight, through the flesh, as there too Eve was delighted; afterwards consent, by the spirit, as there too Adam consented; then defence, through pride, as Adam too, when sought out, excused himself; he feared indeed, but also swelled. For when punishment is feared but the face of God, being lost, is not loved, fear is from swelling, not from humility; because he is proud who does not forsake sin if he may go unpunished. In deed, first the fault is committed in secret; afterwards it is laid open before men without shame; then it is brought into habit; afterwards it is fed either by false hope or by despair. In so many ways the human race weeps for its fall. “Why did I not die in the womb?” The womb in which man is conceived in sin is evil suggestion; but would that he had died in it, that is, had known that he would die, lest the suggestion draw him to delight.
25_marg695: When I came out of the belly. Morally. Because delight snatched the conceived sin outside; but [why did I not] fall in that delight rather than lose my wits as far as consent to the deed? He was received on the knees, because through the consent of the spirit, with all the senses subject to it as knees, he completed the fault. He was also suckled at the breasts, when he is fostered by empty confidence and smooth excuses. So too in deed. The womb is hidden fault. He comes out who does not blush to do openly what he did in secret; whence: “they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom.” But why did I not wish to put myself to death from the life of the flesh in hidden iniquity, or, when I came out into action, why did I not at least then know myself lost? He is fostered on the knees to grow who, not ashamed of his open evil, is strengthened by wicked habits, so as to thrive for worse things. But why these things? that is, would it were not so! He is suckled, because after the fault has come into habit he feeds himself with false hope of God’s mercy, lest he return to amendment; for after habit, even if he wishes, a man resists sin more weakly; whence, enervated, he bends to false comforts, as though God spares these things too; to which is added the flattery of many like him; whence: “if sinners shall entice thee, consent not to them.” Besides, despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. The first three ways, in their order, are more easily corrected, the fourth with more difficulty. Hence Christ raised three dead: in the house, one who lies hidden in sin; outside the gate, one whose iniquity is made public; buried under the mound, that is, one weighed down by the mass of habit. A fourth he hears of as dead and does not raise, because one pressed by evil habit hardly rises again if he is fed with flattery; which is: “let the dead bury their dead,” that is, overwhelm them with favours; or if despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. So Job sees to what great precipices of this exile man has come down, after he lost paradise through fault, and accuses himself of having sinned in the first parent. If that had not been, he adds what rest he could have enjoyed: “For now I should have been asleep and still, and should have rest in my sleep”: if man had not sinned in paradise, he would at some time have passed without death to the homeland of the angels, to which the redeemed are to be carried after death; and had fault not come forth, the saints would rest in peace of heart, and, all clamour, unrest and tumult of temptations removed, would withdraw within the secret of the mind to the contemplation of God; who now cry out as though awake, while they bear the strife of their own flesh against the spirit.
25_marg696: By “now,” which belongs to the present time, he signifies what stands always in the present, that is, eternal rest.
25_interl1959: I would rest in eternal goods
25_interl1960: by despising the tumult of earthly desires
25_marg697: Should have rest with kings: that is, with the angels, who rule those beneath them; who are also consuls, because they counsel us by announcing God’s will. Or he calls kings the holy preachers, who rule themselves; and consuls of the earth, because they counsel earthly men well. So he says that if man had not sinned, he would have gone up, even unredeemed, to where the apostles and holy preachers arrive after the redemption with great labour; who are not kept waiting like the ancients, but enter heaven soon after death. “Who build themselves solitudes”: every earthly man is crushed in heart by dense tumults of thoughts, and trampled by the press of desires as by crowds. But to build solitudes is to drive the tumults of earthly desires from the secret of the heart and to pant for the love of inward rest, so that one can say: “One thing I have asked … this will I seek after,” etc.
25_marg698: With princes, that possess gold. The princes are the rulers of the Church. Gold: wisdom, by which eternal goods are bought, as temporal ones with gold. The houses are the consciences. Silver: the divine words. So the princes, that is, the rulers succeeding in the place of the apostles, possess gold by living wisely, and fill the house of conscience with the divine words with which they instruct them. So Job, foreseeing the future, considers with wonder with which elect he would have rested in eternity without toil, had no one sinned through pride. And he says: “For now I should have been asleep and still,” etc.; because if no rottenness of sin had corrupted Adam, he would not have begotten from himself sons of hell, but those alone would have been born from him as elect who are now to be saved by redemption. He who foresaw the future now recalls the past.
25_marg699: Or as an untimely birth: because what is born untimely, before its time, is dead and at once hidden away. These are the saints with whom he considered he could have rested, who were from the beginning of the world before the time of the redemption, and yet put themselves to death to the world. The first time, before the law, which brought forth fathers dead to the world, was as the womb of an untimely birth; and they themselves were as dead from the womb, who without the tables of the law feared God by nature and, believing in the Redeemer to come, slew their pleasures.
25_marg700: Hidden: because, few being recorded by Moses, the greater part of them is withdrawn from knowledge; and they are said no longer to exist, because their great number is kept in no written record among us. Or those who, conceived through the law, did not see the light of the Lord’s coming, to which, faithfully believed in, they could not attain. In them the inward conception produced the form of faith, but did not bring it to fitting sight. Now he lays open the rest of this light, and shows in plainer words what is daily done there concerning the conduct of the wicked.
25_marg701: Or as they that being conceived: we call ‘conceived’ not only those who had the written law, but all from Abraham, to whom the promises were openly made, whom the spirit of prophecy shone upon, as Job himself.
25_interl1967: in respect of this light and rest
25_interl1968: in a manner, in the present
25_interl1969: in the hope of that light
25_marg702: There the wicked cease from tumult: that is, in the light of Christ, for which the ancients waited, the gentiles cease from the crowd of the world’s desires, and with a calm mind already foretaste eternal rest. And this is: “and there the wearied in strength are at rest.” Those strong in the unclean world are said to be not wearied in strength. He who is strengthened in the love of God wholesomely fails in his own strength, and the more strongly he seeks the eternal, the more, wearied, he dies to earthly things. Whence: “My soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord.” By saying “there” he shows the light as the place in which the elect are held.
25_interl1972: in the rest of the saints
25_marg703: And they sometime bound: the just, though at rest from desires, are yet bound while in the body by the trouble of their corruption; for the body weighs down the soul and the flesh fights against the spirit. There are bodily bonds too: hunger, thirst and the like, which cannot be loosed here, but they will be loosed from all of them “into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.” See the steps: the wicked, converted, cease; the trained rest in the inmost bosom; loosed from the bonds of corruption, they come to freedom. But what they do here meanwhile he adds: “they have not heard the voice of the oppressor.” The oppressor is the devil, who once paid man the coin of deception and daily exacts the debt of death. His voice is temptation: he hears who is tempted and resists; he hearkens who consents. The same is said of inward peace, because what the mind greatly loves it repeats more often.
25_marg704: The small and great: because here there is a distinction of works, there there will be one of dignities. Whence: “In my Father’s house there are many mansions.”
25_interl1979: he does not fear the judge
25_marg705: The servant: he who sins is the servant of sin, who here is never made free while he fears the judge; but there he will be free, where there will be no doubt of pardon. There will indeed be memory of fault there, not such as defiles the mind, but such as, without hurt, binds it more closely to bliss and joy; as when healed we recall our pains without pain, and so give the more thanks to the physician.

25_marg706: Having contemplated the rest where one is free from the master, he despises the prosperity of the world, which draws one back from it. “Why is light given to him that is in misery,” that is, prosperity in the misery of the pilgrimage? Because even if it does not wholly crush the just man, yet it divides his mind between the love of God and the care of himself. Whence he adds: “and life to them that are in bitterness of soul.” Bitterness belongs to every just man, either weeping for what he has done amiss, or because he is kept back from his homeland. Such a man longs to die wholly to the world; but because the world does not always die to such a one, but its glory is given to the sad and groaning, he complains: “and life to them that are in bitterness.” For such a man fears to be held by the world; because unless in some way he lived to it, it would not love him for its own use; as the sea keeps living bodies within it, but soon casts out the dead. So to those who wish to die wholly to the world, the world itself still lives, when, loving though unloved, it binds them by certain occupations. For the saints often desire to extinguish themselves from all life of temporal glory, but by God’s hidden judgment they are often compelled to be occupied in honours laid on them or to preside in government.
25_interl1982: they desire to die to the world
25_marg707: That look for death: that is, they desire to put themselves wholly to death to the world; but by God’s hidden judgment it does not come, because they are compelled to be occupied in honours that bind them, which they bear out of the fear of God; within there is the desire of piety, and outwardly the ministry of their order is fulfilled, lest through pride they contradict God’s disposition; and so they profit many, and, seeing themselves imperfect, they rise the higher through humility; and because they are kept back from their desires, by the very delay they are enlarged for them. Whence, to express the desire of those who seek, he adds: “as they that dig for a treasure.”
25_interl1984: eternal rest, or the knowledge of the Godhead, that is, wisdom
25_marg708: As they that dig for a treasure: because he who seeks a treasure by digging, when he has dug deeper, thinking himself now near the treasure, burns the more for the work at hand; so the just man, the nearer he is to the end and the reward, the more delightedly he sweats at the work. Or because no one dies perfectly to the world unless he is hidden from visible things within the invisible places of the mind. Those who desire mortification are compared to those digging for treasure, because we die to the world through invisible wisdom, which is dug out like a treasure; for wisdom does not lie on the surface of things but lies hidden in the invisible. This is sought by digging the heart, that is, that the mind may cast every earthly thing out of itself and so recognise the treasure of virtue that lay hidden from it. And because they seek death as a treasure, they rejoice greatly when, as a body in the grave, so the soul, dead to the world, is hidden in divine contemplation, where it is at rest from all the din of the world. Or he who digs for treasure rejoices if he finds a grave, where of old the dead were laid away with riches; because he who seeks wisdom finds, in the just once buried to the world, examples of contemplation, by which he grows rich.
25_marg709: To a man whose way is hidden: see, when it was asked “why is light given to him that is in misery,” he shows here that the way is hidden to man, because if he now does well, he does not know what he will do at the end. Or sometimes things thought to please God displease him. “And God hath surrounded him with darkness,” because, though he desires heavenly things, yet he does not know what is disposed within concerning him. There is also about him the darkness of ignorance: he is forgetful of the past, does not find the future, hardly knows the present, cannot penetrate the inner workings of God’s dispensation. But he who looks hard at this darkness weeps and with every effort seeks the light above. Whence it sometimes happens that in devout weeping the brightness of inner joy breaks out. Whence follows:
25_marg710: Before I eat I sigh, etc. To eat is to be fed by the light of contemplation, which none has but he who first groans in this exile, as where there are no goods, and sighs with desire. He describes the force of his tears: “and as overflowing waters.” Overflowing waters are borne with violence in many rolling waves; so in mourners there are many rolling waves, while they do not know what is decreed by God, while they recall their past and dread the future, and fear lest they go astray in their good deeds. When the scourges of God chastise them they suspect they have offended. Whence he adds:
25_marg711: For the fear: for they weep because they fear to be forsaken, and lest the loving stroke be not of discipline but of vengeance. Whence: “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” For sometimes it is grace that we call wrath, and sometimes wrath that we call grace. Hence it is needful to fear in all things: in prosperity, lest these things be given for greater blinding, not for comfort, as is wont to happen to the good; lest in adversity it be the beginning of punishment.
25_marg712: Have I not dissembled? Although we always sin in thought, word and deed, yet when one is raised up by prosperity the mind is carried away more unbridledly through these three: because when it goes ahead with power it thinks high things of itself; and because no one resists, the tongue is unbridled; and because it may do what it likes, it thinks everything it likes rightly lawful. But the holy man then all the more holds back his heart from glory, lest by pride he lose what he does rightly in power (as the king of Babylon, lifted up above men over the city he made, was made lower than men); he restrains his tongue too from insults to his inferiors, and his work from the wandering of restlessness, holding himself back from lawful things. For he alone does not fall into unlawful things who warily restrains himself from the lawful. So Job sets forth what he was like in power, as an example.
25_marg713: Have I not dissembled? Power held must be thought of for its usefulness and dissembled because of swelling; and the powerful man must know that he has power in order to do good. “Have I not kept silence?” See what he is in his mouth. “Have I not been quiet?” See what he is toward unlawful works. Or to keep silence is to hold back the mind from the voice of desires; to be quiet in power is to leave off the din of earthly business; because he who is not free of these hides from himself the light of the vision of God. Hence fish without fins are not eaten, because those that have fins leap above the waters; and only these pass into the body of the Church as food, because in that they serve lower things, they sometimes climb up to higher things with the mind, lest they lie always hidden in the depths; who then order outward things well when they flee to inward things and rest in the bosom of a calm mind; as Jacob is said to have dwelt at home, while Esau is called “a skilful hunter.” But it is plain that he scourges even those who do these things, in order to purge them, because our perfection is not without fault; whence he adds: “and indignation is come upon me.” Hence, with great art, being about to speak of the blows, he first set out his right deeds, so that each may consider what punishment awaits the wicked if he so chastises the just here; as: “if the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly appear?”
25_marg714: Job’s friends had come out of piety, but they spring forward into words of contention, not with a wicked intention, but because they believe he has been struck for iniquity. They ought rather to have weighed his words by his past life, and, even if they thought otherwise, to have spoken humbly; not to add a wound to the stricken man by immoderate words, but to join him in weeping, not to show off their knowledge. Yet their sayings are in many things right and strong and great in themselves; whence the Apostle uses their authority; yet the Lord rebukes them, but by comparison with a better, saying: “you have not spoken the thing that is right before me, as my servant Job hath.” Although wonderful things are said, they are said proudly against the holy man’s adversity; so Paul weighs them by their worth, God rebukes what was spoken incautiously by the character of the persons. Among right things they slide into perverse ones; so heretics hide evil things in good, that they may be received, and infect good things with evil, that they may corrupt.

25_marg715: If we begin to speak, etc. They begin softly, but break out into harsh things. So heretics put forward smooth words, lest they be guarded against, but bring in harsh ones after.

Of these is Eliphaz, who from his own experience thinks the same of all.

25_marg718: Behold thou hast taught many: they are certain goods which even he who wants to accuse admits. How great was he before, who, though occupied in ordering so many of his own affairs, also freely taught others, showing right things by deed and word. But what the accuser says good of him he turns to an accusation, saying: “But now the scourge is come,” etc., as if: you have not kept the right things you used to say. But note that the wicked speak even of the good deeds of the just, which, being known, they cannot deny, lest they seem wicked, and so that they may be the more believed in the evils they bring in; and they turn these very goods into a heap of guilt. Here, then, Job is rebuked as having said right things but not kept them, as though a wicked man by his own testimony; lower down he is noted as speaking badly, that he may be silent. And these are the two ways in which the wicked attack the good: saying either that they speak wicked things, or that they do not hold to the good they speak.

25_marg719: Thou faintest, etc. Where is thy fear? As if he wondered at virtues lost, which he puts in fitting order. As in the way of the world boldness begets strength and fear weakness, so in the way of God boldness begets weakness and the fear of God strength; because he who is joined to God is raised by a certain power above all things. Fortitude is shown only in adversity; whence patience is added, because he has made progress in fortitude, as it were, who bears others’ evils unmoved. From patience perfection is born; whence man is said to possess his soul in patience, that is, to live rightly in all things and to master all the motions of the mind by virtue; for he who conquers himself is strong against all things. But since he has rebuked him by inveighing, he now adds, as though exhorting:

25_marg721: On the contrary I have seen those: he sows sorrows who speaks them; he reaps them who prevails by speaking frauds. Or he sows sorrows who does perverse things; he reaps who prospers in them. These do not perish, as he says, but live here more happily than the just. For God allows some to prevail here, so that the life of the just may be more cleanly purged; others he punishes soon, lest he be thought to neglect human affairs and pass over many evils, so as to strengthen the hearts of the innocent who are faint-hearted. He would have spoken more truly of all at the end; it could have been said generally that the innocent and upright does not perish, because even if he is worn down here, he is restored with true salvation with God; and the wicked perish, because even if they grow high here, at the end they will be struck the harder. But because he says “Remember,” it is plain that past things are brought back to mind, not future things foretold.
25_marg722: Perishing by the blast of God: we blow air when we draw it from outside in and give it back from inside out. So God is said to blow in requital, because from outward causes he conceives within the counsel of judgment, and from inward counsel sends forth the sentence outwardly; that is, from our evils which he sees outside he disposes judgment within, and from the inward conception brings about condemnation outside. Or God is said to blow, that is, to be angry, by a likeness, because when we are angry we are puffed up by the blast of fury. So God blows in anger when he thinks of vengeance, when after long patience he who is calm in himself seems stormy to the guilty, since they are troubled before him by their guilt. Typically. The same of the heretics. The lion: the devil, for his cruelty. The lioness: the city of the world, Babylon, joined to the lion. The whelps: all the reprobate begotten by them. From these the saints guard themselves; but the heretics, secure, think they have overcome everything. As if to say: we are not scourged because we conquer the strength of the devil, and the voice, that is, the glory of the world, and the teeth, that is, the persuasion of the reprobate. The tiger, again the devil, for his manifold cunning; or the ant-lion, weak against those who resist, strong against those who consent; which they say has perished because it has no prey in them. They repeat this for joy, because what is said for joy is often repeated. Such men think they surpass all by wisdom. Whence he adds: “Now there was a word spoken to me,” etc. Heretics pretend to hear hidden things, whence they also preach secretly, so that their preaching may be thought holier, not equal to others’. “By stealth,” because they do not enter by the door with the others, but seek chinks of wicked understanding; and because a thief fears the light, he adds:
25_interl2014: The roaring of the lion. After warning him gently, he rebukes him openly. The roaring of the lion, that is, the severity and terror of Job himself; the voice of the lioness, the talkativeness of his wife; the teeth of the whelps, the greed of his sons, is destroyed. He exults at the roaring as at a thing condemned. He compares Job also to the tiger, for the spots of pretence. For the hypocrite, who seems upright, has hidden vices which, breaking out sometimes, change his colour. The prey is the glory of the just, which he snatches for himself. So, thinking that holy Job had held the goods he knew in him through hypocrisy, he says: “The tiger hath perished,” that is, the variety of your pretence is extinguished, because the flattery of praise has been taken away. For ‘tiger’ the Septuagint here reads myrmicoleon, which in Latin is ‘lion of ants’, or, more expressly, ‘ant’ and ‘lion’. It is a small animal which, hiding in the dust, lies in wait for ants and eats them; but to birds and other animals it is an ant, by which it is eaten. By this he notes that Job was timid against the lofty and bold against those under him; but now his pride has no prey, because, being struck, he is kept from hurting others.

25_marg724: When deep sleep is wont to hold: that is, while all below sleep in torpor, we keep awake to perceive high and heavenly things. And when they see this sometimes despised, they pretend to fear what they say. Whence he adds:
25_marg725: Fear seized upon me: to seem wonderful in high things, they pretend to be terrified at what they invent; and yet they are bold to bring out what they assert they could hardly hear. Whence: “And when a spirit passed before me,” etc.

25_marg726: There stood one, etc. To show that they have known incomprehensible things, they say that the spirit did not stand but passed; and they pretend that they saw an unknown face, to show that they are known to him who cannot be known by the human mind.

25_interl2031: namely the Son, who is the image of the Father and the art in the creation and government of things, is perceived first, and through him the Father also
25_marg727: An image before my eyes: because heretics often picture to themselves in images the God whom they cannot behold spiritually.
25_interl2032: all these things that follow, to the end of his speech, he perceived in the vision
25_marg728: The voice as it were of a gentle wind, etc. Because they rejoice that they are more intimate than the rest in knowing his secrets. For they do not teach what God speaks openly, but what is breathed to them, as it were, secretly. The things said above can truly be brought forward by those who think rightly; so we repeat them in the person of Job’s friends, who, even if they err in their correction, yet do not err in their knowledge of the truth; or of the heretics, who hold not the life of knowledge but only its words. Here Eliphaz is shown to be of great knowledge, but he was not humble in it, because he arrogated to himself spiritually the common good.
25_marg729: There was a word spoken to me: the Son of God; “in private,” because he “was with God.” This is said to the faithful when he is made known to believers. Or the word is the speech of inward inspiration through the Spirit hidden in the heart, which cannot be known except by him who can have it. Whence of this Spirit it is said: “whom the world cannot receive,” because it loves visible things, while the Spirit ascends to invisible things alone. So what few hear within is unknown to the greatest part of men. Or “in private,” because it sounds silently in the heart without the din of speech. “And by stealth as it were,” because swiftly and secretly; for unless the mind is hidden from outward things it does not penetrate inward ones. It receives not the whisper but its veins. The whisper is the inward speech itself; the veins are the ways by which it comes to our mind, because sometimes it pricks us with love, sometimes with terror, and in other ways. So to hear the veins of the whisper by stealth is to know faintly and secretly the hidden ways of divine inspiration. Or he who whispers speaks secretly and does not utter his voice but imitates it. So when God now intimates something of himself to us, he whispers, not as he is; but he will speak in the future, when he shows himself as he is. Or the veins of the whisper are all created things, by which we gather knowledge of the Godhead. But these too by stealth, because we weigh even his wonderful works only swiftly and faintly; but the more the uplifted mind considers God’s power, the more, held back, it dreads his uprightness. Whence he adds: “In the horror of a vision by night,” etc., that is, in the dread of hidden contemplation, in which nothing is seen plainly, but as it were in images. But to this none attains unless fleshly desires are held down. Whence: “when deep sleep is wont to hold men.” He is awake who attends to the cares of the world; he sleeps who flees them restlessly. This is Jacob, who sleeps on his journey and sees angels; that is, in the course of this life he closes his eyes to worldly things, which fault opened in the first parents to covet. And no one is brought to see inward things unless he is withdrawn from the things that entangle outwardly; whence: “Be still and see that I am God.” But the more the mind, raised in contemplation, beholds higher things above itself, the more terribly it trembles in itself. Whence: “Fear seized upon me … and all my bones,” that is, the stronger deeds; because they do not think their good things worthy of the examination of him whom they behold, which by themselves seemed of some value. Whence it is said: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like to thee?” The flesh has no word, because weak things are wholly silent before you; but the strong things praise the great one and tremble. Hence it is that Manue, having seen the angel, fears, but the woman dares; because when heavenly things are seen, the spirit which sees first is struck with dread, but yet hope presumes; because hope rises up to greater things from that by which the spirit is troubled. So because, when God’s justice is seen, our goods too seem foul, he rightly says: “Fear seized upon me, and all my bones were affrighted.” Hence Paul too, not conscious to himself of his merits, does not presume with God as judge. But when the uplifted mind gazes on inward things it cannot stand above itself for long, because, if the spirit carries it to the heights, the flesh weighs it down by the weight of its corruption. Whence: “And when a spirit passed before me.” The spirit passes while we are present, because we see invisible things not steadily but swiftly; nor is the mind fixed long in the sweetness of contemplation, because, beaten back by the light, it is called back to itself; and, advancing with great strength, it sees that it cannot see what it ardently loves; yet it would not love ardently unless it saw to some extent. And because however much one has advanced he feels the goad of the flesh, he adds: “the hair of my flesh stood up.” The hairs are any superfluities of human corruption, the thoughts of the old life; if we shut these out of the mind we cut the hairs from the flesh, so that we are not wearied by pain. Whence Moses: “let the Levites shave all the hairs of their flesh.” But we see these more subtly in ourselves when we penetrate high things; whence it is rightly said now: “when a spirit passed, the hair of my flesh stood up.” For when the mind sees true things it torments itself more harshly over superfluous ones. So when the spirit passes the hairs are terrified, because before the force of compunction superfluous thoughts flee; because the inward vision kindles the soul against itself, and when it strictly cuts away unlawful things, the mind clings more broadly to contemplation, and almost fixes the spirit that was passing; yet even this lingering of contemplation does not fully lay open the power of the Godhead. Whence he adds: “There stood one whose countenance I knew not.” ‘One’ is said only of him whom we either will not or cannot express; and so here he explains: “whose countenance I knew not”; because man, who by obeying was to become spiritual even in the flesh, by sinning was made fleshly even in mind, so that he thinks only what he draws into the mind through images of the body; but hardly, by striving, with bodily form held down, does he know himself; and so a way is made for him to think of the eternal substance, and, all imaginings cast off, he beholds it to some extent; and even if he does not grasp what it is, he certainly knows what it is not. He seems to stand, since all things pass except those he keeps in himself, as the good. Hence when he says “when a spirit passed” he rightly adds “there stood one,” as if: him whom I felt in passing I found does not pass. He passes, because he cannot be held when known; he stands, because he is known to be unchangeable. But because whoever grasps anything of him beholds it through his coeternal image, he adds: “an image before my eyes.” The image of the Father is the Son, who says: “No man cometh to the Father, but by me.” “And I heard the voice as it were of a gentle wind.” The voice of the wind is the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, who is said to be both gentle and vehement upon the apostles; because he tempers his knowledge to us so that he can be known in some fashion, and not as he is, but slips faintly in, as to the bleary-eyed; vehement, because he who touches gently shakes our poverty mightily. So because the mind of man, however much it stretches itself, hardly ever sees anything of him, it is rightly said: “and the voice as it were of a wind”; but because even a little of divine knowledge teaches us perfectly, he adds what he learned from this hearing:
25_marg730: Shall man be justified in comparison of God? This he knew in contemplation, that human justice compared with divine is injustice; as a lamp that shines in darkness is dark in the sun; which he could know, because he who sees the light knows what to think of darkness.

25_marg735: From morning till evening they shall be cut down, etc. That is, from the beginning of their life to its end they are wounded by committing iniquity, and, cut down, they fall into the depth. Or morning is prosperity, evening adversity; but through both they perish, because through prosperity they grow wanton, through adversity, impatient, they rise up to madness. “And because no one” of them, namely of those from morning to evening, “understandeth” what is kept here for the afflicted good, what is to come for themselves, who think these things good. But David, that is, Christ, finds him and turns him to his love, and feeds him with the food of the word, and makes him guide of the way, that is, his preacher; by whose guidance he destroys the feasters, that is, the gladness of the world, which scorned to have him for a companion.

25_interl2047: it troubles the wise but does not kill him
25_marg739: Anger, etc. After the mockery he adds a sentence which is true, but wrongly applied to Job: “Anger killeth the foolish.” Meekness keeps in us the image of God, who is always calm; but anger scatters it, depriving us of many virtues, because while it takes quiet from the mind, the Holy Spirit does not rest there. But one anger is that which impatience makes, another that which zeal makes. The first comes from vice, the second from virtue, which Phinees had; with this we ought to be angry at the errors of our neighbours as at our own; it is “better than laughter, because by the sadness of the countenance” the neighbour “is corrected.” But it must not rule the mind, but be subject to reason as a handmaid; let it not be immoderate, but in avenging sin consider time and measure, first conquering itself by patience. This anger troubles the wise; but anger through vice slaughters the foolish.
25_interl2048: the lower; or the one who loves eternal things
25_marg740: And envy slayeth the little one: that is, while he envies one he thinks greater, as the devil envied man, Cain his brother, whose sacrifice he grieved to see preferred, and Esau too his brother. So the little one is slain by envy, because unless he were lower he would not grieve at another’s good. Or the little one is he who loves earthly things, the great one he who loves eternal things. So the little one is slain by envy, because no one dies of this plague except him who craves these earthly things, which do not come whole to many. Hence, if we desire anything, we envy him who receives it wholly, or who, by having a part, narrows the amount for us.
25_marg741: I have seen a fool with a strong root. Morally. Because he is made solid with all his desires in earthly love. Hence Cain first built a city on earth. The stranger to heaven lives more happily here.
25_marg742: And I cursed: because when, at the sight of the prosperity of the wicked, the feet of the weak stagger, the strong, seeing what punishment follows on their glory, at once reject their prosperity. The weak man changes with the state of things: while he sees prosperity he praises it; when it changes he judges it to be nothing. But the firm man considers, along with the glory itself, the punishment that follows, and at once condemns it. But because those who prosper in the world draw many with them, he adds: “His children shall be far,” that is, his followers.
25_marg743: The gate of the kingdom is the day of judgment, in which the elect enter into glory; before it the children of this world are fools, but then they will be destroyed.
25_interl2056: of old, judges sat in the gates of cities, taking care that no one should enter unjustly or be driven out from there
25_marg744: And there shall be none to deliver them: because there the truth delivers those whom here it presses down by discipline.
25_marg745: Whose harvest: each one has a house of understanding, by which he understands and speaks right things. But because he neither loves nor does them, he fasts from the harvest he has; but he who hungers for justice, hearing right things from him, refreshes himself; whence: “What they say, do.”
25_interl2062: with the weapons of pestilent persuasion
25_interl2063: the devil is armed when he bends the wise to himself, deceiving not openly but secretly
25_marg746: And the armed man shall take him by violence: the devil is beaten as one unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to take away all good things at once. But he comes armed when he passes by some good things untouched and secretly corrupts others.
25_marg747: And the thirsty shall drink up: the fool often has riches, a gift of understanding and the sacred words, but does not drink, because he does not exercise himself in them. But another, who has no such gift, has thirst, and by loving and studying attains what the gifted man does not know. This is “the stellio,” as Solomon says, which “supporteth itself on hands, and dwelleth in kings’ houses.” For he helps his understanding with his hands, and leaning on his hands holds the building of the kingdom, like the stellio, a creature that has no wings for flight. But sometimes birds that have wings, that is, the gifted, sit in the brambles. But because it would be asked why the gift is given to the negligent and the studious man is held back by slowness, he answers:
25_interl2064: the slothful man receives the gift so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence
25_marg748: Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: because thereby the one is more justly punished for negligence, the other crowned for his study. But because we are taught to understand right things not only by study but also by persecutions, he adds:
25_marg749: And sorrow doth not spring out of the ground: the ground, that is, the elements of the world, are turned into the punishment of offenders. Whence it is said: “the whole world shall fight with him,” that is, for the Lord, “against the unwise.” But sorrow will not spring only from them, because punishment is not born of the things that strike, but of those who by sinning forced out the blows. But the more the outward punishment chastises, the more the mind is raised to things above; whence he adds:
25_interl2066: because the body is scourged so that the mind may fly to God
25_marg750: Man is born to labour and the bird to fly: because it is impossible to be without labour on this pilgrimage; but in that the flesh is afflicted, the mind is raised to seek high things. Or man, that is, the fleshly man, feels the evils of the world because he greedily craves its goods. But he whose mind passes beyond these, raised like a bird to the heights on the wing of hope, feels no evil, since he rejoices even in scourges. But because no one is able for these things by his own strength, he adds:
25_interl2069: that you too may fly to the labour
25_interl2070: by whom I know this is granted
25_marg751: That is, I ask him by whom I know these things are granted.
25_marg752: Who doth great things and unsearchable: which no one is able to search out, which are wonderful even if they have grown cheap by use. It would be of less greatness to do great things if anyone could search them out, and again of less greatness to do unsearchable things if they were few; and so he adds:
25_interl2072: these things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness
25_marg753: Wonderful things without number: because the greatness of the divine works can neither be discussed as to their quality nor numbered as to their quantity.
25_marg754: I have seen a fool. Mystically. The fool is the people of the Jews, who scorned the wisdom of God in the flesh. “With a strong root,” because it overcame the elect by killing them; but the heretics too reprove its unbelief. This is what Eliphaz despises by cursing. The children are those it begets in unbelief. “Far from safety,” because even if happy here, they will afterwards be punished more heavily. “In the gate,” that is, in Christ, in whose presence the Jews fell who had flourished in the Law before his coming; whom no one delivers, because by killing the Redeemer they lost the deliverance offered them. “Whose harvest”: the harvest is the words of God, which, because the fool had them but did not eat, the hungry Gentile eats by understanding them; the harvest lost, he himself also perishes. “The armed man,” that is, the devil, carries him off by killing the life of faith in him. “The thirsty”: the Gentiles are watered by the streams of the sacred word. The same words are both harvest, because they refresh the fasting mind, and riches, because they order behaviour with great beauty.
25_marg755: Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: he puts this because some thought that all scourges come by natural causes, according to the nature of the elements, and not from the fault of the one struck.
25_marg756: Who giveth rain. Allegorically. These words are mystical, because Job’s friends had been taught by his company. He gives rain to the earth when he pours the grace of preaching into the dry hearts of the Gentiles.
25_marg757: Watereth all things with waters, when he fills man with the Spirit to bear fruit. Man is called all things because he has something in common with all things. Or all things, that is, rich and poor and all the differences of men, because reward follows a good work. He adds:
25_interl2074: those who despise temporal things he raises to heavenly ones
25_marg758: Who setteth up the humble on high, so that those now despised may judge with the Lord.
25_marg759: Those that mourn: because the more they are troubled now by adversity, and chastise themselves by lamenting, the loftier the health they will have, even in this life. These things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness, like those who rejoice when they have done evil. But these grow cheerful from the certainty of eternal salvation.
25_marg760: Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant: when the reprobate devise evil, God sometimes, lest they prevail against the good, takes away their strength so that they lack the effect of the deed, and are guilty before God in conscience.
25_marg761: Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked: because human deeds serve God’s counsels fittingly even when they resist them; as in the selling of Joseph, so that he should not be worshipped; in Saul’s demand for foreskins, so that David should be destroyed; in the death of the Lord, so that not all should believe in him. God grants some things in mercy, permits others in anger, which he then turns to the use of his own counsel; so that the things which fight against his counsel serve his counsel, and what is done without his will is not contrary to his will. Whence: “Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done.”
25_marg762: They shall meet with darkness in the day. Mystically. Because in the very presence of the truth they were blinded by the error of unbelief, seeing the miracles of Christ and doubting his Godhead.
25_marg763: As in the night: by groping we seek what “we do not see with our eyes.” The Jews had seen miracles and still, as though groping, asked: “If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.” But Christ could not be held long in their hands. Whence he adds:
25_marg764: But he shall save … from the sword of their mouth: the sword of the mouth is the accusation of the Jews. The hand of the violent: the Gentiles who crucified him. But Christ overcame these by rising again, in whom, the needy, that is, the humble people of the faithful, the hope of the life to come is made solid. But the iniquity which now opens its mouth wide in insult to Christ will shut it through punishment; or, converted, it ceases from its injuries.
25_marg765: The same things of the wicked in general. “They shall meet with darkness in the day.” The mind of the envious man, when it is pained at another’s good, is darkened by the ray of the sun. “And grope at noonday as in the night.” The day of good work shines outwardly in the neighbour, but they grope as in the night, because, blind with spite, they busy themselves to find something to blame. Behold Lot, that is, the just man, with the wicked opposing him, is shut within the house and protected, that is, he returns to his mind and stays within. The blind Sodomites go round about, that is, the envious search out his deeds and words, and do not find the door, that is, an opening for blame, but grope at the wall, because everywhere the praiseworthy action of the just man meets them. “They shall grope.” But the poor in spirit, that is, he who is not lifted up in himself, is saved “from the sword of their mouth,” that is, from wicked persuasion. “And the poor from the hand of the violent,” that is, from hostile power, so that he is neither drawn away by the flatteries of persuasion nor broken by the pain of torments. The poor man is not drawn away, because his hope, fixed in eternal things, is made solid against these. When the poor man comes to the fruit of this hope, the proud man falls dumb and draws in his mouth, because torments bind the tongue that spoke against the just in detraction. But that the elect may escape punishment and reach the reward, he must be purged here by scourges. Whence he adds: “Blessed is the man whom God correcteth.”
25_interl2084: God sometimes lets the soul be wounded by the longing of its desire, so that it may rise stronger and be healed
25_marg766: And because he is blessed: “refuse not therefore the chastising of the Lord.” He refuses it who complains that he suffers unjustly. So Eliphaz, thinking that Job is struck for cleansing, not for the proving of his fortitude, because Job speaks freely, asking the causes of his striking, thinks he refuses the chastising of the Lord. So heretics turn to evil what is rightly done by the Church.
25_marg767: For he woundeth: in two ways God wounds those whom he brings back to salvation. Sometimes he strikes in the body to heal the mind; sometimes, without outward scourges, he strikes the hardness of the mind with longing for himself, and so heals it, which lay dead and secure in the world. But while the mind pants after God and despises all worldly things, at once all things are turned into temptation for it and afflict it; but while it is worn by passing labour it is freed from lasting labour. And so he adds:
25_interl2087: by six he understands all the evils of the present world, which runs its course in the six days assigned to work
25_marg768: In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh: the number six, which the seventh follows, signifies the work and course of the present life, because on the sixth day God, completing all things, made man, “and on the seventh he rested,” which has no evening, that is, no end. So he delivers in the seventh trouble, so that in the seventh evil may not touch; because here he wears down in fatherly teaching, but on the day of judgment hides from the lash.
25_interl2089: even then he breathes into his faithful, without sound, what is to be done
25_marg769: In famine: he counts up the evils of the present life and the helps of God. The famine of the mind is the silence of the word of God; when this is withdrawn, the temptation of the flesh, which is the battle, grows strong. But God, even in famine, snatches the soul from death, because he refreshes it with his word.
25_interl2090: in the temptation of the flesh
25_marg770: And in battle: he makes them strong against the temptations of the flesh. But one so made sometimes fears detraction. Whence he adds:
25_interl2091: from the word of detraction or insult
25_marg771: From the scourge of the tongue: that is, from the reproach of insult, for which a man, mocked, ceases from good. Whence David: “and from the sharp word.” From this the holy man is hidden, because while he does not seek praise here, neither does he feel insults. But because after these someone fears the tortures of the body, it follows:
25_marg772: And thou shalt not fear calamity, of persecution. But because such a man prepares for himself security in the terror of the judgment to come, he adds:
25_marg773: In destruction and famine: the destruction is hell, which torments without; the famine is hunger, because they will be separated from the sight of the eternal bread. As they sinned within and without, so they will be punished within and without. Or “from the scourge of the tongue,” that is, from the sentence of eternal damnation, which is: “Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire.” And the just man will be hidden from the calamity that comes, because in that strictness he will be comforted with the gentle voice: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat”; and he will laugh, cheerful from glory, no longer suffering with the damned, clinging to divine justice by sight; and it would be a lessening of beatitude if he wished anything he could not fulfil. But because here he tastes the beginnings of the security to come, so that he may not fear the old enemy, so that he may not shudder at his assault in the moment of death, he adds:
25_interl2096: at the going out of the present life
25_marg774: And the beasts of the earth, which at the time of death are let loose to snatch souls; but he who did not follow them when they flattered does not fear them when they rage; and the beginning of reward is security of mind at death. But when one lives well, he must take care not to glory in being singular, despising others, but to think again of the common good. Whence he adds:
25_interl2097: with the elect of the Church
25_marg775: But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands: the lands are, as it were, the divided nations of the Church, differing in customs and language. The stones are the elect, who are set in the building. So he who lives rightly joins himself to the stones by a covenant, because in forsaking the world he binds himself to the saints by imitation; whence the attack grows, by which, however, worn down, he is more humbly subject to God. Whence he adds:
25_interl2100: evil spirits will not attack you
25_marg776: And the beasts of the earth: not ‘at peace’ but ‘peacemaking,’ because they do not have peace but make peace; because the more fiercely a man is attacked by the devil, the more he is driven to love, and a firmer peace is made with God. Or the beasts are the motions of the flesh, which, pressed down by continence as in a cage, even if they roar in tempting, yet do not break out into the deed, as into the frenzy of biting; in this they are peacemaking. Or, because they disturb, that place where one lives with no contradiction is loved the more, and so they drive to the love of inmost quiet.
25_marg777: And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle is in peace, etc. Peace is either begun, which is conceived here from the longing for God, or full, which will be in the future from the sight of God. So when the mind is subjected to God, or the flesh to the mind, the tabernacle of the just man, that is, the body which the mind inhabits, has peace, the motions of the desires being reined in under justice. But this chastity of the flesh is nothing if gentleness of mind in the love of neighbour is not present. Whence he adds:
25_marg778: And visiting thy beauty thou shalt not sin: our beauty is our neighbour, in whom we see what we are; he visits him who goes to him with the steps of love, and, having looked at himself, comes down to him. And this is the tree that brings forth seed after its kind, that is, the mind which considers another from itself and brings forth the shoot of right work. Behold Paul, who comes near to all, coming down to them indeed but not falling. And he fully conquers sin who weighs from himself how he may be widened in love of his neighbour. But when the flesh is restrained and the mind exercised in virtues, it remains that he teach by speaking the life he keeps in his conduct, because from the seed of good work he gathers rich fruits of preaching. Whence he adds:
25_marg779: Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied: for he receives the gift of speaking well who lives well, and his conscience does not hinder him as he speaks. Hence it is that the Egyptians, made slaves, receive corn for seed, who, while free before, had received it for eating; because when we are fully subject to God we are filled with the word of preaching. Before, as free men, we are fed with the sacred word, and yet are taken up with some things we seek in the world. From preaching follows a great offspring of the faithful. And this is:
25_marg780: And thy offspring like the grass of the earth: that is, countless. Or it is compared to grass because, forsaking the withering glory of the world, it grows green with inward hope. But it is not enough for the just man to do these great things outwardly unless he also penetrates to eternal things by contemplation. Whence he adds:
25_marg781: Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance: the grave is contemplation, which hides in its inmost places those dead to the world; and the active life in a way buries, covering those dead to wicked ways. But contemplation buries more perfectly in abundance, because it has first gathered the works of the active life. He is not a perfect preacher who puts works after contemplation, or contemplation after works. Whence Christ, the pattern of life, works miracles in the cities by day and prays through the night on the mountains. Those who contemplate, fixed in the love of God, drink in what they pour out for the good of their neighbours.
25_marg782: As a heap of wheat is brought: because the time of action comes first, of contemplation last. And the perfect man must first exercise his mind in virtues, and afterwards store it in the barn of quiet. Or the grave is eternal rest, in which one rests the more truly the more perfectly the life of corruption is put to death. He enters it in abundance who, after gathering the works of this life, wholly dead to this changeableness, is hidden in the secret place of the true light, like wheat. Because the just feel persecutions in a time not their own, but in their own they go in like grain into the barn.
25_interl2102: as if: I have not lied
25_marg783: As we have searched out: by this he notes that he spoke above of the grave, the beasts, the stones, the tabernacle and suchlike not according to the surface, but sought the inner things in them.
25_marg784: Which thou having heard: words of boasting. Even if he taught well, it is unskilful to want to teach a better man; whence the sayings of the friends, even if right, are reproved as not rightly said.
25_marg785: O that my sins, etc. Allegorically. Touched by scourges, he is provoked by words, so that, roused to defend himself, he might fall into obstinacy; but as, struck, he gave thanks in silence, so, provoked, he answered rightly: “O that my sins were weighed.”
25_interl2105: as if: O that the balance would come, that is, Christ, who has two scales, mercy and justice; mercy is light in forgiving, justice of greater weight in correcting and punishing
25_marg786: A balance: Christ, holding in the Father’s hand the scale of mercy and of justice, shows sin to be light by loosing it through mercy, and calamity to be of heavy weight by dying. He also gives this grace, that the calamity itself may be known. For blind man rejoiced in exile as if in his homeland; but God, appearing outwardly, calls man back within, so that, having seen what he lost, he may grieve heavily at what he bears. So he says: “O that … were weighed,” that is, the evil of our damnation is believed light, but O that he would come who, showing the homeland, might teach that the exile is heavy. Calamity is compared to the sand which is driven out by the surge of the waves, because sinning man, moved by the waves of temptations, went out from the inmost things to the outward. It is called heavier because the punishment is shown to have been hard, while the fault is lightened through mercy. But he who through the grace of Christ has a foretaste of the homeland groans amid present things, where the ignorant laugh, weighing the judgments of God by which he is afflicted. And this is:
25_marg787: Therefore my words are full of sorrow: For the arrows of the Lord: that is, the stroke of God’s punishment, which does not leave me uncorrected as it leaves many, but drinks up my spirit, that is, checks my pride, so that I say: “My spirit hath fainted away.” And I not only groan at what I suffer, but fear what you threaten. And this is:
25_marg788: The terrors of the Lord war: lest eternal death follow after this. But because he longs for the coming of the balance, he adds with what ardour the Gentiles and Judea thirst for it.
25_marg789: Will the wild ass bray, that is, the ass of the field. The ass is the Gentile people, which, as nature brought it forth outside the stalls of discipline, so remained wandering in the field of pleasures. The ox: the Jew, who, set under the yoke of God, gathering proselytes, drew the name of the Law through the hearts he could. Of both peoples many, like Job and Simeon, awaited the coming of Christ. Their grass and hay is the Incarnation, with which they are filled: “for all flesh is grass.” Refreshed by its grace, the wild ass no longer groans, and the ox does not have the manger of the Law empty, since it has received him whom the Law itself foretold. Hence, when born, he is laid in a manger, that he might refresh with the hay of flesh the animals fasting in the Law. But because before the coming of Christ the Law was held not spiritually but carnally, he adds:
25_interl2113: the unsavoury thing can be understood either as the Law without spiritual understanding, or as the philosophy of the Gentiles concerning the incarnation of the Word of God
25_marg790: Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten: salt is the virtue of hidden understanding, without which the Gentiles would not be subject to the Law commanding hard things, nor taste that which, tasted carnally, brings death; because it binds offences with hard punishment, and because it teaches guilt but does not blot it out. But when they recognized the truth in it, they eat, pressed by their desires, what before they would not touch, seeking amid those carnal things him whom they love ardently. But these things fit Judea too, which through the Law had salt from the knowledge of the one God, and scorned to receive the unsavoury Gentiles; because the divine sentence, with death set before it, had forbidden Judea to make a covenant with foreigners and defile its life. Hence he says: “Or can a man taste that which when tasted bringeth death?” But, according to the elect converted to Christ, when its own people rejected the word of God it turns to the Gentiles, and those whom it did not even touch in fellowship it now receives, hungering to convert them, suffering the straits of preaching, which is despised among its own.
25_marg791: Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten: the same. MORALLY. He longs for the balance; we already live by faith in it, but yet for our cleansing we suffer its arrows, and fear with the terror of what is to come. But because we are sons, we ought not to fear him as Lord, but love him as Father and pant after him, where we may be fed with food, that is, his eternity, for which we now bray. Whence: “Will the wild ass bray?” The wild ass is the people which in the field of faith is bound by the thongs of no office. The ox: prelates, pressed by the yoke of offices. The food of both is the eternal refreshment, which, fasting in exile, they ardently desire. But the wicked oppose this intention by their words and ways, which are unsavoury things offered to the good, that they may let them into the belly of delight; among which words, pressed on the ears importunately, beget temptation in the heart; and although reason rejects them and the tongue condemns them, yet what is judged outwardly is hardly conquered within. So, when the saints, raised up to eternal life, drive unsavoury things from the heart, they also separate themselves from such words; and this is: “Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten?” But those already set on high, apart from fools, often, while they take care only to bear their own hard things, are not girded up for the love of truth. Whence he adds:
25_marg792: Or can a man taste: it is hard to seek what tortures, what drives away life; but often, when one is on high, he bends down to bear the evils of fools, so as to draw them. For with his desire for heavenly things increased he is pressed hard, and for the sweetness of those things he does not fear the bitter things of the world. Whence, after the impossible taste of death, he adds:
25_marg793: The things which before my soul would not touch: that is, the evils of the world are now sweet foods for love of heaven. And since these are sweet: “Who will grant that my request may come?” namely:
25_interl2115: here it is plain that he did not refuse the chastising of the Lord; because some refuse it, the Lord in anger draws back his hand from correction, even when it has begun
25_marg794: That he that hath begun may destroy me: the adversary destroys, and man falls away from virtue. God destroys, and, broken from vices, he is made solid in virtue. So he who longs to draw near to God through scourges says: “that he that hath begun may destroy me”; because sometimes God begins the destruction of vices, and man, advanced in that very beginning, is lifted up; and so the enemy, shut out, creeps back more heavily, taking other spirits with him, and destroys the virtues.
25_marg795: That he may let loose his hand: that is, exercise its effect. For while, against one puffed up by long prosperity, he does not exercise his love through scourges, he holds his hand bound, as it were, from striking vices; whence he says to the sinning people: “I will be angry with thee no more,” and: “my jealousy hath departed from thee.” “And cut me off”: for when pain or temptation strikes us, the pride of the mind is cut down and falls, so that it now seeks the hand of one who lifts it up.
25_marg796: And that this may be my comfort, that afflicting me: as if: some he spares here so as to strike them for ever; but let him strike me here, not sparing, which is my comfort. For the saints fear being spared here. That he said this not with a swollen but a humble mind he shows in these words:
25_interl2118: that is, I will not murmur at his examinations
25_marg797: Nor I contradict the words: the words of God to us are not only things said but also things done, as here the striking of Job, which he does not contradict by murmuring; for he even calls holy him whom he endures striking him.
25_marg798: For what is my strength: the strength of the good is one thing, of the wicked another; for theirs is to conquer the allurements of the flesh and the world, to endure evils here for eternal things. The strength of the wicked is always to love present things and to hold out unfeelingly against the scourges of God, not to rest from craving temporal things even in adversity, to put hope in themselves. Of both Isaias says: “They that hope in the Lord shall change their strength.” For in saying not ‘shall take’ but ‘shall change,’ he made it plainly known that the strength which is laid aside is one, that which is begun another. The wicked man bears evils and dangers for the world; the just man is weak to suffer these for the world; he sees the end, how short this life is, and refuses to suffer for what he does not love. So he says:
25_marg799: For what is my strength … or what is my end: that is, I cannot bear evils for the world, because I am not strong in desiring it; because when I consider the end of this life, why should I suffer for that which I scorn? For I am not like the hardness of the wicked, who are unfeeling as stone and brass. Stones when struck give no clear sound, which brass does; but because a stone lacks life, it has no feeling in its sound. So some are so hard that even when struck they give no sound of humble confession. Others give it, but not from the heart; and so they do not feel the good things they speak, and, not fulfilling them, cry out without life. But Job is neither so hardened as to be silent from confession when struck, nor ignorant of the meaning of his voice. By denying that he is strong through madness he shows that he is strong through a state of health. But lest he claim this for himself, he puts whence he has it, and, so to speak, the weak man has strength; whence he adds:
25_marg800: Behold there is no help: also, for the merit of greater strength, he adds how he is forsaken by those near him:
25_marg801: And my familiar friends also: if he is despised outwardly, within he presides on the throne of judgment. For he breaks out into sentences.
25_marg802: He that taketh away mercy from his friend: a friend is any neighbour; when we do him good, he helps us to life. From love of God love of neighbour is born, because he who neglects God does not know how to love his neighbour. Hence, about to say: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour,” etc., he first said: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.” And through love of neighbour the love of God grows strong; whence: “he that loveth not his brother whom he seeth, how can he love God whom he seeth not?” Yet this love of God is born through fear, but by growing is changed into affection. And God, so that it may be seen how near or far each one is from charity, strikes some; in which he both teaches them and betrays false friends, and gives those not struck an occasion of good work. So he who takes away mercy from the stricken forsakes the fear of God, because he openly shows that he did not love him, and wickedly sets himself up against God, whom he acknowledges neither as merciful in himself nor as just in the stricken. In Job is signified the life of the whole elect people, of which he is a member. The reprobate are joined with the good in faith and sacraments but not in charity; whence they are also called brethren. And he compares those who pass by to a torrent which passes from the mountains into the valleys, which, gathered by winter rains, dries up in summer. For those who forsake things above for the world seek the depths from the mountains. In the winter of this life many, to be dried up in the summer of judgment, pass swiftly, that is, without obstacle or difficulty, because the ascent is in labour and the descent in pleasure. A rock is pushed upward with labour, easily it slides back to the bottom; things grow with labour that quickly fall. Or they pass suddenly into the valleys, that is, to the lowest places of punishment, they from whom the days of life are snatched daily. But there are some who wish to act rightly, but some things in the present stand against them in their weakness, and while they fear to suffer these, they offend God. These are they who fear the hoary frost, which freezes below; and the snow, which falls from above, that is, eternal punishment, falls upon them; and those who fear things to be trodden underfoot from below suffer things to be feared from on high. These, if they are glorious now, at the time when they are scattered will perish outwardly too, having lost all these things, they who long ago perished inwardly by neglecting eternal things; of whom it is rightly said:
25_marg803: And after it groweth hot: that is, when through knowledge of punishment they begin to burn, they will be separated from the delight of the flesh which they held with desire. The wicked do not understand eternal things except when they are already punished for earthly ones; then the mind boils, and kindles itself with the fire of a late repentance; then its hardness is melted through punishment. Hence the prophet: “vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear.” This they are to suffer then; meanwhile they are entangled in these things.
25_marg804: Are entangled: everything entangled is folded back upon itself; so the wicked, sometimes wishing for good things, stretched as it were outside themselves, are folded back, when tempted, to their accustomed evils. Or they are entangled who, even if sometimes, one wickedness overcome, they lift a foot, another reigning entangles them back even into that which they had conquered; as he who has scorned avarice is still lustful, and for the price of lust returns to avarice; so the vices hold their runaway by taking turns, and bind his steps as with snares. Whence often, weary, they return to their pleasures and do not care for the things that last. Whence he adds:
25_marg805: They shall walk in vain, and shall perish: because they carry nothing with them of the fruit of their labour. But the just man does not appear empty in the sight of the Lord; for he carries the sheaves of justice. And he frightens men from imitating those by their end.
25_marg806: Consider the paths: Thema means the south wind, Saba a net. The south wind, which loosens the limbs with warmth, is here the slack looseness of living. The net is the bond of action; and man is entangled in loose acts while he does not perfectly forsake the world, while he goes not with strict zeal but with loosened steps, like one held back from the things of God by fleshly love of parents. He says “Consider,” because we love perverse things when doing them, but when we see them in others we judge them; whence, returning to ourselves, we blush for such things.
25_marg807: Wait a little while: because whatever ends is little; but he who thinks this long does not care for eternal things. Having spoken of the shortness of life, he rises against the wicked with the voice of the just.
