25_interl2120: the wicked come to the good to accuse them, and when they cannot, they blush
25_marg808: They are confounded: because, namely, the wicked try to draw the good back from hope through harsh things; if they succeed, they exult; if not, they blush to have been cruel in vain. Whence he adds also what happens in the requital:
25_marg809: They are come also: at the judgment the wicked come to the just, because they will see their glory, so that they may grieve more heavily seeing what they have lost. Then shame covers them, when conscience burns them as a witness. The same spiritually. Job’s friends are confounded, because while they cannot bend me to despair they are confounded; they are come, when they now recognize the steadfastness of my mind within, and they blush. He shows them to be of the number of those who do not fear God unless terrified by their own or others’ adversity.
25_marg810: Now you are come: as if: I feared God even before adversity; you, who do not fear God out of love, are afraid only because of the blow.
25_marg811: Did I say: Bring: the Church does not need the substance of heretics, of whom Job’s friends are a figure, that is, fleshly wisdom; and it refuses to hear from them even the right things which they sometimes say against the devil about conversion, because by these they draw men to unbelief. The hand of the enemy is the strength of Satan. The mighty are the evil spirits.
25_marg812: Teach me: this is either joined to what goes before, or said by itself as a rebuke.
25_marg813: Did I say: Bring? Against the rich of the world, the poor man of God; against the powerful, the oppressed; against the wise, the fool, answered three things: because the poor man does not seek their substance, nor the oppressed help against the mighty, that is, the evil spirits, nor the fool the teaching of fleshly wisdom. For the good, with mind fixed on high, despise all these things as though far below; whence also, humble within, they contradict the powerful of the world freely, where love sharpens their words; they are neither free from pride nor submissive from fear, but uprightness makes them free, and their weakness humble; and what they despise in themselves they despise in others also.
25_marg814: Why have you detracted, etc. He who corrects others ought to be clean; for how does an eye weighed down by dust see a spot in another? Or how does a hand that holds mud wipe away filth? Hence it is said figuratively to David: “Thou shalt not build me a temple, because thou art a man of blood”; because he who is given to fleshly acts must needs blush to instruct the minds of others spiritually. So he said: “Why have you detracted,” that is, with what rashness do you blame things heard, you who, not knowing the causes of my striking, bring forward blameworthy things to rebuke me? Two kinds of speech are harmful: that which praises perverse things, and that which even reviles right things; in the one is favour, in the other anger; for this he reproves Job’s friends. One arrives at this vice from idle words. Whence he adds:
25_marg815: And you utter words to the wind: to utter words to the wind is to say idle things, by which the harmful tongue is let loose, and to speak of others as is usual; afterwards it leaps forth into detraction of them too, from which come quarrels and hatreds, and peace perishes. Hence Solomon: “He that letteth out water,” that is, lets the tongue loose into a flood of talking, “is the head of quarrels”; because he who does not rein in his tongue scatters concord. Hence Ecclesiastes: “He that putteth silence on a fool appeaseth wrath.”
25_marg816: You utter words: those who slip away through harmful words fall from every state of uprightness; because the mind, like water, when hemmed in returns to the heights whence it came, and when let loose runs away through the depths. Likewise, by the restraint of silence it returns to the knowledge of itself; but by superfluous words it is scattered out of itself and laid wholly open to the enemy. Whence it is said: “As a city that lieth open and is not compassed with walls, so is a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking.” Silence is the wall of the mind, within which, however, it is sometimes pressed too tight; and when it is restrained from speech immoderately, it boils within with thoughts, and despises others who speak the more freely because the more secretly; and when it suffers some injustice, the pain boils more within, because it does not flow out through a calm tongue. Also, when it sees the evils of others, it denies them the use of medicine. Whence the prophet: “Woe is me, because I have held my peace.” So let the tongue have a door, which is now shut, now opened.
25_marg817: Upon the fatherless: see how great a weakness he weighs himself to be; and though he complains that they wish to overthrow him, yet he testifies that he is a friend, because charity, even when hurt, does not cease. The Church does the same against heretics. And the good, being strong, do not fear to suffer adversity; whence he adds: “However finish what you have begun.” Nor, being kind, do they cease to preach the truth to their very persecutors; whence he says: “give ear,” etc. For they are not well armed with the shield of patience against what is inflicted, by which they may be safe, without the sword of the word by which they may conquer. This is what the Apostle says: “Charity is patient, is kind.” If one is lacking, it is not charity: namely if one bears with those he does not love, or does not bear with those he loves.
25_interl2131: as if he said openly: though you are ungrateful for correction, yet I do not hide my inner things from you
25_marg818: See whether I lie: because the humble man does not command what he says by authority but persuades by reason; but because opponents, given the occasion of reasoning, break loose into contention, he adds:
25_marg819: Answer, I beseech you, without contention: because heretics, in their questionings, do not aim to reach the truth, but to seem victors.
25_marg820: And speaking that which is just, judge ye: because he who speaks is subject to the judgment of the hearer. Between his heart and his tongue let there be a fair judge, so that nothing goes forth hastily from the heart through the tongue, but he examines it before he speaks. And because they first judge rightly of their own words, he adds about others’ words:
25_marg821: And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue: because folly does not sound to you in me if it does not proceed from your own conscience. So the Church first destroys the falsehoods of its enemies, afterwards opens the truths, for which there is no room while false things are held for true. By the tongue is meant open speech; by the jaws, hidden pondering; because what the Church preaches outwardly it keeps by living.
25_marg822: The life of man … is a warfare: he expresses what he rightly thinks. Warfare, or temptation according to another translation, which comes to the same thing, because temptation is a warfare, that is, a fight against demons. And it is not said that life is tempted, but that it is temptation itself, because, being now corrupt, it begets troubles for itself out of itself; and though now among good things, yet out of weakness it always brings forth what virtue must kill, and it feels evils springing up within the very goods, as sloth in the leisure of contemplation, vainglory in abstinence. But by the name of warfare something more is hinted: that it is both a fight and daily tends to its end; whence the course of a soldier’s service is also expressed.
25_marg823: And his days are like the days of a hireling, who wishes the days to pass quickly so that he may come to the reward of his labour. So is every just man; and as the hireling sweats at others’ labours but prepares his own reward, so the just man is subject among worldly and evil things so that he may lay hold of heavenly things. Take care that the day does not go empty of work and the reward be lessened. He suffers hard things that he may be crowned the more; though the wage is already in his heart, yet the heat is felt the more heavily in the body, so that afterwards there may be refreshment in rest. And this is:
25_marg824: As a servant: every elect man is well called a servant so long as he is under the yoke of this corruption, before he comes into the liberty of glory.
25_marg825: As the hireling: who would grow weary from the heaviness of his work if he were not relieved by the hope of the end; but when he has seen it he thinks nothing of what he feels.
25_marg826: Empty months: empty of the things of the world, because the good do not seek them by their acts; and they endure the wearisome nights of adversity when they are already in the torment of the body. Or empty months, because now there is labour but not yet reward.
25_marg827: Wearisome nights: he counts those who heap up for themselves the adversities of the present time by exercising themselves in virtues. The Church has empty months in the weak, who do earthly things without the reward of life; wearisome nights in the strong, who bear manifold things. And it is well said not days but months, because they feel not in the actions themselves but at the end that they have acted in vain. Or by night ignorance is meant; he who returns from it to the light washes with weeping what he did emptily. So he, as a servant longs for the shade, has empty months, because the more he seeks the eternal refreshment, the more he sees how emptily he laboured for this life. And as the hireling waits for the end, he counts wearisome nights, because the more he sees the reward from the end of the work, the more he groans that he long did not know what he seeks and that he laboured in vain.
25_interl2135: when shall I come to the day
25_marg828: If I lie down to sleep, etc. According to the history, the mind of one in pain is expressed, which, driven by grief, wanders through various desires: in the night it longs for the day, in the day for the evening; because pain does not let what is present please, and, having found this heavy, it awaits something else with consoling desire; but not even so does the pain end. Whence:
25_interl2136: namely, in the day I say
25_marg829: And shall be filled with sorrows. And this is the cause of the sorrow:
25_interl2137: because he sat on the dunghill
25_marg830: Is clothed. The same more subtly in the Church. By sleep, the torpor of idleness; the evening, which suits sleep, figures the desire for idleness. By rising, the exercise of action. So the mind of man, because it would not stand when it could, now cannot stand even when it will, but is always changed by desires, so that at rest it longs for action, busy it longs for rest. Or to sleep is to lie in sins, from which the just man tries to rise; but when he has risen he feels himself lifted up by the very virtues. Hence he also seeks to be tempted by adversities, by which he may be better kept, saying: “prove me and try me.” Or the evening is the temptation to sin, and it provokes the more just man more sharply. Whence Moses too says that one is led from morning to evening, when the shadow of temptation follows the light; which yet in the elect is not night but evening, because it darkens the light but does not put it out; and it is not even feared, but awaited as something that will profit them. But however much they strive, they have no whole health here; whence he adds: “and shall be filled with sorrows even till darkness,” because he does not find security until he wholly leaves the time of temptation. And he adds the cause of the sorrow.
25_marg831: My flesh is clothed: that is, the fleshly life which I lead is either defiled by evil working, or, though restrained from that, is darkened in memory by the images of sins, which rise like dust before the eyes. The Church in some feels the rottenness of the lust of the flesh; in some, given to earthly acts, it is sprinkled with dust. Of both he adds:
25_interl2138: the outer part of the body, which, when it draws no moisture from the inner parts, withers and is drawn together
25_marg832: My skin: the skin in the Church are those who give themselves only to outward cares, whose hearts despair dries up; and so they are drawn together, not stretched out through long-suffering toward eternal life. They cling to present things; which happens because they do not attend to how fleeting this life is. But the Church does the opposite.
25_interl2139: therefore the things that flow in do not please me
25_marg833: My days … more swiftly: as the web grows thread by thread, so life grows day by day; but the more it grows the more it tends to the cutting. But the swiftness of life, which is always failing, passes even the haste of the web. And so the elect do not fix their heart on it. Whence he says:
25_marg834: And are consumed, etc. That is, I place no trust in these things; what the reprobate do, I do not.
25_marg835: That … is but wind: eternal life is solid; this life is judged neither solid nor lasting. And so: “Remember,” that is, look kindly on one passing swiftly; because the consideration of human brevity is an offering pleasing to God. And because after life passes there is no place to deserve pardon, he adds:
25_interl2144: so as to do right works
25_marg836: And … shall not return: that is, after death the mind, seeing its requital, is not called back to show good works; whence the rich man, despairing of himself, which is an increase of punishment, prays for his brethren. Behold, life passes; what follows remains.
25_marg837: Afterwards too: “Nor shall the sight of man behold me.” That is, the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of sinners, as when he looked upon Peter. He does not free after death him whom grace does not reform before. Not the sight of man, but “thy eyes”: that is, as strict judge you will see in order to strike; and I, who here, awaited for repentance, stood, will now be no more. This fits the just man, who fears everything he does and knows beforehand that, mercy removed, he would perish; and he does not stand before the eyes, because life is hardly enough if justice presses on him: “Nor are the stars,” that is, those who shine with holiness, “pure in his sight.” The guilt and punishment of the human race are briefly added:
25_marg838: As a cloud is consumed: a cloud, made thick, is raised to the heights, is driven by the wind so that it runs, is dissolved by heat so that it vanishes. So the heart of man shines forth by its talent, is driven by the breath of demons through evil desires, but at the regard of the judge fails as by the heat of the sun; and after it is handed over to the places of punishment it does not return to that to which it clung by love, which is the house of the mind. Or hell is despair, into which one dead in sins falls, and afterwards there is no way of return. The despairing man is compared to clouds, because he is darkened by gloom and made thick by many sins, but is scattered by the brightness of judgment. Such a man does not return to his house, that is, to the heart, of which it is said to the man who was healed: “Go into thy house.”
25_interl2149: because he raised himself to the heights, driven by the wind of temptations
25_interl2154: or: in the pain of heart
25_interl2155: that is, I will spur myself to compunction
25_marg839: Neither shall his place know him any more: man’s place is God, who created him to abide in him; man deserted him by sinning. But God sought the runaway through the Incarnation. But afterwards he does not know the one condemned who now acts more wickedly, saying: “I know you not.” Fearing this, the just man repents anxiously, and does not spare his mouth, but confesses his sins. The affliction of the spirit, which is the fear of foreseen judgment, opens the mouth. The reprobate also confess their sins, but not with a contrite spirit so as to weep for their evils. But this bitterness of mind makes him speak against himself and quarrel, and now attends to other things which, secure, he passed by, and he puts before himself the good things he received from God and the evils he gave back. But, repenting thus, spurning pleasures for eternal things, he still feels opposition from the corruption of the flesh.
25_interl2157: he speaks as if I must be bound fast
25_marg840: Whence he adds: “Am I a sea?” The prison is the flesh, which hinders from high things. The sea: the hearts of the fleshly. The whale: the devil, who swims through slippery thoughts. He, then, with his fleshly ones, is rightly ploughed by the prison of his punishment, so that they may not do whatever evil they wish. But I, who am already in heaven in heart, why am I pressed by the prison of the flesh? This is said not proudly but out of love of the truth. But God puts it off for our good. Kept back from true rest, he returns to the heart as to rest against the strife of the flesh. And this secret place of the heart is called a bed or couch, where, weary from outside, he turns over the hidden words of his thoughts. But there too there is strife; because while the flesh, like the wall of the house, is shaken, the bed too is disturbed; and the more he thinks, the more he sees how strict the judge is, what shame it is to be confounded before the angels and all the saints, what punishment then follows; and so he is frightened as by sleep and vision, because he imagines it somehow, but does not see the thing as it is. But literally too the devil thrusts prosperity on the covetous and adversity on the timid through dreams, so as to affect them more; and the saints too, whom he is less able to tempt awake, he tempts more heavily asleep; which God kindly permits, so that not even sleep may be empty of the reward of suffering. Hence God is said to do what the evil spirit does. He has set out how many stumbling-blocks there are on every side; now he adds counsel against them.
25_interl2158: against this, that he is delicate in the flesh
25_interl2159: the mind, in which I rest
25_interl2160: in the secret place of the heart
25_interl2161: afterwards, while I await the just judge
25_marg841: So that … rather chooseth: the soul is the intention of the mind, the bones the strength of the flesh. What is hung is lifted from the bottom. So the soul is hung up toward eternal things, so that the bones may die; because for love of eternal life it kills in itself all the strength of the outward life, so that it despairs, that is, wholly forsakes the goods of the present life, lest it put hope in them; and further it uses them lawfully, but the perfect man fails in them. And because I despair of these:
25_interl2166: namely, that I may come to eternal life
25_interl2168: I have no consolation in earthly things
25_interl2169: that I may be consoled with eternal things
25_marg842: Spare me, O Lord: that you may give eternal things, because by contempt of those these are better hoped for. While he asks to be spared he proves that he did not despair of God. That “he chose hanging” is “I have done with hope”; from the same he brought in “spare me”; that “the bones choose death” is “I shall live no longer,” this the third time.
25_marg843: My days are nothing: he who considers eternal things, returning to himself, rightly calls these days nothing, and dreads to be strictly judged. Whence he adds:
25_interl2170: by the gift of reason, the pouring in of grace
25_marg844: What is a man: God magnifies man with many a spiritual gift, and sets his heart upon him, because he judges more strictly for what he has given. But what is man? as if: even though magnified beyond himself by your gifts, yet because he is flesh, if he is judged without mercy he cannot bear it. Whence he adds further:
25_marg845: Thou visitest him early in the morning: it is early morning when man comes from the night of vices and ignorance to the light; in which he is also at once proved; for lest he glory that he has good things from himself, he is allowed to be shaken by temptation, so that the height of God and his own weakness may be seen; as Solomon after wisdom is tempted by harlots. Man suffers this in the whole of this mortality. Whence: “How long wilt thou not spare me?”
25_interl2174: how long do you allow me to be struck by temptations
25_marg846: My spittle: spittle slips from the head into the mouth, and is swallowed from the mouth into the belly. The head is God, from whom we take our beginning. The belly: the mind, which takes the food of understanding and rules all the members of actions. The spittle: the savour of inmost contemplation; in this way it passes to the mouth but not into the belly, because our understanding is now steeped in it, but the mind is not fully satisfied. It is in the taste, not in the fullness. Christ mixed this with the clay of human thought, and, man in the world, the man born blind is enlightened. But God will spare man fully when he lets him swallow the spittle, when he admits him to the perfection of his contemplation. He who wishes to deserve this confesses the evil he has done.
25_interl2175: that I may be washed from my faults
25_marg847: I have sinned: what shall I do to thee? as if: I find nothing to offer you in recompense, because all the virtue of man is weak for washing away guilt. Or “what shall I do to thee?” as if: all good things profit not you but us.
25_marg848: O keeper of men: because he has so forsaken us that we cannot keep ourselves, and if we attempt anything we are weighed down by sins. Whence:
25_marg849: Why hast thou set me opposite to thee: when man believed the serpent he became God’s enemy, and scorned to seek him. And God set him opposite himself, counting him an enemy for his pride. But this opposition of guilt is to man a weight of punishment, and he carries himself as a heavy weight while he bears so many things in the flesh, so many in the soul. So he had to be put under who proudly raised himself up; this is what is said: “a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam.” Job says this with a groan; that things are so, he does not blame justice, but seeks mercy.
25_marg850: Whence he adds: “Why dost thou not remove?” Behold the longing for the Mediator, “who taketh away the sins of the world.” Or sin will be fully taken away when man is changed into incorruption. So he longs for the Redeemer or for the resurrection; whence he joins both the punishment he deserved from his origin and the judgment he fears from his own action. Behold now it was said to sinning man: “Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return.”
25_marg851: Why hast thou set me opposite to thee: because, made lower, he is now opposed to the higher, that is, to God; and so our lower part, sensuality, has been made opposed to the higher, that is, to the spirit, so that they always fight.
25_marg852: In the morning: that is, at the coming of the judge, when all things are open. God’s seeking is to judge strictly, before whom not even the just man stands; but this is the comfort of deliverance, that the humble man says he cannot suffice. So he bewails the death which is now, and fears the judgment which threatens.
25_interl2179: he sets upon him about hypocrites
25_marg853: Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said: How long, etc. It must be known first of all that, as Eliphaz chiefly charged the most holy Job with pride, though he also touched briefly on hypocrisy, so this man means chiefly to charge him with hypocrisy. But before he does so he puts something first, from which it is weighed how burdensome Job’s words were to him, namely words of edification. As though, then, he could no longer bear him speaking well, he broke out indignantly into these words, saying: “How long wilt thou speak these things?”, as if to say: why do you speak useless things? “And the words of thy mouth like a strong wind?”
25_marg854: How long wilt thou speak these things: because words of edification are heavy to the wicked man, as though he cannot bear them; and because he does not wish to be corrected, he accuses what is well said.
25_marg855: Like a strong wind: while he attributes manifoldness to his speech, he blames the poverty of his understanding. And note that there are four kinds of speaking. Some are full both in mouth and in sense, who are to be praised; some narrow in both, who are to be pitied; some full in sense but unable to speak it out, who are to be helped; some poor in sense but torrents in tongue, who are to be despised; which this man twists into a charge against Job.
25_marg856: Doth God pervert: Job had neither denied nor been ignorant of these things; but it is the way of the wicked, lest they seem ignorant, to speak boastfully of good things known to all as though unknown. So Baldad, as though Job had grieved over the snatching away of his goods, praises the justice of God, but in the manner of false men, who praise God in prosperity, thinking these things owed to them as to just men, and say that others are scourged as for guilt; but if any adversity touches them, they blame God’s examination. So heretics, when they see the Church corrected by God, swell with perverse preaching, saying that they prosper by their merits and that she is worthily afflicted; and so they seek an opening to creep in. Reproaching also the deaths of others, as though they perished justly, they strike others.
25_marg857: Whence he adds: “Although thy children have sinned.” “If thou wilt arise early”: as if: let them be in the light, the Church in the night, which they call to rise through the knowledge of God and to wash away the past through the prayer of repentance, if clean in thought, upright in work.
25_marg858: He will presently awake unto thee, who now sleeps as to helping you, since you are straying.
25_interl2188: that is, he restores to you the security of tranquillity
25_marg859: And will make the dwelling of thy justice peaceable: that is, he will restore the tranquillity of the present life, which alone they reckon to be God’s reward.
25_marg860: That … thy former things: because they promise both that lost things will be recovered and still greater rewards of the present life, or the dwelling of justice. They call the counsel of the mind that which is made peaceable, because if they draw men to their side, they fall silent from contention. They also promise riches of understanding, saying: “Insomuch that thy former things.” But because their words are not easily believed, they bend the sayings of the fathers into an argument for their error.
25_marg861: Whence it is added: “For inquire of the former generation,” etc. They warn not to look but to search, because they do not wish to be seen what is clearly plain to all.
25_marg862: We are but of yesterday: sometimes they teach morally that present things are guessed from the past, namely from their passing, that these things are nothing. Whence he adds: “we are but of yesterday,” because if the former generation is recalled, this life is known to pass quickly like a shadow.
25_interl2189: as if: in the fathers you will learn that God does well to the good, but the hope of the hypocrite will perish
25_marg863: They shall teach: they praise the fathers with us, so that they may attack us the more from that.
25_marg864: Out of their hearts: as if: you have simplicity of spirit in your mouth, not in your heart; they the opposite. Often the wicked, not attending to themselves, tear at the good, and either bring forward good things which they learned not by seeing but by hearing, or thrust on others the evils they themselves do; and so they excuse themselves in deeds and judge in words. So Baldad, a pretender to justice, says wonderful things against hypocrites, and presumes to teach the just man about things that would suit the wicked. A fool, who, while his gardens thirst, pours water into the river.
25_marg865: For he says: “Can the rush be green?” He compares the hypocrite to a rush or sedge, which grows green with the warmth of holiness, without the fruit of work; yet not without water, because he receives graces, to prophesy, to cast out demons, etc., but green in colour; while he seeks praises outwardly, proud, he grows on high, but is empty of fruit. The rush in flower is the hypocrite in praise. The sedge is not plucked by hand, because rising with sharp edges it cuts the hand; so the hypocrite, if plucked by the hand of correction, is angered for his wounded reputation and cuts at the life of the one correcting him, so as to show himself innocent not by his own acts but by others’ crimes.
25_marg866: Before all herbs: the just too are herbs according to the flesh, because “all flesh is grass”; who wither, because their works fail with the life of the flesh. But the hypocrites’ wither before, because they soon forsake good things once they have obtained the things for which they pretended. “These are the grass upon the tops of houses, which withereth before it be plucked up.”
25_interl2194: namely, in the day of requital
25_marg867: Even so are the ways of all: see to whom he compares the rush or sedge. The hope of the hypocrite is glory and suchlike worldly things, which perish; eternal things remain.
25_interl2195: which, even if it pleases now, will yet displease
25_interl2196: when a great thing is sold for a cheap price
25_marg868: His folly shall not please him: folly is to sell a great thing for a cheap price, that is, to do laborious good things for favour. In this he now delights, but in punishment it will displease him, and then he will know that all the things that passed away were nothing.
25_marg869: Whence: “And his trust shall be like the spider’s web.” The spider’s web is woven with care and scattered by a puff of wind. So whatever the hypocrite sweats out, the breeze of favour carries away.
25_marg870: He shall lean upon his house: the house of the mind is any thing which the soul inhabits through love. So the house of the hypocrite is favour. Or the house is confidence in his holiness, which will stand before men but not before God.
25_marg871: He shall prop it up: what cannot stand by itself is propped so that it may stand. So the hypocrite, when he sees his life falling in the judgment, props it with a count of his works, saying: “Lord, have not we prophesied in thy name, and cast out devils?” But the house of praise so propped does not rise, because in all he did he never lifted his mind from the earth; and so he is not raised to the reward of requital; so he will be rejected in the judgment. But before, he is held to be such by men.
25_marg872: He seemeth to have moisture: the rush, the hypocrite, seems moist in the night, that is, appears to men steeped in the grace of holiness, but before the sun, in the day of judgment, he will wither.
25_interl2201: but the present reward will not stand, because
25_marg873: And at his rising his blossom: every plant is first brought forth from the earth, is touched by breeze and heat, nourished by rains, and at last brings forth the shoot of its seed. But the rush is born with its flower and brings forth the shoot of its seed along with itself. So the saints here grow by doing good, feel the heat, and at last at the end seek requital. But the hypocrite, as soon as he begins something good, receives the reward of praise, forgetting even what he was before; and the good things that become known before their time perish the more quickly, namely while the mind is not yet strengthened by humility; as new plants wither at a touch, a new wall falls easily which, when dried, does not yield even to the ram. Hence Moses: “Thou shalt not plough with the firstling of a bullock.” The hypocrite, even when he acts rightly, wishes to be seen by many. And so he adds about the rush:
25_interl2203: he who carries treasure on the road wishes to be robbed
25_marg874: His roots … upon a heap of stones: from the root are the thoughts. Stones, because ‘men’ is not added; and men are both good and bad. So the hypocrite, who abides among stones, multiplies his thoughts in seeking the admiration of men; for through all that he does he seeks praise with hidden thought, having openly what enemies may plunder. Like Ezechias, who, after many benefits done to him, showed all his goods to the messengers of the king of Babylon; whence he soon hears that all will be carried away to Babylon; so, while praise is sought, virtue and beauty are handed into the hands of the enemy. Whence Job says:
25_interl2205: men, whose favour he seeks and among whom he dwells. He says ‘stones’ because he cannot bear fruit among them
25_marg875: And among the stones he shall abide: because he stands where he makes solid the intention of his mind; and, even if he is full of good things, “if one swallow him up,” that is, if God takes him by death “out of his place,” that is, from the favours of this life, he will say: “I know thee not,” as is also said to the foolish virgins. And deservedly, because it is not enough for him unless he makes others like himself too; and this is what he says: “For this is the joy of his way,” etc., so that he may be punished for their guilt too. But
25_interl2208: that is, from the favours of this life
25_interl2213: because he rejoices to have harvests
25_marg876: God will not cast away the simple, whose simplicity is now called foolishness by the cunning of the double-minded.
25_interl2215: in the present or in the future
25_interl2216: that is, help, so that they may be raised again
25_marg877: Nor reach out his hand, to lift them up from the depth in which they seek glory. The evildoers are hypocrites, who do not even do good things well. Or because outwardly they show themselves pure and simple to their neighbour, within they hide their doubleness; against whom Moses says: “Thou shalt not wear a garment woven of wool and linen.”
25_marg878: Until … be filled: not that he will do so after, which is certain, but not before, which may seem doubtful to men; as if: neither before the judgment does he forsake the simple, nor does he cease to strike the wicked.
25_marg879: Thy mouth be filled with laughter: that is, the mind with the joy of eternal security; whence: “and thy lips with rejoicing.” Jubilation is when such gladness is conceived in the heart that speech cannot unfold it, yet the mouth sounds it.
25_interl2217: this is said of Job on behalf of all the good
25_marg880: They that hate thee: confusion will clothe the enemies of the just in the judgment, because then, when the judge is seen, all their evils are turned over before the eyes of the mind, and the guilt that weighs them down clothes them on every side. They come to this because here they loved only passing things.
25_interl2218: as if he said: you who will be good after repentance
25_interl2219: the world, in which they pitched their tent, will perish; what then for them?
25_marg881: Whence he adds: “And the dwelling.” That is, the building of eternal happiness, which they multiply only for it to fall on top of them, so as to defend themselves here from needs as from heat and rain; in which the mind dwells that the good traveller despises.
25_marg882: And Job answered, and said: the perverse, to whom the person speaking is displeasing, attack everything he says, whether wicked or right; but Job, to whom not the person but the fault is displeasing, seeing that Baldad had said right things, “Doth God pervert judgment?”, and had brought forward true things against hypocrites, approves what he heard. Truly I know that the humble man, set under God, receives justice; the man who sets himself beside him loses it, because he who compares himself to him, claiming for himself what is God’s, deprives himself of the good he received. And he considers too that every merit of our virtue, if strictly judged, is a fault.
25_interl2220: that is, that God does not overthrow or pervert judgment
25_marg883: He adds: “If he will contend with him,” by presuming on his own merits and claiming the glory of his virtue not for God but for himself.
25_marg884: He cannot answer him one for a thousand: that is, he cannot lift himself up against him, even about the very beginning of a good life, which is signified by one. A thousand is put for the whole, as: “the word which he commanded to a thousand generations.” The unit is multiplied into ten, ten into a thousand; so because we begin from one so as to come to a thousand, by one the beginning of a good life, by a thousand the perfection of life is understood. So he who receives the highest goods, if he is lifted up by them, shows that he does not have even the beginning. And lest the weak man contend, let the sight of God’s power frighten him.
25_marg885: He is wise in heart: do not think your hidden things lie concealed, because he is wise; once known, you will not escape, because he is strong, and he who resists him brings himself to confusion.
25_marg886: Who hath resisted him, and hath had peace? He who creates orders created things so that they agree with him, and in this is their peace; and he who tries to fight against his ordering loses peace; as the angel, lifted up by his own restlessness, and man, who is vexed by the trouble of the flesh, because they would not be subject to their maker, both lost peace.
25_marg887: Who hath removed mountains, etc. Having spoken generally of the confusion of pride, he shows by the ruin of Israel what punishment awaits the proud.
25_marg888: Who hath removed mountains: the holy preachers, from the Jews to the Gentiles; which the Jews did not know, who were overthrown in this, thinking it a joy to themselves that they lost the light when the mountains were removed.
25_marg889: He shaketh the earth out of her place, because he drew the Jews out of their borders through the Romans.
25_marg890: The pillars: the priests, princes and doctors of the Law were shaken, because they themselves were not allowed to live for themselves, since they drove out the apostles; moreover they were forsaken in the darkness of their error.
25_interl2228: that is, the brightness of the preachers
25_marg891: Who commandeth the sun: the sun shines by day, the stars by night; because the preachers both open the contemplation of the true light and instruct rightly about earthly things; “under a seal.” We shut something under a seal so that we may bring it out when the time comes; so Judea is now deprived of light, but at the end will be visited. So Elias and Enoch are now hidden, afterwards they will appear. The glory of the preachers, driven back by the Jews, is spread through all nations.
25_marg892: Whence: “Who … spreadeth out the heavens,” that is, makes the apostles, driven out by the Jews, honoured everywhere. “Alone,” who wonderfully dispensed this, even when the bitterness of the world raged in the killing of the good. “And walketh upon the waves,” that is, treads them down while he calms them by wonder at signs. Jeremias: “I have set the sand a bound for the sea,” that is, to break the glory of the world he chose the cast-off and the poor; while the sea rages before it, the Church advances.
25_marg893: And this is: “Who maketh Arcturus.” He uses the names of the philosophers so as to express those things by their usual name, as God too takes up the words of men: “It repenteth me,” and suchlike. Arcturus shines with seven stars at the axis of the sky; it always turns and never sets. This is the Church universal, which is signified by the seven churches and the seven candlesticks in the Apocalypse, having the gifts of sevenfold grace; it shines from the axis of truth; it is always troubled, but does not fail till the end of the world; rather, like Arcturus, it turns and is raised up. Whence he soon adds: “Orion,” stars which rise in winter time, and at their rising stir up storms and trouble sea and lands. These are the martyrs, whom, while heaven, that is, the Church, brought them forth, winter, that is, the frailty of the wicked, exercised in storm; and it roused not only the turbulent but the calm too to kill them. “Hyades”: they rise in the forehead of the Bull in spring, when the warmer sun lengthens the days. These are the doctors of the Church, who, after the martyrs were taken away, came to the knowledge of the world at a time when, winter held back, faith shines and burns more brightly. ‘Hyetos’ in Greek is ‘rain’ in Latin; hence the Hyades are named from the rains which they bring when they rise, from which the crops grow more richly; then a new sun shines more brightly in the minds of men. After these it remains that the Church should come to see the inner things of the homeland above. Whence he adds: “and the inner parts of the south.” The south wind is the fervour of the Holy Spirit. Its inner parts are the hidden orders of angels and the secret recesses of that homeland, which the warmth of the Spirit fills, where the souls of the saints, and afterwards the risen, are hidden like stars in hidden places, where the sun is seen at noon. These stars are the eyes of the bride; the inner parts of the south are what lies hidden within. Job, wondering at the things said outwardly, tries to tell of the inner things, all that is done outwardly or inwardly. But because this cannot be unfolded, he grasps it better by failing, saying:
25_marg894: Who doth things great: he fulfils it better who confesses that he cannot fulfil it, and he speaks more eloquently who is silent in amazement. Great in power, incomprehensible in reason, numberless in multitude. But why should we wonder at things outside us, when we do not know even what is done toward us?
25_marg895: Whence he says: “If he come to me.” He comes when he gives gifts; he goes away when man is provoked by temptations of the flesh; but his coming and going are not known, since the end of things cannot be foreseen; because sometimes one lifted up by virtues falls, and what was thought grace was anger; and one weakened rises humble, and it is grace which seems anger; and yet man, blind as he is, will render an account of his acts to God.
25_marg896: Whence he adds: “If he examine on a sudden.” He examines suddenly when he calls the unsuspecting to judgment; but no one is able to answer, because even the life of the just gives way if mercy is lacking. Or he examines when he knocks with hard things, so that man may know what he is; but he cannot answer, because, being dust, he says nothing against the divine judgments; which is shown more plainly when he adds:
25_marg897: Who can say: Why dost thou so? We ought to revere the deeds of God, because they cannot be unjust; and not to discuss them, because to seek the reason of his counsel is to be proud against it. But he who looks at himself as weak, though he does not see God’s counsel, has its reason; and the humble man appeases the anger which the proud man kindles unquenchably.
25_marg898: Whence he says: “God, whose wrath no man can resist.” Moses and Phinees and other saints often resisted the wrath of God; but God himself so raised them up to resist him that, in the things men justly suffered, their piety, which is so great before God, might prevail. But in the things defined before God no one resists, when he himself does not breathe into them to pray; so that even Moses himself did not enter the land of promise. No one resists the wrath of God, as is plain in the Jews, whom he forsakes, taking up the Gentiles; and he bends to himself those who bear up the world, that is, who bear the cares of the world, the princes of the earth, called basileis in Greek; laos is ‘people.’ Basileus, that is, the base of the people which he supports. So those who bear up the world are the powers of the nations, or the angelic virtues, by whose ministry the world is ruled. Who then opposes him to whose power even the angels bow? Or one who is bent does not see above himself; so the angels too are bent, because they do not grasp the height of God. Turning from these to himself, he humbly holds himself cheap before the power of God, saying:
25_marg899: What am I then: that is, if an angel is not able to consider him, with what mind do I dispute about his judgments, I who am pressed down by the flesh? Our words to God are works; but with these man cannot speak with God, because in them there is no confidence before the fine judgment of God.
25_marg900: Whence he adds: “I, who although I should have,” etc. “Would make supplication.” After justice he needs prayer to God, so that what is too little in itself may avail through the mercy of the judge, even if justice is full in the more perfect. “Any just thing” is said because the mind of man hardly carries out what it grasps, and what it grasps is little. And prayer, because it is shaken by many thoughts, fears to be rejected even if it is heard.
25_marg901: Whence he adds: “And if he should hear me when I call.” For since, as David says, now “they mount up to the heavens,” when they reach the heights, now “they go down to the depths” through foul temptations, they have no certainty of being heard. See how finely he judges himself and lays open his weakness. “What am I?” He does not trust in justice but flees to prayer; he who said “although I should have any just thing” says fearfully of prayer too: “if he should hear me when I call.” Job looks round so, because he sees that he cannot bear the force of the judgment.
25_marg902: Of which he says: “For he shall crush me in a whirlwind.” He who despised him when awaited in calm will be crushed in a whirlwind. “In a whirlwind,” because he fears that works will be strictly required there in the commotion of the elements, since he sees that some are condemned without works for original guilt; in whose voice he says: “and multiply my wounds without cause,” because they themselves did nothing. Whence it is said: “None is clean in his sight, not even the infant of one day.” “Without cause”: by the reckoning of human sense; but with God it is just that the tree should keep in its branches the bitterness it drew from the root. These things are said spiritually too of Job, who foresaw the scourges of God in the whirlwind, fearing, and, having foreseen, bore them. Whence he says: “and multiply my wounds without cause,” because he was struck not for guilt. Whence above: “that I should afflict him without cause.” He adds the continuance of these wounds:
25_marg903: He alloweth not: a full proving; torments tear without, temptations chasten within; whence he says he is filled with bitterness. But the equity and power of the one striking soften the force of the pain.
25_marg904: And this is: “If strength be demanded.” As if: no one dares, because he examines merits who does not search them out by another’s testimony, but, a silent observer, waits long. No one else can be a witness for me, because I cannot even be one for myself.
25_marg905: And this is: “If I would justify myself.” I am not able to be a witness to my innocence, nor do I know that I have it. And this is: “Although I should be simple.” He who knows the good he does, is he not proud in some way? Again, he who does not know the good in himself, how does he guard it? Against both it is needful to value right things, that they may be guarded, and as least things, lest we be lifted up. But there are some things that cannot easily be known; for sometimes what virtue begins, fault finishes. Hence Moses: “Thou shalt follow justly after that which is just,” so that one defends justice for love of it, not of reward. And because he cannot fully examine himself, he bears this exile of blindness with distress.
25_marg906: Whence he adds: “and I shall be weary of my life.” But there is comfort in this darkness when the just power of God is brought back to mind, which both punishes the wicked and passes beyond the just.
25_marg907: And this is: “One thing there is.” Either the innocent man is consumed, because from the consideration of inmost purity he seems to be nothing; the wicked, because, being known, he is condemned; and this word of thought I have brought forth within me. Or he consumes the innocent and the wicked, because by the merit of the first fault they are drawn alike to the destruction of the flesh. Against these losses of the human race he seeks the grace of the Redeemer, who by the single death of the flesh might destroy our double death, of flesh and soul.
25_marg908: And this is: “If he scourge, let him kill at once.” For God to laugh is to be unwilling to pity affliction; whence he says to the reprobate: “I also will laugh in your destruction.” Every desire is a punishment while it is put off; whence Solomon says: “Hope that is deferred afflicteth the soul.” This was the punishment of all the elect before the coming, at whose prayers God laughed while he put them off. Or the laughter of God is gladness, because he rejoices when he is sought more ardently by us. So he gives him joy from punishment who, through holy desires, chastens himself for love of him. He reveals that he alone bore the death of the flesh.
25_marg909: The earth is given: the earth is the flesh; the wicked one, the devil. His hand: the killers of Christ, against whose mind the devil could do nothing, so he killed the flesh through his henchmen. The judges of this earth were the priests and Pilate, whose face, that is, hearts, the wicked one covered, so that they should not know God. Because the devil with his followers is one person, Scripture often speaks of him so as to pass suddenly to his body. The persecuting people is well understood by the name of the wicked one, when he says: “and if it be not he,” that is, if that people is not wicked, who is ever to be thought wicked? Turning his eyes from the unbelief of the Jews to himself, he grieves that he goes out of the world before Christ comes.
25_marg910: And this is: “My days have been swifter than a post.” It is a runner’s task to announce what is to follow; so all the elect before the coming, announcing Christ, were runners; but because they die before, they grieve that they pass more swiftly than a runner, so as not to see present him who alone is called good. Of whom he also adds:
25_marg911: As ships: he who carries fruit enjoys the smell, but brings food for others; so the ancients were fed by the smell of the one to come, but by prophesying brought the fruit itself to us. Fruit is usually mixed with chaff so that it may be carried unharmed to land; so in the sayings of the fathers the chaff of history keeps the spiritual things. They often turn from the height of the Godhead to the Incarnation, like the eagle, which fixes its eyes on the sun, yet bends them to a carcass when it needs food; and the carcass is Christ in his death, by which we are fed. But because the people of Israel, once full of the spirit of prophecy, did not remain in the faith which it foretold, it lost prophecy; the speech turns, in compassion, to their hardness.
25_marg912: So: “If I say: I will not speak so.” Israel would not speak as before, when it denied him whom it foretold; in which its inner face is changed by the filth of unbelief, so that it is not known by God; whence it remains for it to be tormented with eternal sorrows.
25_marg913: “My days have passed more swiftly.” The first man was so made that his life could be stretched out through time, not run out; but because he sinned he suffered the running down which man always endures and yet desires while he longs to live. He groans at the losses of this running down in the voice of the human race. “They have fled away”: because man would not stand toward the light, by fleeing he lost his sight, so that he cannot see the good which is, for which he was made. “As ships carrying fruits”: the fruit of the land through the waves. Man’s land is paradise, in which he would have remained innocent, but through guilt he came to the waves of changeableness. The fruits of the land: the speech of the cleansed; the power of work; the understanding of God, which, because man would not eat it in the land of rest, he carries over the sea, and tries to keep amid so many temptations, not without wood, that is, the cross by which we are remade. Or a ship that carries fruit has a sweet smell but has no heavy weight; so man too, driven out, when he raises himself to seek again things above, perceives the smell of heavenly things by remembrance, but, not having the weight of life, is driven lightly here and there; and like the eagle, which flies on high but by the craving of the belly seeks the earth, so man, made on high, fell to earth for the taste of forbidden food, where he feeds on the flesh of pleasure. But when we treat of these things a question presses: why did God make one he foresaw would perish? Why did the good and almighty not make such a one as could not perish? Lest this thought break out into pride, he humbly checks himself, saying: “I will not speak so,” but, weak, I will be restrained from such an inquiry. In which the face of the mind is changed, because, seeing itself weak, the mind which sought high things reveres what it does not know. In which there is sorrow, because he is greatly afflicted who is blind to understanding the things that concern himself. To these common evils he fears to join his own.
25_marg914: Whence he adds: “I feared all my works,” etc. They were good indeed, but even these are to be feared by those who truly wish to please God. For two things are to be feared in good works: sloth and fraud. Lesser love of God makes sloth; love of self makes fraud, when for good deeds the silent gratitude of the human heart, or the breeze of favour, or any outward thing is desired. But blessed is he who shakes his hands from every gift: the hands of heart and of mouth. Against these, fear must be had, which strengthens us in the knowledge that he will not spare the offender; for even if he calls sinners to repentance, yet he never passes over sin without punishment: either man punishes it or God; whence even after baptism we die for original sin. But while he trembles more than is right, he is weary of living, as if he would not come to life even through labours.
25_interl2229: after fear he comes to tears of despair, so that the humility of entreaty may carry good work up to its reward; but neither life nor tears make perfectly clean while this corruption holds; whence he adds: “If I be washed,” etc.
25_marg915: Whence: “But if so also I am wicked.” He does not regret having laboured, but grieves that amid his labours he is uncertain of the reward. The just man is uncertain in such a way as to trust, and trusts in such a way as not to grow sluggish in security.
25_marg916: “In vain,” I say, because: “If I be washed.” He who crushes himself so as to be afflicted with lamentation washes himself with waters, but not of snow unless humility is present, which shines white before God, while it neither despises another nor murmurs against God. Or snow water comes from the air, while other waters spring from outside. So he who weeps for eternal things is drenched with snow water; he who is pricked in prayer for earthly things, with water of the earth. The hands are the works, “ever so clean,” as though not truly clean under this corruption.
25_marg917: Thou shalt plunge me: that is, you will show me plunged, because the nearer we come to him, the more we recognize our filth from his cleanness.
25_marg918: My garments: the garment of the soul is the body, which Solomon bids “at all times be white”; and if it is mixed with blood, that is, with fleshly desires, Isaias says it is to be burned.
25_marg919: Shall abhor, that is, will make abhorrent; as it is said of Judas: “he hath possessed a field of the reward of iniquity,” that is, caused it to be possessed. In the abhorrence of the garment there is this heavier thing, that it does not know the mind of the one who reproves it.
25_marg920: Whence he says: “For I shall not answer a man.” Among men we both hear objections and answer them and are heard; but in the judgment of God he hears us, because he sees all we do, but we do not hear him, because we do not fully understand what displeases him. He cannot be heard on equal terms, nor is there anyone who can reprove both, that is, God and me. He reproves who goes against one by the authority of reason. So he who does right now contradicts the anger of the judge not with the groan of prayer but with the confidence of authority. Job sees how perversely man did, how strictly God is angry, and that there is no human justice to contradict; and so he longs, namely, for the Mediator to come after, who would both reprove man so that he should not offend, and by suffering stand against God so that he should not strike him. And he put his hand between both, because he both gave man an example of action and showed God in himself works by which he might be appeased, which no one before him could. He also did this more wonderfully, that he corrected the hearts of offenders by meekness rather than by terror.
25_interl2230: as Isaias says: “Cease to do perversely, learn to do well … and then come, and accuse me”
25_marg921: Whence he adds: “Let him take his rod away from me”: the rod of the Law, by which he punishes; but Christ took it away and showed the ways of life by meekness. He willed to be feared as God but loved as Father.
25_marg922: Whence he adds: “I will speak, and will not fear him.” Now he has not fear but affection as toward a father. Behold, the staff, that is, the fear of the Law, when sent, does not raise the boy; but Eliseus himself, fitting himself to the boy and breathing seven times, that is, through the love of the Spirit.
25_marg923: Answer: that is, to repay with deeds worthy of him; but no one fearing like a slave has answered God’s benefits. Only he who does not fear, through the confidence of love, has rendered him worthy service. He is not pure who would do evil if it were allowed.
25_marg924: My soul is weary of my life: to one who loves, this life, which was sweet before, is wearisome; even grieving, he bears it. And this is: “My soul is weary of my life.” But when this life grows cheap for love of the heavenly, he who used to defend his faults now accuses them. And this is: “I will let go my speech,” which I used in my defence, now “against myself,” because by confessing I accuse myself; not as one who still blushes to confess, since he does not forsake evils with so great a desire; but because sometimes one who confesses openly does not groan, but speaks rejoicing of things to be mourned, he adds: “I will speak in the bitterness,” so that bitterness may punish what the tongue accuses. From repentance security is born, and more confidently he asks how he is being dealt with. And this is: “I will say to God: Do not condemn me,” because my punishment puts out your torments.
25_interl2231: that is, by the present affliction; whether for future security, or for what fault in particular, spiritually; because even if just, he still has some evils
25_marg925: Why thou judgest me so: in two ways he judges here. Either he sends a punishment which drags the unchanged to the eternal one; or by this punishment he puts out the future one. So he is troubled by the uncertainty of this judgment, and he who is in doubt about his life asks in thought. But when the virtue of his life is looked at, a comfort is answered as it were by the judge, because he does not strike to destroy one whom even in striking he keeps in innocence. So he says: “tell me why” you scourge, whether for security or for what fault in particular; because even if he is just, he still has some evils; and so he asks that God judge him to himself, so that what God punishes in him he too may punish by weeping. Therefore I seek the cause, for I know it is not unjust.

25_marg938: Whence he says: “Hast thou not milked me as milk?” etc. Man was made as clay, but, begotten, he is milked like milk from the woman, is curdled like cheese in the flesh, is clothed with flesh and skin, is made firm with bones and sinews. 25_marg939: Life and mercy: but he gave these goods in vain unless he himself keeps them.
25_marg940: Whence he adds: “and thy visitation,” etc. The same of the inner man. The inner man is clay, because the grace of the Spirit is poured into the earthly mind and waters it so that it may be raised to God. But lest it grow proud by continual use, the Spirit forsakes it for a time, and, brought back to dust, it dries up, so that it is now driven by the wind of temptation, so that man may know himself; for when man is left and shaken, he thinks more finely of the gifts of God. “Hast thou not milked me as milk?” When the mind is drawn by the Spirit of God from its old state, it is milked like milk, because it is formed in a kind of beginning. It is curdled like cheese when, growing rich in thoughts, it is pressed together, so that it no longer flows away in desires but is made solid in one love. But against these first beginnings the flesh murmurs from its old habit. “With skin and flesh,” that is, the mind is hemmed in by the siege of fleshly motions; but he who outwardly lets them loose for wars, inwardly strengthens it with the bones of virtues, so that it may be humble and strong. And God grants the uprightness of right living because he spares past offences. “Life and mercy”: life is given when kindness is breathed into evil minds; but this is not given unless mercy first washes away the evils done before. Or mercy follows the life given, to keep it, because he visits mercifully, either by pricking to love or by scourging to fear, so that the human spirit may be kept. After he has spoken of the gifts of mercy to himself, he adds generally: “I know that thou rememberest all things,” as if: why do I tremble for myself, who know that all nations are to be gathered? “Although thou conceal these things in thy heart,” because you do not yet judge with open speech. Those certain of pardon are wont to be touched by the memory of their former wickedness and to be knocked at, against their will, by unlawful thought.

25_marg941: Whence he adds: “If I have sinned,” etc. God spares for an hour when he soon washes away guilt by the gift of tears. But he does not allow us to be clean, because even unwilling we bear the memory of evil with delight, which is for scars to fester. This is “the man who,” as Moses says, “is defiled by a dream in the night,” that is, by hidden temptation, who “is commanded to go forth out of the camp,” that is, to despise himself in comparison with the continent; “in the evening he is washed with water,” that is, seeing his failing he washes himself with tears; “after sunset he returns into the camp,” when the flame of thought cools, he takes up the confidence of the fellowship of the good. But when the mind is shaken by the memory of evil, it is sometimes dragged to commit it more heavily than before, and the man becomes wicked, to whom, even if he is raised up, there will be the woe of eternal damnation. But if the just man tries to resist, yet, pressed by labour and lasting affliction, he is not allowed to lift his head; but so he will be freed. God keeps these assaults for his own, so that they may not grow proud in security, but, knocked about, may fix their hope more firmly in God’s help alone.

25_marg942: And this is: “For pride … as a lioness.” The lioness, while greedily seeking food for her cubs, falls into a pit. For it is said that in her path a narrow, deep pit is made, in which a beast is placed, so that the lioness is provoked to throw herself in, from which she cannot get out by leaping. Joined to it is another pit, in which there is a cage, so that when the lioness is pressed from above, wishing to hide herself, she enters the cage; shut in it she is no longer feared, but, fenced round with bars, she is lifted out. So the mind of man, made in freedom, while it wished to feed the desires of the flesh, fell into the pit of deception for the forbidden food, where it endured the cage, that is, the prison of corruption; but, called back to pardon by grace, it is always held tight by the prison, lest it wander through desires. So man, free, fell of his own will; but brought back under discipline he lives better shut in. So too daily, when someone presumes on his virtues, a wonderful dispensation prepares something for him in which, delighted, he falls; from which he does not get out by himself, but, his weakness known, God leads him out as one bound. For the pride by which he lifted himself up for his virtues, he is bound in humility when he has fallen. God turns away from the proud, and the compunction of highest love departs, for he does not even feel his losses; but let God return and strike through grace, because the man visited, advancing, weeps, who perished glad. “Wonderfully,” not penally, because through weeping the mind is raised to the heights and rejoices to be so afflicted, because it advances. But if we grow sluggish in holy desire, he sets before us the examples of those who watch well.

25_marg949: Whence he says: “Before I go.” Hell is called a land because captives are held there. “Before I go”: not that he who mourns goes, but that he goes who does not mourn; as if I said to a debtor: pay before I bind you. “And return no more,” because mercy no longer frees the damned.
25_marg950: Of misery and darkness: because pain torments without those whom blindness of mind darkens within. Or there no one returns to the light any more, as in this land, where, even if there is misery, it is allowed to return to the light by conversion.
25_marg951: The shadow of death: death is separation from God; the shadow, its darkness; because the fire of punishment has burning and not light, so that those who sinned in both may be punished in both.
25_marg952: No order: not that God does not order the torments according to the merits of each; because, even if hell is one, not all will feel it in one way, as now men do not feel the heat of the sun alike. But in the mind of the damned, through the shadow of blindness spoken of before, there will be great confusion, which will torment them within as the flame without. Or there will be no order, because in the punishments the proper nature of things is not kept. Whence he adds: “but everlasting horror dwelleth.” Here fear is of evil to come; when one already suffers it, fear has gone. There fear torments even in the torments themselves. Here the flame that burns gives light; there it burns and darkens. See how heavy the torment, where the torments are at odds with their own natures, as the living were at odds with the will of God. And fear remains there with the punishments because no end of punishments will be hoped for in the future. But the fire, which does not give light for comfort, sometimes gives light for punishment; because by its light they will see in punishment, that they may grieve the more, their followers, for love of whom they offended. That they will grieve at the torment of their friends is proved by the rich man, who, mindful of his brethren, asked that they might not come to the torments; he who saw Lazarus would see them in punishment.
25_marg953: Sophar: they follow one another in turn, as the very situation is against a strong athlete.
25_marg954: Shall not he that: he begins with insults. It is the way of the wicked not to agree with things rightly said, but to answer against them; to whom even few words seem many, because they are against the views of those who think nothing right except what they themselves think.

25_marg958: And I wish, etc. The perverse wish good things in words, so as to seem kind, and so that the evils of the present may be shown. Hence this man too says: “I wish that God would speak with thee,” as if he said: you now speak to yourself; you think of God carnally; you are empty of the spirit of truth; as if: I pity your ignorance rather than your punishment.
25_marg959: His lips: that is, the judgments by which, as by opened lips, he shows men his will, which lies hidden in his secret dispositions. With opened lips this teaching is done, so that he may show the secrets of wisdom. The public works of the wisdom of God are that he kindly orders those whom he made freely, breathes good things into them, perfects and keeps them, which is plain to all. His secret works are what he does on the contrary in the wicked, whom he forsakes; which few can search into, but none can find out. Yet he sees it in some way, and finds by not finding, who understands that they are incomprehensible, so that he may humbly fear and say: “Who art thou that repliest against God?” This man, skilled through the study of knowledge, ignorant through the boldness of pride, wishes for a better man what he has. The law of God is charity, through which the precepts of life are in the mind, which is called the fullness of the law. Manifold, because it spreads out to all the deeds of virtues and draws back from every evil; and he who attends to it carefully recognizes how much he sins against God daily; and if he recognizes his sins, he bears scourges patiently.
25_marg960: And this is: “And thou mightest understand that he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth.” Unjustly he charges the just man with iniquity; but this insult comes from zeal for God and is pardonable. 25_marg961: Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God: the kindness of visitation, which shows us the way, so that we may follow one not yet seen, until we come to contemplation. These cannot be comprehended, because we do not know whence, where, or in what ways the gifts of his Spirit come; whence: “and thou knowest not whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.” In the future the Almighty will be found by sight, but not perfectly, because his essence will be fully seen by no one.
25_marg962: He is higher than heaven: because by the uncircumscribed nature of his Spirit he transcends all things.
25_marg963: He is deeper than hell: because in transcending he bears up from beneath.
25_marg964: Longer than the earth: because he exceeds the measure of the creature by the lastingness of eternity. “Broader than the sea,” because he so possesses times as to narrow them under the presence of his power. Or the heavens are called the angels, hell the demons, the earth just men, the sea sinners. So neither do the angels reach his height, and he judges the cunning of the demons far more finely, and his patience surpasses the long-suffering of the just, and his presence fills the deeds of sinners everywhere. Or man is heaven by contemplation, hell by the darkness of temptations, earth while he bears fruit, sea while he is driven by changeableness. But man’s contemplation fails in God. And if he examines himself in temptations, he fears God’s finer judgments, and his requital at the end surpasses his works. And however much the mind wavers in searching out the strictness to come, it does not know it; whence: “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” Or, according to the Apostle: the breadth of God is love, which gathers in even persecutors; the length, by which, bearing long, he leads to the kingdom; the height, because he transcends even the understanding of the glorified; the depth, because he incomprehensibly carries out judgment on the damned in hell. He shows the same things now too: breadth by loving, length by bearing, height by surpassing understanding and prayers, depth by judging the unlawful motions of thoughts. But how unsearchable the height and depth are, no one knows except him who by contemplation is carried to the highest things, or who, resisting hidden motions, is troubled by temptations. Hence it is said to Job, despised: “He is higher,” etc., as if: when are you able to know his height and depth, you who neither know how to be carried to the highest things by virtue nor how to reprove yourself in temptations?
25_marg965: If he shall overturn: he overturns heaven when he destroys man’s contemplation; hell, when he lets one fearful in temptations fall into worse; the earth, when he cuts off the fruit of good work through adversity; the sea, when he confounds our wavering by the terror of judgment. Heaven and hell are pressed together at once when contemplation lifts up and temptation darkens the same mind; whence: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind.” Earth and sea at once, when sure faith in eternal things strengthens the same mind, and from some little changeableness the breeze of doubt turns it, as in him who said: “I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief.” This happens by a hidden dispensation, so that when the mind is raised it is attacked by the remnants of wickedness, so that it is either exercised by resisting or broken by being led astray.
25_marg966: Whence he rightly says: “Who shall contradict him?” or “Who can say to him: Why dost thou so?” Because no one can withstand the judgment of God, or penetrate it by searching. Why he overturns or presses together, he adds: “For he knoweth.” When the mind is lifted up by pride because things go well, God forsakes it even in its virtues, so that man may find what he is. And because God, by bearing with them, sees vices grow up, by judging he confounds good things. Iniquity is put after vanity; all things that pass are vain; if they bind us, iniquity begins. Or vanity is called the lighter guilt, iniquity the heavier. And from lighter things, use making everything light, man is led to heavier. Hence Solomon: “He that contemneth small things shall fall by little and little.” Vanity is said to be known and iniquity to be considered, as it were more carefully, because God leaves not even lesser things unpunished, and girds himself more intently to strike greater ones. Where vanity with iniquity drags one, namely to swelling, he adds: “A vain man is lifted up into pride.” The vain man is made bold by guilt; forgetting himself, he loses humility; and, serving his desires, he shakes himself free of the yoke of divine love, so as now to go freely through pleasures. By the wild ass’s colt he notes every kind of wild beast, which, let loose to the motions of nature, is not held by the reins of masters; so he who is not held by discipline runs boldly, a wanderer, through his desires in unbridled freedom.

25_marg967: But thou hast hardened thy heart: the heart is said here to be hardened not through virtue but through unfeelingness. And he says to spread the hands to God, that is, to be proud of the virtue of one’s works against the grace of the giver. But he who until now has rebuked the just man now adds as though teaching: “If thou wilt put away from thee the iniquity that is in thy hand,” etc. Iniquity in the hand is guilt in work; injustice in the tabernacle is iniquity in the mind. To lift up the face is to raise the soul to God through the efforts of prayer; this face a stain defiles if the conscience of its guilt accuses it.

25_marg1028: With my teeth: the teeth are the inner senses, which search into each thing. 25_marg1029: And carry my soul in my hands, etc. To carry the soul in the hands is to show the intention of the heart in working, which is done for the edification of the neighbour. 25_marg1032: Hear ye my speech, etc. By naming hidden truths he shows that he has figurative speeches. Whence he adds in the voice of the faithful people: “If I shall be judged.” This does not disagree with his own person either, of whom the Lord said even greater things: “that there is none like him.” He says more humbly that he is just, not more than others. What is it that he said above: “I will reprove my ways in his sight,” and below: “thou wilt consume me for the sins of my youth,” and now says: “If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just”? But, attributing iniquity to himself and his cleansing to God, he both knows himself a sinner of himself and is not ignorant that he has been made just by gift.

25_marg1065: But man when he shall be dead: man dies by the very loss of justice; he is stripped of the garment of innocence granted in paradise; he is consumed by the destruction of the flesh that follows. Where then is he who is not in his love, where true being is?

The present life is compared to the sea and the river, because now it is touched with the bitterness of adversity, now we are filled with the sweetness of prosperity.

25_marg1067: Till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake: because when the end of this world comes, the human race will awake from sleep. Or Christ is the tree which, cut down by the Passion, grows green by the Resurrection, through which the boughs, that is, the faithful, grew. 25_marg1149: My cheek: Peter is the jaw, who kills and eats. Samson holds the jawbone of an ass and kills his enemies; that is, Christ holds simple heralds in the hand of his power and kills the fleshly from their vices. The jawbone, thrown on the ground, poured out waters, because the bodies of the heralds, given over to death, show great miracles.
25_marg1150: God hath shut me up, etc. The people of the elect is shut up with the unjust man when its flesh is given over for a time to the persecutors of the old enemy. It is delivered not in spirit but into the hands of the enemies, because the less they can take it in mind, the more cruelly they burn against its flesh.
25_interl2514: the Church in time of peace fed her own with the wealth of preaching
25_interl2515: because the mind of the weaker falls when unprepared
25_marg1151: I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden broken, etc. He signifies the mind of the weak, because, while they do not know how to foresee adversity, it is the heavier to them the more unexpectedly they bear it. Or the Church suffers these things in some of her own who slip back, who after the wealth of doctrine are sometimes turned by sudden vices.
25_marg1152: He hath taken me by my neck, etc. The neck here signifies the upright bearing of freedom, which the enemy holds in time of persecution. He constrains it when the weak do not dare to preach freely the true things they think. Or he calls his neck those in the Church who, under pretext of defending uprightness, serve the vice of pride; this the enemy bends by the strictness of his persecution.
25_marg1153: And hath set me up to be his mark: a mark is set up so that it may be struck by the shooting of arrows. So the faithful people is set up as a mark for its enemy, because he always attacks it with his acts when he afflicts it with his persecutions. Whence the Apostle: “For yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto.” As if he said openly: why do you wonder at our wounds in this time, who, if we seek eternal joys, have come to this, to be struck?
25_marg1154: He hath compassed me round about with his lances: the Church is surrounded by lances from her enemy when in her members she is attacked on every side by the cunning assailant with the darts of temptations.
25_marg1155: He hath wounded my loins: when the enemy draws the faithful people to lust, he strikes it in the loins. And he is said to wound together with us, because what he suggests wickedly to us we, following, fulfil of our own will, and as it were wound ourselves together with him.
25_interl2517: this is not literally of Job; and by this note that all these things are said mystically
25_marg1156: He hath not spared, and hath poured out my bowels on the earth: he calls the bowels of the Church the minds of those who hold her mysteries in themselves; when the old enemy drags them to worldly business, he pours her bowels on the earth. “He hath not spared,” that is, he has not left off.
