So because he from whom it came forth is invisible, and it is uncertain to us in whose mind, being understood, it rests, it is rightly said: “Whence then cometh wisdom? and where is the place of understanding?”
25_interl2994: “For man shall not see me and live,” because no one sees spiritually and lives fleshly, but dies to the flesh
25_marg1556: It is hid from the eyes of all living: because so long as one lives here, God cannot be seen in the form of his nature; but through images he was seen by Moses and Jacob and others.
25_marg1557: And the fowls of the air know it not: because, set in this corruptible flesh, they too do not pierce the power of his nature by seeing, though they now fly by the merit of holy contemplation. In sacred Scripture birds are sometimes given to be understood in a bad sense, sometimes in a good. For by birds sometimes the powers of the air are designated, opposed to the efforts of the good. Whence it is said by the voice of Truth: “Because the seed which fell by the way side, the fowls came and ate it up”; because surely the malignant spirits, besieging human minds, while they thrust in harmful thoughts, tear the word of life out of the memory. And again: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests,” etc. By the name of foxes, the deceitful and fraudulent; but by the name of birds these same proud demons are designated. But on the other hand birds are usually put in a good sense; as in the Gospel the Lord, when he announced the likeness of the kingdom of heaven from a grain of mustard seed, said: “It is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of the air lodged in the branches thereof.” For Christ is the grain of mustard seed, who, planted in the burial of death, rose up a great tree. For he was a grain when he died, a tree when he rose again: a grain through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of majesty. The branches of this tree are the holy preachers, of whom: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth,” etc. In these branches the birds rest, because holy souls lift themselves from earthly thought on certain wings of virtues, and in their sayings and consolations breathe again from the weariness of this life.
25_interl2996: that is, the finders of death and destruction, namely the malignant spirits, have said: “With our ears we have heard”
25_marg1558: Destruction and death have said: With our ears we have heard the fame thereof: because to see God is the same as to have him; so the wicked do not see this wisdom, because, driven back through pride, they could by no means have it. And to have heard its fame is to have known its power from its might.
25_interl2998: the way is through the passage of the humanity, the place through the seat of the Godhead; or its way is that it comes to the heart of man, the place the heart in which it abides
25_marg1559: God understandeth the way of it: as if he said: it is known to God either when Wisdom comes to men through the flesh, or how it remains invisible with the Father even when it has appeared outside. For the place, not a local one, of Wisdom is the Father, according to that saying: “I am in the Father.” Or God understands its way, because to discern it belongs to the divine sight alone. Or by what means the understanding of wisdom comes to the heart of man. Or whose mind does not lose the understanding of life it has received. But because this Wisdom, made manifest through the flesh, was to fill the hearts of the elect in all parts of the world:
25_marg1560: There follows: “For he beholdeth the ends of the world.” For God to look on is to re-form to grace what was lost.
25_marg1561: Who made a weight for the winds: in Scripture souls are usually signified by the swiftness and height of the winds; which, when grace from above fills them, it makes heavy with ripeness put in or usual, so that they do not leap away from attention to God with light movement. Or to make a weight for the winds is to temper the glory from virtues granted to the elect here with weakness mixed in.
25_interl3000: unless this be a guard, from his own weakness
25_marg1562: And weighed the waters by measure: he calls waters the minds filled with the Holy Spirit, which he weighs by measure, because the saints, who are caught up to the highest things by the Spirit lifting them, are held down by certain temptations lest they grow proud with any haughtiness. He lifts them indeed, but with measure: they do not advance as much as they wish, lest they be lifted up. Elias did wonderful things, but fled from a woman, struck with fear.
25_interl3001: because the Spirit and Word of the Father, which if it can be known, he told man what he can take from it
25_marg1563: When he gave a law for the rain: the rain is the sayings of the preachers, which persuade gently. A law is set for the preacher, that by living he may fulfil what he persuades. He calls the sounding storms terrible words about the judgment to come. And he set a way for the storms when he made an entrance for his preachers to hearts struck with terror of the judgment. But the law is set first so that afterwards the way may be opened, because that voice pierces the hearer’s heart which keeps in work what it has sounded.
25_marg1564: Then he saw it, and declared: he saw this Wisdom made flesh, that is, made it be seen and declared by the preachers, and made it be prepared and searched by the hearers. For whoever has taken care, by living well, to have it favourable on the day of judgment prepares it for himself.
25_marg1565: He saw it, and declared, and prepared, and searched it: he saw, because it is form; declared, because it is the Word; prepared, because it is the remedy; searched, because it is hidden. It must be noted that these four aforesaid fit God the Son of God himself.
25_interl3002: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”
25_marg1566: And he said to man: Behold the fear, etc. Because we cannot pierce the nature of wisdom, what it is in itself, by God’s condescension we have heard what it becomes in us. For it is certain that he has it of whom it is not uncertain that he fears God.
25_marg1567: Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: as if he said: if you fear God, it is plain that you are full of wisdom, which among men is called the fear of the Lord. But because he truly understands the force of divine fear who guards himself from all wicked works, he adds: “and to depart from evil, is understanding.”
25_interl3003: he hints that he speaks mysteries in figures
25_marg1568: Job also added, taking up his parable: in this last speech he designates the last time of the Church, when she is forced to bear being mocked by her adversaries, that is, the fleshly and the heretics or the gentiles, whom she now strives to hold down by the authority of wisdom, lifted up with unbridled boasting. And blessed Job, holding the figure of the Church, which will then be in straits and yet will remember our quiet, both tells her past things and announces to others the things to come. For the Church will be pressed by such evils that she will long with a sigh for these wretched times of ours.
25_interl3004: the Church will be pressed by such evils that she will long with a sigh for these wretched times of ours
25_marg1569: Whence he says: “Who will grant me, that I might be according to?” A set number of days is called months. And by the name of months he signifies gatherings of souls. So the Church remembers how great gains she brought back from the souls gathered by her preaching.
25_marg1570: Fittingly the last speech treats of the last times, when the error which is now hidden will be open.
25_marg1571: The months past: days, while they are gathered into months, are taken away, because the Church, while she gathers shining souls, hides them in inner places. Or the month is put for the perfection which will be theirs in rest, for whom it is now in working; which the Church now remembers.
25_interl3005: he recounts what she was like in those months; now the weak are kept in the bosom of peace, but then they will fall
25_marg1572: According to the days in which God kept me: because then, in those who fail through persecution, she will reckon that same keeping which she now sees in these.
25_marg1573: When his lamp shined over, etc. The light of sacred Scripture is called a lamp. So now the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because the sacred words light up the darkness of our mind.
25_marg1574: And I walked by his light in darkness: the Church, even if she does not pierce the hidden things of another’s thought, because she does not, as it were, know the face of God in the night, yet sets the steps of good work guided by the light of the speech from above.
25_interl3006: in these words the pretence of religion too is not undeservedly lamented, because some even now do not desire to be Christians but to seem so; to whom, namely, God is in public, not in secret
25_marg1575: As in the days of my youth: the Church was grown up when, filled with the Spirit, she was fruitful in conceiving sons through the ministry of preaching. The little Church had no breasts, since before she advanced she cherished none by preaching; grown up, when joined to the Word of God, she begets sons by preaching; but then she will be barren with old age.
25_interl3007: that I might advance secretly within
25_interl3008: and I kept it outside too
25_marg1576: When God was secretly in my tabernacle: he calls the dwelling of the mind a tabernacle. Whoever thinks silently on God’s commandments, God is secretly in his tabernacle. For to show how much he advanced within, he declared that God had been secretly in his tabernacle; and to show also how much he kept the works of uprightness outwardly, he adds: “When the Almighty was with me.”
25_marg1577: There follows: “and my servants round about me.” Those are called servants who serve the heavenly commandments, who are now round about her, because they are found in almost all nations.
25_marg1578: When I washed my feet with butter: the feet of the Church are the ministers of lower works, who, while they carry on outward things for necessary uses, cling to the earth like feet by their lowest ministry. But those who preside ought to minister to such men the pouring of fatness by the voice of frequent admonition, which Job did for his own. For feet are usually torn by the roughness of the road. The feet of God are the preachers, who are not without fault but are washed with butter, because by the fatness of good work the dust gathered, or the glory of preaching, is poured over and cleansed. Or the feet, as it were weary, are anointed with butter when the preachers are cherished by the good works of those who minister to them, that is, by the fruit rather than the gift; so it is from the voice of the head. From the voice of the body, the feet are those who minister outward things.
25_interl3009: Christ, at whose teaching rivers flowed everywhere
25_marg1579: And the rock poured me out rivers of oil: because in her the preachings of Christ of inward anointing flow out. From this rock the rivers of oil came forth, the books of the evangelists. Or he calls the gifts of the Spirit rivers of oil.
25_marg1580: When I went out to the gate of the city: by the gate of the city every good action is designated, by which the soul enters the assembly of the heavenly kingdom. So now the Church goes out to the gate of the city, because, to obtain entrance to the heavenly kingdom, she puts herself forth in holy actions. It was the custom of the ancients that the elders should sit in the gate and judge the cases of those coming in, so that the people of the city might be peaceable, into which the quarrelsome might not enter; which Job too did.
25_marg1581: And in the street they prepared me a chair: because in the breadth of great authority she shows the freedom of her teaching. For she who preaches with public voice the right things she perceives sits as it were in the street on a chair, when she fears nothing over her preaching and, pressed by no one’s errors, hides herself under silence.
25_interl3013: because they fear to be caught in their hidden things
25_marg1582: The young men saw me, and hid themselves: he says young men because they are supported by no weight of counsel; old men, those ripe with the long age of character. And the sense is: the unripe dread the vigour and uprightness of the Church; those of long age glorify it.
25_interl3014: the light flee; the perfect, by rising up, revere the merits of life
25_marg1583: The princes ceased to speak: he calls princes or rulers the authors of heretical wickedness. And the sense is: when I was allowed to preach with public voice, everyone who was not subject to the truth dreaded me.
25_marg1584: The finger: they lay it on the mouth when they show, by false complaints, that they are held back not by the reason of speech but by the hand of power.
25_interl3015: who draw the erring after them
25_interl3016: because even if they do not dare to speak perverse things freely, yet they hide them within themselves
25_marg1585: The rulers held their peace: surely those who try to draw erring peoples after them are now curbed, so as not to dare to speak perverse things, both by the weight of authority and by the force of reason. Their tongue cleaves to their throat, because even if they do not dare to speak perverse words aloud, yet within themselves they hide all the false things they plan to put forward against the true faith.
25_marg1586: And their tongue cleaved to their throat: against this Jeremias says of the last times: “The lamias have drawn out the breast,” that is, the heretics, who have a human face but through ungodliness beastly hearts. Then they will preach their error freely. For at that time, when holy Church is pressed by adversity, freedom of speech is given to all the wicked preachers. Then they suckle their whelps, because, as wicked followers, while they slip perverse things into the souls of little ones, they strengthen them by nourishing them toward ungodliness.
25_interl3017: he says that he was held in reverence by those who heard and saw, against the rebukes of his friends
25_marg1587: The ear that heard blessed: there he said what he showed by teaching, here what by mercy; there he brings forth and fills with words, here he defends from evils.
25_marg1588: The ear that heard me blessed me: what he was like in speech, what in work, is shown. He blesses the words of the Church who completes in work what he has heard. He bears witness to her who answers the examples of her life by living well.
25_marg1589: Because I had delivered the poor man that cried out: the Church delivers the poor man crying out when she looses the faults he has committed for the sinner who begs pardon.
25_marg1590: And the fatherless that had no helper: she delivers the fatherless when each one, the old father the devil being dead to him, runs to the bosom of holy Church and finds in her the help of exhortation.
25_marg1591: And the fatherless that had no helper: these are the works of great mercy: to deliver the poor, to snatch away the fatherless about to perish, to console the widow. These the Church shows both bodily and spiritually.
25_interl3019: see how gentle is he who above was stern, when he said: “The young men saw me, and hid themselves,” etc. Rulers must hold both: namely, that the vigour of discipline should rule gentleness, and gentleness adorn vigour; and so each be commended by the other, so that vigour be not stiff nor gentleness slack
25_marg1592: The blessing of him that was ready to perish: the blessing of him that was ready to perish comes upon her when she forestalls the destruction of the sinner and leads him back from the pit of fault by holy exhortations.
25_interl3021: not of the young man or young men
25_marg1593: And I comforted the heart of the widow: the heart of the widow receives great comfort when the faithful soul learns in the words of the Church something about the coming of him to whom she is spiritually joined.
25_marg1594: I was clad with justice: he is clad with justice as with a garment who protects himself on every side with good work and leaves no part of his action naked. For that Pharisee who went up to the temple to pray opened the city of his heart to the enemies lying in wait through haughtiness, which he had closed in vain by fasting and alms. The other places are fortified to no purpose when one place, by which an entrance lies open to the enemy, is not fortified. Eleazar, killing the elephant, fell beneath it; so he who overcomes vices, if he is proud, falls beneath them. He dies under the enemy he killed who is lifted up over the fault he overcomes.
25_interl3023: on every side, so that there is nowhere an entrance for the enemy; otherwise it avails nothing
25_interl3024: because the judgments of the just, through the glory of great work, lead to the crown of reward
25_interl3025: the good man always judges within himself what he owes to God, what to his neighbour, and cleanses himself of vices
25_marg1595: And a diadem … with my judgment: the judgment of the just is called a diadem, because by it they long to be rewarded not in earthly and lowest things, but above.
25_marg1596: With my judgment: I was clothed with judgment, which is compared to a crown, which is placed on top, because he seeks to be crowned in heaven, not on earth. He opens his good things so that his friends may be raised up, not rebuking, but may imitate them in silence. The memory of former things also avails against despair, in place of rebukes.
25_marg1597: I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame, etc. For blessed Job had both given his hand to the one himself, and upheld the other by carrying him himself, because he knows that the mind is weighed by God more than the deed. The Church is an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. For she enlightens the blind by preaching, and upholds the lame by helping. For he is blind who does not yet see where he should go; and he is lame who cannot go where he sees. Or the gentile people is called blind, and the Jewish people lame; because the one did not have eyes, that is, the law, because, not having received the law, it did not see where it ought to have gone; the other, on the contrary, held the law indeed by knowing it, but did not stretch out in it the step of right work.
25_marg1598: I was an eye to the blind: after justice, mercy; because he does well the things that are merciful who first keeps the just things, so that mercy may be drawn from the fountain of justice. For how is he merciful to another who is unmerciful to himself and does not yet love himself? To whom is he good who is wicked to himself?
25_interl3028: what he bestowed he gave from affection, not from fear of judgment
25_interl3029: because the force of mercy had imitated nature in him, so that he looked on them as sons through love, over whom he presided as father through protection
25_marg1599: I was the father of the poor: for the poor in spirit are begotten by her preaching.
25_marg1600: And the cause which I knew not: the Church, when through the elect she judges the evils of the fleshly, searches out what she does not know, because she searches out by working the evils she does not know, correcting them through judgment.
25_marg1601: The cause which I knew not: just in his own actions, merciful in the weakness of his neighbours, he is also energetic in the business of the poor, so that he who seeks eternal things may stretch out to all merits. Whence Solomon: “He that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Yet lesser things are to be left for greater.
25_interl3031: whence let no one be hasty in sentence
25_marg1602: I broke the jaws of the wicked man: the wicked man is the devil. By the jaws his hidden snares; by the teeth the committing of open fault is shown. So it is first necessary to bring to light the hidden contrivances of his counsels, so that we may be able to call back our hearer’s soul from open falling.
25_interl3033: the soul which he had already bitten by breaking it with sin, by turning it to the salvation of life
25_marg1603: And I said: I shall die in my nest: by the name of nest the calm rest of faith is expressed, by which each weak one is nourished. So the voice of those who will then be is anticipated by the voice of blessed Job, who believed that in the time of peace they would pass to the things above, that is, fly from the nest.
25_interl3035: that is, growing little by little; or at last there will be prosperity and strength
25_marg1604: And as a palm tree: it advances slowly but stays long in its greenness; and at the bottom it is slenderer, at the top it thickens near the fruit (unlike other trees); and below it is rough, above it is fair to touch and sight. So she believed she would multiply her days like a palm, who promised herself the leisure of peace for a length of many days, and thought that the minds of the faithful would rise stronger right to the end; which is now not so. The Church believed she would multiply her days like a palm, who, a danger suddenly arising, grieves that the grace of her peace, both slowly won by the faithful, has been cut off more swiftly by the unfaithful. The Church is like a palm, despised below and girded with rough things, fair above; and whereas others are strong in earthly things and weak in heavenly, for which they will do or suffer little, she is weak toward the earth, strong above; nor does she, like some, do more at the beginning and less at the completion.
25_interl3037: because with spiritual mind she always attends to knowledge
25_marg1605: Root: of the Church, Christ made flesh, who, invisible in Godhead, was opened through the flesh and known to the peoples.
25_marg1606: My root: by the name of root hidden thought is designated. The root is opened beside the waters when the thought of the mind is hiddenly opened to receive the streams of truth.
25_marg1607: And dew shall continue in my harvest, etc. Understand: “I said.” The harvest of the Church is taken to be when perfect souls, drawn away from their bodies, pass like ripe crops cut from the earth to the heavenly barns. Dew will continue in the harvest, because grace coming from above makes us worthy to be gathered from lower things.
25_marg1608: My glory shall always be renewed: she bewails as it were lost glory, because she knows that those whom she believed were serving as soldiers of a new life are serving old desires.
25_marg1609: And my bow in my hand shall be repaired, etc. Scripture is the bow, from which terrifying sentences come to the hearts of men like striking arrows. The bow is repaired in the hand when whatever is known of the sacred word is fulfilled by living; which at the end will fail in many, and which is so even now.
25_interl3042: these things are true of Job, but in the figure of the Church
25_interl3043: not like these erring men who now run ahead as if teaching
25_marg1610: They that heard me, waited: she remembers past times, in which everything said by her was heard by the faithful with fear; and she bewails the impudence of her adversaries.
25_marg1611: And being attentive held their peace: they hold their peace at her counsel who do not dare to attack her words, but believe them.
25_interl3044: see the reverence of the hearers
25_marg1612: To my words they durst add nothing: the heretics presume to add something to her sayings when they try as it were to amend the uprightness of her preaching.
25_interl3045: see the dispensing of the teachers
25_marg1613: And my speech dropped upon them, etc. In this dropping of speech is taken the measure of preaching according to the capacity of the hearers.
25_marg1614: They waited for me as for rain: we wait for the words of holy preaching as for rain when with true humility we acknowledge the dryness of our heart, so as to be watered by the drink of holy preaching.
25_interl3046: Christ himself is late, at the end of the world
25_interl3047: Christ at the end of the world gave himself for us as an evening sacrifice
25_interl3048: whence: “I will give you the early and the latter rain”
25_marg1615: And they opened their mouth as for a shower: because while we receive the words of holy preaching in the last part of the age, we open the mouth of the heart as for a latter shower.
25_marg1616: If at any time I laughed on them, they believed not: the Church says this from the voice of the head. For God to laugh is to prosper the way of the saints by following favour; but we do not believe our Redeemer when he laughs, when we receive the grace of his favour, many gifts of his already bearing witness, and yet still waver under his judgment over our weakness. Job showed himself such to those under him that even laughing he could be feared; so a prelate ought to be feared when laughing and loved when angry, lest too much freedom make him cheap or immoderate severity make him hateful.
25_interl3049: the eyes of the wise man are in his head, that is, Christ, whose works he sees are to be imitated; but “the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth”
25_marg1617: And the light of my countenance fell not: the light of blessed Job’s countenance does not fall on the earth, because he did not look on earthly things with desire. The light of the Lord’s countenance too does not fall on the earth, because the brightness of his vision does not appear to sinners. The Church too does not preach bright mysteries to earthly men.
25_interl3050: because the good care first for eternal things, then for earthly; in them the Lord sits first, in others last
25_marg1618: If I had a mind to go to: the Lord both comes when he wills and, when he comes, sits first; because both his coming into our heart is free, and the longing of desire for him in our thought is not equal to other desires.
25_marg1619: And when I sat as a king: the Lord sits as a king in the heart, because he rules in thought the motions of minds that clamour round, which stand round him like an army. Or he sits as a king with his army standing about, because a crowd of virtues stood round him presiding over the minds of the elect. He is also the comforter of mourners, by the promise in which he says: “I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.” If we refer it to the Church, in her the order of teachers presides as a king, which the crowd of the faithful stands round; which comforts the hearts of mourners, while it gladdens minds afflicted by the hardship of the present pilgrimage with the promise of the eternal homeland. To sit is the rod of rule; to console, the ministry of devotion.
25_marg1620: A comforter of them that mourned, etc. He who has heard of God’s justice so as to fear, let him hear of his mercy too so as to trust, so that there may be fear and hope together.
25_marg1621: In the ark with the tables there are both the rod and the manna; that is, with knowledge of sacred Scripture, in the breast of the ruler there is the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness.
25_interl3051: from here on he shows, in the last time, things contrary to those said before; because they began from the Church, not the Church from them
25_marg1622: But now the younger in time scorn me: those younger in time mock the Church when those who have gone out from her despise the words of her teaching.
25_interl3052: even if they seemed to have some right things, yet because they did not think rightly about the Lord, she does not set them with the dogs of her flock, that is, does not count them among the right preachers
25_marg1623: Whose fathers I would not have set, etc. The flock of the Church, then, is the multitude of the faithful. The dogs of the flock are the holy teachers, who have stood forth as teachers of the faithful. So the Church disdains to set the fathers of the heretics with the dogs of her flock, because, judging between them, she spits out the inventors of errors and scorns to number them among the true fathers.
25_interl3053: because without charity, without the look of holiness
25_marg1624: The strength of whose hands was to me as nothing: the strength of the hands is greatness in working; but the strength of the hands of heretics is said to be as nothing to holy Church, because she sees that whatever they do, true faith being lost, is of no merit.
25_marg1625: The strength of whose hands: the more they err, the more they show themselves great in works; and sometimes they do miracles, yet are not holy for that. For the proof of holiness is not to do signs, but to love each one as oneself, and to think true things of God and better things of one’s neighbour than of oneself.
25_interl3054: that is, of the miracles they do, because they are not humble; or of the Christian name, which they attack
25_marg1626: Barren with want and hunger: for by immoderate daring, the more they long for knowledge of the knowledge from above, the more they lose it.
25_marg1627: And hunger: because they long to know whence to be learned and talkative, not to be ordered in character; whence they scarcely grasp outward things, who think they have pierced secret ones.
25_marg1628: And this is: “who gnawed in the wilderness,” etc. The heretics, who are separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, are said to gnaw in the wilderness. That is gnawed which cannot be eaten; because those who strive to understand Scripture by their own power, not helped by grace from above, cannot eat it, but gnaw it as with certain bites, while they do not reach its inner parts. Or the covetous gnaw with the tooth, taking others’ things by force; but those lick who take them by the flattery of the tongue.
25_marg1629: Disfigured with calamity and misery: they are said to be squalid with calamity and misery, because they are despised both for the ruin of their character and for the perversity of their senses.
25_marg1630: Disfigured with calamity and misery: calamity is as it were sickness; misery is the neglect of it, by which it becomes heavier. No one would be squalid if he did not add the misery of pleasure to his necessities.
25_marg1631: And they ate grass, etc. To eat grass is to understand the plainer sayings of Scripture or to keep the least precepts. But they eat the bark of trees who in the sacred volumes revere only the surface of the letter. Or surely to eat grass is to imitate certain light and tender things of the ancient fathers; but to eat the bark of trees is to do their works on the surface, but not to keep a right intention in those same works.
25_marg1632: For what is designated by grass but the tender life, close to the earth, of those who begin well? And what by the bark of trees but the outward works of those who already long for lofty things? So to eat grass and the bark of trees is to scatter, by pestilent persuasions as by certain teeth of their malice, either the efforts of those who begin well or the workings of some who already, like trees, stretch toward higher things. The reprobate eat grass when they consume the beginnings of the weak by mocking them. They eat the bark of trees too when by the hand of perverse counsel they strip the covering of good works from the life of those growing rightly. These in certain acts they strip like trees, but those like grass, because, despising them, they drag them along and as it were eat what they tread on. The strength of some, already rising on high, they partly pull down; but the tenderness of others, still placed below, they utterly crush. Or grass is earthly consolation, bark the outward glory which God sometimes gives to his elect, when he lifts them up with outward honours and makes them honourable above others. But the wicked sometimes despise their life indeed, but long to obtain their happiness in this world. So because they seek here the flatteries of passing consolation, they eat grass. And because in their thoughts they meditate on their outward glory, they eat the bark of trees. And since in all these things they serve avarice alone, they are filled with the root of the juniper.
25_interl3055: because in errors they seek earthly gains
25_interl3056: avarice lies hidden in the heart, but brings forth openly in work the prickings of all sins
25_marg1633: And this is: “and the root of junipers was,” etc. Junipers have as it were thorns instead of leaves. And a thorn is every sin, because while it draws to delight it tears the mind as by pricking. So by the root of the juniper avarice is designated, which is “the root of all evils,” as it were of thorns; which is the food of the heretics, because mostly they pursue only outward gains in their words.
25_interl3057: all the present life, compared with the things above, is at the bottom; in which, when they find even a little gain, they run with a cry, quarrelling over it and breaking the look of holiness laid over them
25_marg1634: Who snatched up these things out of the valleys: they snatch them out of the valleys because with a proud spirit they gather these things from the humble sayings of the fathers. And while they boast that they have found them for their own fathers, they run to them with cries, because everything they perceive they try, from longing for praise, to spread abroad to the ears of men.
25_marg1635: All these things are about the heretics, or about other fleshly men who press on her within.
25_marg1636: They dwelt in the desert places of torrents: he calls the inventors of perverse doctrines torrents, which, cold from the heat of charity, swell as in the numbness of winter time, but are dried up by the arguments of Catholics as by the heats of the sun. So those who follow their errors dwell in the desert places of torrents. The inventors indeed have been put out by the truth, but their disciples still defend what they taught. Or the torrents are the holy heralds, whose desert places are the earthly things the wicked love.
25_marg1637: And in caves of earth: for heretics meet in secret little gatherings, so as to give their error by hiding the reverence they cannot give it by reason; whence stolen waters are sweeter. Or caves are evil thoughts where hypocrites lie hidden. The gravel is the present life, which is always being driven along; the foot of one who clings to it is set on the surface of the gravel, but slips to the bottom; so he who, for love of the world, does even lawful things goes down even to evil ones.
25_marg1638: Or upon the gravel: we call gravel the tiniest stones, which river water drags along. The heretics dwell upon the gravel, because they drag along those minds of men which are made firm by no weight of stability.
25_interl3061: over which they ought to weep
25_marg1639: They pleased themselves among these kind of things: by the name of briers he signifies the prickings of sins. Perverse minds rejoice in the iniquities they ought to weep over. Whence Solomon: “Who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things”; because surely they attend to the passing things they receive and neglect to look on the abiding goods they lose.
25_interl3063: because they boast with gladness of that by which, in ruining others, they carry thorns, as if leaders to justice; or the wicked delight in things by which yet they are pricked with adversities, which they had learned from fools; or there is no one who does not disagree with the condition of his fortune
25_marg1640: Whence it is openly added: “and counted it delightful to be under the briers.” They rejoice in temporal things indeed, but yet, since they cannot manage them without tribulation, the wretches are pricked by the care by which they are pressed. And this is what Jeremias says: “He hath inebriated me with wormwood”; because the human race, even if it receives many bitter things, yet like a drunkard does not understand what it suffers, but rejoices as if in good things, gaping so after earthly things. Whence Osee: “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love to tread out the corn”; because even when she could freely be free from the labours of the world, yet from habit she returns, even uncompelled, to the same habit of labour, so that, used to weariness, it does not please her to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when she may.
25_marg1641: The children of foolish and base men: the children of those who were the masters of errors; who, by teaching perverse things, are foolish through ignorance; by living wickedly, base through action; who have been made exiles from the land of the living.
25_interl3066: even if they long to be seen; or in the Church, for the vileness of their works, they do not appear to God
25_interl3067: and who before were as it were revered while they were in the Church in appearance
25_marg1642: Now I am turned into their song, etc. The time of the Church is expressed in which she is publicly mocked by the reprobate.
25_marg1643: And am become their byword: she will be made a byword by the wicked, because when they see the good die by torments they take from them a likeness for cursing, saying: “Pardon to you as to that butchered one.”
25_marg1644: They abhor me, and: the wicked flee far from the Church, not by steps of the feet but by qualities of character. And to spit in her face is to confound the just even in their presence, and to send loose words against them in insult like dribbling spittle. But because holy Church knows to attribute her good things to the mercy of the Redeemer, she knows to attribute her evils to the justice of the judge.
25_marg1645: There follows: “For he hath opened his quiver,” etc. By the quiver the hidden judgment of God is designated. So when the Lord sees sins and yet does not move his hand to vengeance, he holds as it were a closed quiver; but by striking he shows how much he was displeased by what he long saw and bore with in us.
25_marg1646: The quiver is the hidden counsel from which he sends forth the arrow, that is, the open sentence. We see that man is scourged, but not for what cause; but in the chastening the force of the counsel is opened.
25_interl3069: but we grieve the more at what we suffer from those in whom we trusted
25_marg1647: And hath put a bridle into my mouth: for the holy teachers, when they see the hearts of those who resist forsaken by God, fall silent, afflicted and groaning, lest they speak to the unworthy, who would become worse as well.
25_marg1648: She spares the wicked by keeping silent, yet urges her life on them by patience.
25_marg1649: At the right hand of my rising, my calamities: our Redeemer is called the rising (the East). For because light rises from the east, he is rightly called the rising by whose light of justice the night of our injustice is lit up. So at the right hand of the rising calamities arise, because those too leap forth to persecution who were believed to be elect, to be at the right hand. And he rightly asserts that they arise forthwith, because, since those who persecute were not strangers, evils come from them suddenly and forthwith. But if the faithful are truly called the right hand, calamities arise at the right hand of the rising, because when persecution breaks out the just suffer the onslaughts of the wicked.
25_marg1650: They have overthrown my feet: by the feet of the Church her lowest members are signified, which, while they serve earthly works, can be deceived the more quickly the less they understand lofty things.
25_marg1651: And have overwhelmed me with their paths as with waves: the path of the adversaries is compared to waves, because the life of the wicked, troublesome with insolent restlessness, falls like a tempest to sink, so to speak, the ship of the heart.
25_marg1652: They have destroyed my ways: let blessed Job say this of the malignant spirits; let the Church say it of the persecutors, who destroy her ways when they trouble the way of truth in the minds of some weak ones by foul persuasion.
25_marg1653: They have lain in wait against me, and they have prevailed: those lying in wait prevail when they pervert, by pretending good things, those whom they cannot openly drag into evil.
25_interl3070: as if God had forsaken for a time in order to test
25_marg1654: And there was none to help: mostly the just, caught in tribulation, reckon that the hand of the helper is slow, when the savagery of the persecutors straitens them a little longer; and the remedies of the deliverer are swift indeed, but seem slow to pain.
25_interl3071: or the wall is the fortification of discipline
25_marg1655: As when a wall is broken: the Redeemer is a wall to us, who forbids the course of the malignant spirits to reach our hearts; but the wall is as it were broken when by the persuasions of the wicked the faith which is in our Redeemer is scattered in the hearts of some; whatever happens, because power is given by God to the enemies.
25_marg1656: And a gate opened, they have rushed in upon me: when power is given to the perverse in this life, what else is opened but the gate of error? As if a wall were broken and a gate opened, the wicked rush in upon the good when the perverse, having received temporal power, try also to destroy the defences of faith in the hearts of some.
25_marg1657: And have rolled themselves down to my miseries: the reprobate roll themselves down through their own miseries to ours too, when they drag even some united with us into the evils in which they themselves are entangled.
25_marg1658: I am brought to nothing: in the reckoning of the wicked we are brought to nothing when we do not hold the temporal goods which they love as the highest.
25_marg1659: I am brought to nothing: allegorically. To such men whatever they see of the virtues of the good is nothing; even if at times they think of eternal things, passing delight takes it away.
25_marg1660: All these things that are said allegorically are also to be taken according to the history, which is plain.
25_marg1661: As a wind thou hast taken away my desire: the faithful people declares that it suffers what it grieves that those it loves suffer. So the wind takes away desire when any passing thing destroys the longing for eternity.
25_marg1662: And my prosperity hath passed away like a cloud, etc. A cloud stands out on high, but the breath drives it on its course. So prosperity passed like a cloud, because the glory of the perverse, the higher it is, the less it is fixed. Having completed the desires and acts of the weak, he returns to the voice of the elect.
25_interl3072: in the future it will grow green again, passing beyond itself
25_marg1663: And now … within myself: now our soul fades and is weakened within ourselves, but is restored in God; and it becomes so much the farther from the greenness of joy as, still driven back from the light of its maker, it retreats into itself. Because in the time of the last persecution many will fall and few will stand, here he says few things of the good and more of the perverse. Whence he soon returns to those who fall.
25_interl3073: afterwards there will be days of gladness
25_marg1664: In the night my bone is pierced with sorrows: he speaks of his own things so that they fit the falling too; because a multitude of worms swarming through the hollows of his ulcers tore the holy man’s body. But the bone of the Church is pierced with sorrows in the night, because the saints, pressed by the darkness of tribulation, are bored through by affliction, so that even those who had the vigour of strength in her now have as it were a certain hole of fear.
25_marg1665: And they that feed upon me, because the malignant spirits, who consume the fleshly members of the Church, know so much the less how to rest from temptation as they are weighed down by no weight of flesh.
25_marg1666: With the multitude of them my garment is consumed, etc. What else is taken as Job’s garment but his body? But the garment of the Church is the souls of individuals, which surround her by believing and faithfully clinging to her. So he says: while those who torture are many, very many are destroyed who clung to her by the bond of love.
25_marg1667: As with the collar of my coat: the collar of the coat goes round the neck. But if the neck is squeezed, the use of the voice and the breath of life are killed. And the reprobate squeeze the Church at the neck, that is, in the preachers, as with the collar of a coat, because by their persecutions they try to put out in her the life of faith and the voice of preaching.
25_interl3075: if any prefer to die rather than keep silent, they are held cheap
25_marg1668: I am compared to dirt: in the judgment of the reprobate the Church of the elect is compared to dirt, because, trodden under for a time, she is despised. She is likened to embers and ashes, because they reckon that she has come only to the evils which they see shown in her bodily.
25_interl3076: therefore I wish to be changed; but because God delays, therefore I groan
25_marg1669: I cry to thee: the Church in the time of her persecution stands by faith, cries by desires, but grieves as if she were not regarded, while she sees her wishes put off in tribulations; which happens so that the merits of the sufferers may grow.
25_marg1670: Grief urges the patience of the saints into speech, and, delayed so as to advance, they fear lest they fail.
25_interl3077: striking strictly and not sparing fault
25_marg1671: Neither cruelty nor changeableness comes into God; but he added “to me,” so that the cruelty and change may be not in the quality of the judge but in the mind of the sufferer.
25_marg1672: Thou art changed to be cruel toward me: it is said of God after our manner, so that by things near to us we may sometimes climb to the highest. But nothing worthy can be said of him.
25_marg1673: And in the hardness of thy hand: the hand of God is said to be contrary to our will when by striking it pursues what displeases him in us.
25_interl3078: the lifting up of temporal and fleeting happiness happens only so that it may dash one down the worse, suddenly, into the lowest things; in Job it seemed to be so in others’ eyes, in the weak it truly is
25_marg1674: Thou hast lifted me up, and set me as it were upon the wind: because the glory of the present life is seen as on high, but is made firm by no stability; he who rejoices in passing prosperity is set, as it were lifted up, upon the wind. These words, which fit the person of Job, he adds not as to what he was but as to what he seemed to be. For he did not suffer this fall in mind, because no adversity cast down him whom no prosperity had corrupted. In the Church too the weak, who rejoice in passing successes, seem lifted up upon the wind; but in the time of persecution, when the breeze of prosperity has passed, their lifting up at once collapses.
25_marg1675: I know that thou wilt deliver me to death: for no one comes here who does not go on by the steps of his corruption toward the death of the flesh.
25_marg1676: Hell was the house of all before the coming of Christ; no one escapes the death of the flesh; and these things fit Job himself. Mystically, the weak, who, living fleshly, come to the house of death. But because some fall into pleasures who return through penance, for whom stripes are instruction, not destruction, he adds: “But yet thou stretchest not forth thy hand to their consumption.” The Lord does not stretch out his hand to the consumption of sinners when by striking he rebukes them from sins and saves those who fall, while he wounds in bodily health those falling into fault, so that, laid low outwardly, they may rise inwardly.
25_interl3080: since he adds this not of himself but of others, he shows that he signifies in himself the persons of many
25_interl3081: it is more to give of oneself than of one’s goods
25_marg1677: I wept heretofore for him that was afflicted: compassion is more than a gift, because often even one who does not have compassion gives something. But one who truly has compassion never refuses what he sees is necessary to his neighbour. The Church, when she sees the afflicted in the laments of penance, joins her weeping to them in continual prayer.
25_marg1678: In the time of the last persecution the Church brings back to memory the good things she did in the time of peace; longing for eternal joys, but, while they are put off, pressed by evils.
25_interl3083: to have them as soon as possible
25_marg1679: He adds: “I expected good things, and evils are come upon me.” The faithful people expects good things but receives evils.
25_marg1680: I waited for light, and darkness broke out: she waits for light and runs into darkness, because she hopes, by the grace of reward, to be present now at the joys of the angels, and yet, put off longer here, she bears the hands of persecutors, like Tobias.
25_interl3086: who, knowing her secrets, the better they know where she is most pained, the worse they do not rest at all from afflicting her
25_marg1681: My inner parts have boiled without any rest: for the inner parts of holy Church to boil is to bear in the cruelty of persecution even those whom she had carried before like her bowels through the love of faith.
25_marg1682: My inner parts have boiled without any rest: she would grieve less at these evils if they were done by an adversary; but they torture more heavily when done by those from whom good things were hoped; and this is her inner parts.
25_interl3087: but these I bore heavily even before
25_marg1683: The days of affliction have prevented me: for the Church of the elect knows that she will suffer many evils in the last persecution. But the days of her affliction forestall it, because even in the time of peace she bears heavily the life of the wicked among her, who already show in their wicked ways what is to come.
25_interl3088: even if lifted up, as he says above: “Thou hast lifted me up,” etc.
25_marg1684: I went mourning, etc. The holy man, lifted up with goods and honours, went mourning, because even if the glory of power showed him set over men, yet within by his mourning he offered to the Lord the sacrifice of a contrite heart. The Church too goes mourning through prosperity, because she reckons nothing truly prosperous until she grasps the good which she singularly seeks.
25_marg1685: Or: even if he abounded in so much, mourning held him within under discipline, and from the licence of power he did not break out into impatience. Whence: “without indignation, I rose up.” Impatience is almost always the friend of power.
25_marg1686: Calves to be slaughtered are left in free pastures; the one to be kept is pressed by the yoke. Those come through pleasant meadows to the pit; this one through a rough road to the homeland.
25_marg1687: Without indignation; I rose up, and cried in the crowd: often the tumults of seditious men provoke the minds of those set over them; who, if they are good, have a cry against the tumults of the insolent but have no fury, since they do not cease to teach those whom they bear with mercifully.
25_interl3089: in time of peace the Church suffers within her the wicked and the feigned; so too Job was good among the wicked, which is the perfection of goodness
25_marg1688: I was the brother of dragons, and companion: by the name of dragons the malicious; by ostriches, which have wings and do not have flight, pretenders are designated, who have only the look of holiness.
25_interl3090: in whom the Church was fair, now she is foul
25_interl3091: because power is given to them too against the Church; but Job says he suffered outside and within
25_interl3092: as Paul burned with the dryness of weariness at some falling, when he said: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”
25_marg1689: My skin is become black: by the name of skin the weak of the Church are signified, who serve outward usefulness. By the bones the strong, who care for heavenly things, in whom is the framework of the body. So the skin is blackened and the bones dry up with heat, because while the weak leap forth to iniquity, and, often having taken a place of honour among the reprobate, serve against the Church, the strong who are in her are tortured with zeal for the faith.
25_interl3093: when preaching is silent, the elect man grieves
25_marg1690: My harp is turned to mourning: as if he said: in the time of my peace I preached through some, who also tame the flesh, small things after the manner of a harp, through others great and sounding things after the manner of an organ. But now the harp and the organ are turned to mourning, because when I see myself despised I bewail those who do not hear the song of preaching.
25_marg1691: Or: the harp sounds through strings, the organ through pipes. The string of the harp is the intention of those who work rightly, which is stretched through affliction of the flesh toward another life, the flesh dried, so that the string may have a fitting sound. If the string is stretched too little it does not sound, but if too much it sounds hoarse; because abstinence avails nothing unless the body is well tamed, or if it is worn down too much; because vices are to be put out, not the flesh.
25_marg1692: I made a covenant with my eyes: now he lists his own virtues in order, so weaving the history of his life as to put in among them very rarely something that can be understood mystically. “I made a covenant with my eyes.” For so that he could keep the thoughts of his heart chaste, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first look carelessly on what he would afterwards love unwillingly. It is said to the serpent by God: “Upon thy breast and belly shalt thou go.” On the belly when he works lust in deed through human members; on the breast when he defiles in thought; but because one comes to the deed through thought, which is placed in the breast, therefore Job, because he fortified his thought, overcame breast and belly with one guard, saying: “that I would not so much as think,” etc. Which he added because he put out not only the act of lust but the thought, which is abundant justice.
25_marg1693: Up to here he has listed the evils he suffered; now he begins to tell the good things he did. Because death enters through the windows of the senses, he guards them outside, lest through them the soul desire outward things. They ought not to look at what is not lawful to be desired.
25_interl3095: as if: if I were not clean
25_marg1694: For what part should he have in me: as if he said: the maker of the heights refuses to have me as his possession if my mind wastes away before his sight with weak desires. For no good things please God without cleanness of mind.
25_interl3097: because other good things do not please without cleanness
25_interl3099: I would not be the part of God, because
25_marg1695: Is not destruction to the wicked? Then there will be aversion to the reprobate, when they see themselves made anathema from the inheritance of the strict judge.
25_interl3102: because no good or evil things are without retribution
25_marg1696: Doth not he consider my ways? By the name of ways he declares actions; by the term steps, the motions of minds or the advances of merits. And if the Lord considers the ways of each one, he so numbers the steps that not even the tiniest thoughts, and the slightest words which have grown cheap with us by use, remain unexamined in his judgment.
25_interl3103: and since God sees all, I wish to be perfected in the example of Christ
25_interl3104: vanity belongs to lightness, deceit to malice. So he uses the right order, because through light things one comes to malicious ones
25_marg1697: If I have walked, etc. Knowing he is seen, he takes care; yet he is not secure and perfect, because among the ancients he weighs, in the precepts of the Christ to come, how much he lacks of perfection. So he says: “If I have walked.”
25_interl3105: he is weighed in this, that he is called to the example of his life
25_marg1698: Let him weigh: as if he said: as far as the measure of human life goes, I do not see evils in me. But unless the Mediator appears, who surpasses all, I do not know how far I stand from true simplicity.
25_marg1699: In a just balance: by the name of balance “the mediator of God and men” is designated, in whom our merits are weighed equally, and in whose precepts we recognize what we lack in our life. And the sense is: if I have ever done anything lightly, anything ruinously, let the Mediator appear, that in his life I may recognize whether I was truly simple. For he who had surpassed the powers of his times was seeking the Mediator of God and men, so that, weighing himself in him, he might recognize whether he had truly kept a simple life.
25_interl3106: God is said to know when he makes us know
25_interl3107: that is, let him make me know
25_interl3109: through consent, not through what one suffers unwillingly
25_marg1700: If my step hath turned, etc. The step turns out of the way as often as our thought leaves the road of uprightness through consent to error.
25_interl3110: if sight serves evil thought, work soon follows
25_marg1701: And if … hath followed my eyes: for as temptation is drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes, conceived within, it forces the eyes to serve it outside.
25_marg1702: And if a spot hath cleaved to my hands: as if he said: I neither wished to see what I might desire, nor by seeing followed what I desired. Nor did a spot cleave to my hands, that is, fault to my actions; because if he ever thought anything unlawful, he did not let it reach as far as works.
25_marg1703: Then let me sow and let another eat: to sow is to preach the words of life; to eat is to be filled with good works. And the sense is: let not me but another do what my mouth speaks. For a woman suckles her son when awake and kills him when asleep; so a master awake in knowledge and asleep in life, if he nourishes the hearer by watchings and preaching, kills him by the sleep of the body.

But he would reckon he did wrong to devotion if he ate alone what the Lord had created for all in common. Nor does he attribute this devotion to himself but to the grace of God; he says: “For from my infancy mercy grew up with me.” He makes known that he obtained these bowels of devotion by his maker’s grace; because, as he was not formed in the womb by his own work, so neither was he devout from the womb by his own power. For mercy, even if it was of his choice that it should advance with him, yet it was not of his choice that it should come out of the womb with him. The virtues are companions: let not humility, when it reveres a neighbour, forsake liberality, nor liberality swell up toward the needy. Neither through ungodliness fail to cover one who shares your nature, nor through pride cease to revere him whom you cover; as it is said: “That they may receive you into everlasting dwellings,” where it is shown that we offer gifts to patrons rather than give gifts to the needy.

Great riches are the abundant sharpness of counsels which the hand of the seeker finds, that is, which the thought of the one handling them brings forth. So he finds great riches who, by searching the sacred words, obtains abundant understanding. And it is not a secure gladness to know them, but to keep them; because of him to whom much is committed more is required, and while it is given out at interest it is lost unless it is paid out carefully. Understanding either grows numb with idleness or vanishes with haughtiness; and so he says: “If I have rejoiced.” But when he carries out what he understands, from the fact that it is shown outside he often slips; but blessed Job, as he did not extol the gold of understanding, so neither the light of working. And after such great things as he said above, what great thing is it not to have worshipped created things? He says that he did not even see them, that is, that he did not look with desire at the beauty of the present light; so that he delighted neither in gold nor in bodily light; like him who says: “I have not desired the day of man”; in which he cannot rejoice because he did not see them through desire. If, I say, I did this or that, then instead of wheat, that is, greater goods, thistles, the least evils; instead of barley, that is, the least goods, thorns, greater evils. For the thistle is softer than the thorn, which is harder for pricking. And it is, to say it briefly: if I did this or that, instead of the goods that refresh for ever let evils that prick be paid back to me. Or in wheat the spiritual work that refreshes the mind; in barley the dispensing of earthly things is figured, in which we prepare food as for fleshly beasts, which also has some chaff mixed in. And here even that ruler against whom the land cries sometimes sows wheat and barley; but the subjects who are weighed down in many things do not think those few good things good which are in some way defiled. So he says: if I did not do the great things I ought, let me receive the prickings of murmuring from those under me, even for the good I did. So prelates must take care not to give an example of evil, and subjects not to judge the deeds of prelates easily, contradicting the order of God who gave them power, as it is written: “All power is from the Lord God.” And of these it is written: “Obey your prelates,” lest it be said of you: “And they murmured, and perished by the serpents.” Of those, then: “The glory thereof as the flower of the grass.”

25_marg1746: So these three, etc. At last we have set out blessed Job’s sentences, full of mystic power, in which he answered against the words of his friends; now it remains for us to come to the words of Eliu, which must be weighed with so much the more serious circumspection as they are also uttered with a more fervent spirit through the boldness of youth. Blessed Job, known to God alone and to himself, was to be brought to our knowledge in his calm; he was touched by the scourge, so that he might spread the scent of his strengths the wider, as, like spices, he gave off a better fragrance from being burned. He knew how to rule those under him devoutly in good times and to guard himself strictly from evils. He knew how to use well the things he had, but we did not know whether he would remain patient when they were taken away. He knew how to pay daily sacrifices to God for his children while they were safe, but it was uncertain whether he would offer him the sacrifice of thanksgiving even when bereaved. So, lest prosperity cover any vices, it was fitting that pain should lay this open. So licence to tempt was given to the cunning enemy against the holy man. He, while he longed to destroy his good things, known in many ways, showed also the good of patience which lay hidden. For he burned the flocks, put out the households, crushed the heirs, struck the health of the body, and, to hurl the dart of a heavier temptation, kept back the wife’s tongue, so that grief through the losses of things might lay low the holy man’s strong and solid breast, and cursing through the words of his wife might pierce it. But as many wounds as he raging inflicted, so many victories he unknowingly supplied to the holy man. His friends, who inveigh against him as if while advising, express the figure of the heretics, who under the appearance of advising carry on the business of leading astray; whence also, while they make speeches to blessed Job on the Lord’s behalf, they are rebuked by the Lord, because all heretics, while they strive to defend God, offend him. Whence it is aptly said to them by Job: “I desire to reason with God, first shewing you to be forgers of lies, and maintainers of perverse doctrines.” So it is plain that they bear the figure of the heretics, whom the holy man refutes as serving the maintaining of perverse doctrines. So in the three names of Job’s friends three falls of ruin in the heretics are expressed. For unless they despised God they would never think perverse things of him; and unless they drew themselves into oldness, they would not err in the understanding of the new life; and unless they destroyed the contemplation of the good, the judgments from above would never reprove them with such strict examination for the fault of their words. So by despising God they keep themselves in oldness; and by keeping themselves in oldness they harm the contemplation of the upright with their wicked speeches.
25_marg1747: Was angry and was moved to indignation: Eliu is interpreted ‘this is my God’ or ‘God the Lord’; by him the faith of the arrogant placed within the Church is rightly designated, because they confess God the Lord. Barachel, ‘blessing of the Lord.’ Buzite, ‘contemptible’; because it fits arrogant preachers that in the eloquence of preaching they receive the blessing of divine grace, but in their haughty ways they show it to be contemptible. Ram, ‘lofty.’ For the people of the faithful is lofty, which here despises the lowest and cast-off things of life. So Eliu is said to be of the kindred of Ram, because every arrogant preacher placed within the Church is joined to the holy peoples by the truth of faith, though he is separated from their life by the wickedness of haughtiness.
25_marg1748: Now he was angry against Job: for the followers of vainglory, when they set themselves above men, rebuke some for foolish senses, others for unworthy merits; that is, they reckon some know nothing, others do not live well; even while they justly accuse all placed outside the Church of thinking wicked things. They also despise those within for the contempt of their life; and those outside they press by the truth of what is said, those inside they press by the manner of saying, that is, by the vice of haughtiness.

And mostly they revere the talents of those who are wrongly wise more than the simple life of the innocent. And though the Church is older than the heretics, because they went out from her, yet Eliu is described as younger, because after the wars of the heretics had been waged, men fervent in talent came forth to the contests against the enemies, and from that they began to be arrogant. After these too the younger Eliu is joined in reproaching blessed Job, from whose person the kind of certain teachers who are faithful, yet arrogant, is designated. His words we do not easily understand unless we weigh them from the Lord’s rebuke that follows. For the Lord says of them: “Who is this that wrappeth up sentences in unskilful words?” And when he says sentences but does not add at once what kind, he surely wants good ones to be understood. For when sentences are named, unless they are also called bad, they cannot be taken badly. For we take sentences in a good sense when they are put without an added rebuke, as it is written: “The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that speak sentences.”

25_marg1751: But, as I see, there is a spirit in men: it is no small condemnation to glory privately in a good which is given in common; to know where the good began and not to know how to use the good one has received. For there are four kinds of swelling: when a man reckons he has good from himself; or, if he believes it is given from above, yet thinks he has received it for his own merits; or when he boasts of having what he does not have; or when, despising others, he wishes to appear singular. This fourth kind comes nearer to the devil, who wished to be above the angels; because into this kind every human mind frequently slips, so as to glory in having singularly what it has. For whoever rejoices to have good singularly, whoever seeks to seem loftier than others, imitates him who, despising the good of the fellowship of the angels, setting his seat in the north and proudly longing for likeness to the Most High, tried through wicked desire to break out as it were to a certain summit of singularity. From this the Lord checked the disciples returning from preaching, lest they rejoice in the singularity of miracles, saying: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven”; who was singularly lifted up, so that in his ruin they might learn what to fear from haughtiness.
