25_marg1757: Therefore because I have waited, etc. The end of speech for the wise is usually to speak until they impose silence on their adversaries; for they do not desire to show themselves, but to check those who teach wicked things. But after it has been said of Job’s friends: “They were afraid, and answered no more,” or: “they left off speaking,” Eliu adds and says: “I have waited, and they have not spoken: they stood, and answered no more.” And Eliu multiplies words when they are now silent, because the arrogant man hastens not to overcome the sayings of his adversaries but to display his own wisdom.
25_marg1758: So there follows: “I also will answer my part,” etc. Every arrogant man reckons this his part, if he not so much has knowledge as displays it; because surely all the haughty do not long to have knowledge but to show it. Therefore it is rightly said by Moses: “The vessel that hath no cover, nor binding over it, shall be unclean,” etc. But holy preachers reckon it their part if within they themselves rejoice in wisdom, and outside they check others from error. Nor do they so go out of themselves in speaking as to put the joy of the mind in the display of discerning speech; but they meditate on the good of knowledge in the secret of the heart, and rejoice there where they perceive it, not where, among so many snares of temptations, they are forced to become known.
25_interl3183: because the proud see the saints speak great things and be honoured for it, and they follow these things only so as to be held famous
25_marg1759: I am full of matter to speak of: it often happens that wise men, when they consider that they are not heard, impose silence on their mouth. But when they see that crimes grow while they keep silent, they bear a certain force of their spirit so as to break out into speech of open rebuke. Whence Jeremias, when he had imposed silence on himself, saying: “I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name,” at once added: “And there came in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I was wearied, not being able to bear it.” But often, in like manner, the anxiety of vainglory, by no means containing itself within silence, inflames the mind of the arrogant to the urge of speaking as if with the zeal of charity, and drives it to unbridled speech; whence Eliu, stretched by the spirit of haughtiness and not containing himself within the bars of silence, says: “I am full of matter to speak of,” etc. By the belly the bosom of the heart is taken, by the new wine the fervour of the Holy Spirit. For Eliu is shown in the puffing up of haughtiness as if he were kindled by the ardour of the Holy Spirit; he compared the spirit of his sense, in that he kept silent, to new wine without a vent.
25_marg1760: And he rightly says: “which bursteth the new vessels,” because the fervour of the Holy Spirit is scarcely contained not only by the old but even by the new life; so the new wine bursts the new vessels, because the power of his fervour goes beyond even spiritual hearts. He calls weak consciences, or the earthly vessels of bodies, vessels.
25_marg1761: I will speak and take breath: he rightly says: “take breath,” because as it is the toil of the just to see wicked things and not correct them, so it is a heavy toil for the arrogant if they do not show what they know. For they can scarcely bear the force boiling within if they make known a little too late all that they perceive. So it is necessary that when a good thing is done, their haughtiness be first overcome in the heart, lest, if it comes forth from the root of wretched haughtiness, it bring forth the wretched fruits of wickedness.
25_interl3184: because as it is the toil of the just to see evils and not correct them, so it is a toil for accusers if they do not show what they know
25_marg1762: I will not accept the person of man: he rightly does not level God with man, because he does not know how long he will remain here or when he will be taken to God’s judgment; and he rightly says: “after a while,” because however long the time of the present life has been, it is by that very fact the shorter in that it does not last. For it is not fitting that whatever is bounded by an end be judged long-lasting. But among these sentences, which he utters solid from the truth, he breaks out again into words of haughtiness, saying: “Hear,” etc.
25_interl3185: among true sentences he again breaks out into words of haughtiness
25_marg1763: Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches: it must be weighed from how great haughtiness it comes down, that he warns blessed Job to hear him, that he declares he has opened his mouth, and promises that his tongue will speak within his jaws. For it is the property of the arrogant not to be able to minister rightly the right things they know, nor to bring in humbly the things they teach.
25_interl3186: what I perceive against you, I tell prudently and quietly
25_marg1764: Let my tongue speak within my jaws: to speak within the jaws is to speak quietly and not to shout with cries. The arrogant within the Church are said to speak as it were within the jaws when they do not cry out against adversaries living outside, but rebuke those placed within the Church. And often the arrogant pretend to flee arrogance, and speak privately to individuals as if secretly, so that they may glory both in their sense and in their contempt of arrogance. Sometimes they are so shameless that, while others keep silent, they praise what they say.
25_marg1765: So he adds: “My words are from my upright heart.” Simplicity of speech is the praise of great virtue; which, because the arrogant do not have it, they assert they have, so as to be heard more securely. And they announce that they will speak purely, because men of this kind fear their doubleness will be caught, and they mix true things with false so as to be believed the more quickly. So because Eliu both declared that he would speak purely and, by calling his sayings sentences, ran ahead with favour, he now adds that same sentence he promised, saying: “The spirit of God made me.” He tells that he was made by the spirit and given life by the breath. For of Adam’s making it is written: “He breathed into his face the breath of life.” And note that he uttered a true sentence when he said he was made by the Spirit of God, but uselessly and not in its place. Whence Moses: “The man that hath an issue of seed shall be unclean.” The seed is speech, which makes the hearers fruitful; but if it flows out unseasonably it defiles the one who emits it, so that even what he has thought rightly is fouled, and he is not believed and loses the power of begetting. But let us hear whether these things which he rightly asserts are rightly followed through.
25_marg1766: If thou canst: again he breaks out into the arrogance of proud haughtiness while he tells the order of the true condition. And he repeats the same thing in other words, saying: “Behold God hath made me as well as thee.” The arrogant remember that they were made equal with men, but set themselves above them by the swelling of knowledge; and in that they are no longer equal, they bring back to a marvel the fact that they were equal by birth.
25_marg1767: But yet … my wonder: Paul humbly calls his high things “the word of consolation,” speaking to the Hebrews; this man calls his least things a wonder and eloquence; because it is the property of the arrogant that before they speak they reckon they are saying wonderful things, and forestall their speech with admiration; which the haughtiness of the mind does.
25_marg1768: Now thou has said in my hearing: he adds what he said.
25_marg1769: I am clean, and without sin: against these words, which he relates blessed Job said, he brings forth his sentence, saying: “Now this is,” etc. For surely blessed Job had said truly that he had been scourged without fault. For he said this of himself which the Lord said of him to the devil: “Thou hast moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause.”
25_marg1770: Now this is the thing in which thou art not justified: for he did not know that by his scourges vice is not wiped out but merit increased; and because he had said he was without sin, he rebukes him, scourged, with this sentence. But it must be noted that blessed Job said his foot had been put in the stocks, but he by no means said in this way what is charged against him, that he had been clean and without sin, or unspotted and without iniquity. But Eliu, while he strove to rebuke with severity the things that were said, adds lyingly things that were not said, so as to seem to accuse learnedly. And this because the arrogant long to accuse more than to console, and believe that evils befall men only for iniquities.
25_interl3189: after so many words of haughtiness he opens his knowledge
25_marg1771: I will answer thee: this is said so that the scourged man, considering that God is greater than he, may in all that he suffers set himself below his judgment, than which he does not doubt he is less, and may believe what he suffers from the better one to be just, even if he does not know the causes of that justice.
25_marg1772: Dost thou strive against him: it is the property of an afflicted heart that in all it longs for (and yet feels the order of things to be contrary) it would wish, if it could be, to be answered by divine voices why it is so or not so, so as to consult God about every dispute of things, and rest once the reason of his answer is known.
25_interl3191: but God does not answer individuals with a private voice, because he has established a word by which he satisfies all
25_marg1773: God speaketh once: but Eliu, foreseeing that the Lord established sacred Scripture, and in it answered the public or hidden questions of all, says: “Dost thou strive against him, because he hath not answered thee to all words? God speaketh once,” etc. As if he said: God does not answer the hearts of individuals with private voices, but builds such a word as satisfies the questions of all. For in the word of his Scripture each of us finds our cases if we seek them. For there we are all answered in common in what we suffer particularly; there the life of those who went before becomes the pattern of those who follow. For to bring forward one out of many: see, when we are affected by some suffering or trouble of the flesh, we perhaps wish to know the hidden causes of that suffering or trouble, so as to be consoled in what we suffer by the very knowledge of things. But because we are by no means answered individually about our particular temptations, we run back to sacred Scripture, where we find that when Paul had been tempted by weakness of the flesh he heard: “My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity.” This was said to him in his own weakness for this reason, that it might not be said to each of us one by one. So in sacred Scripture we have heard the voice of God, to Paul when he was afflicted, lest when perhaps we are afflicted we seek individually to hear it with private consolation. For God’s speaking is to beget the Word, because besides the Only-begotten he begot no other word; and for us to wonder at this is in some way to see, as a closed eye perceives light. But because this wonder is not easy for those busied on earth, he shows how God’s speech comes to us through a dream.
25_interl3192: with the mind at rest from the business of the world, as Moses on the mountain receives the law
25_marg1774: By a dream in a vision by night: in sleep the outward senses sleep and inward things are seen. So if we wish to contemplate inward things, let us sleep from outward entanglement. In daylight we see more surely; but in a vision by night we see through images; and the saints, so long as they are in this life, look on the secrets of the divine nature as under a certain imagining, because they do not yet contemplate them more openly as they are.
25_interl3194: that is, when one ceases from outward action, whence there is rest in the mind
25_marg1775: And they are sleeping in their beds: because then we come to know the secrets of the Godhead, when we withdraw from the tumultuous lust of this world into the chambers of our mind.
25_marg1776: Then he openeth the ears of men: for when they are lulled from outward actions, with open ear they hear the causes of the inward examination.
25_marg1777: And teaching instructeth them, etc. Because while they consider subtly either the public scourges or the hidden judgments, they do not cease to afflict themselves by weeping. And it is rightly said: “And teaching instructeth them,” etc., because to the mind that considers and tears itself through penance, the laments of compunction are as it were certain wounds of suffering. For there are four qualities by which the soul of the just man is strongly affected in compunction. Either when it remembers its evils, considering where it has been; of which Paul: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because,” etc. Or when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments and searching with itself, it thinks where it will be; of which: “I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps,” etc. Or when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, it considers mourning where it is; whence: “while we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord.” Or when it contemplates the good things of the homeland above, which, because it does not yet obtain them, it looks on mourning where it is not. Whence the Apostle: “We see now through a glass in a dark manner,” etc.
25_interl3196: he who is turned from the things he has done is delivered from pride, because: “Pride is the beginning of all sin”
25_marg1778: That he may withdraw a man: what has man made of himself but sin? And he longs to avoid what he has made, and returns humbly to the order of his condition; while he flees his own works, he loves himself such as he was made by God. And to be proud against the maker is to overstep his precepts by sinning, because he shakes off as it were from himself the yoke of his lordship, to which he scorns to be subject through disobedience.
25_marg1779: Rescuing his soul from corruption: to pass to the sword is to pass from this corruption of vices to the sword of punishments. But surely he snatches his life there from the vengeance of torment, whose mind he here draws away from the delight of sin.
25_interl3197: we are pricked within, lest there be haughtiness
25_marg1780: He rebuketh also by sorrow in the bed: the bed is taken as temporal rest. So he rebukes by sorrow in the bed, that is, in the rest of the present life he troubles him either by the goads of temptation or by the affliction of the scourge. For he makes the road of this world rough for the elect, lest, while anyone is fed by the rest of the present life as by the pleasantness of life, it delight him more to journey long than to arrive quickly.
25_interl3198: because they were as it were thrust in as companions of the good
25_marg1781: And he maketh all his bones to wither: we take the bones as virtues; and he makes the bones wither, because when in that rest which we prepare for ourselves from this world we are affected by the scourge of temptation, we who could have been puffed up by our virtues are thinned by weariness at the weakness we have come to know; and all that fat and green rejoicing in our strengths will suddenly be dried up by the grief of anxiety.
25_interl3199: so that he may prove what is from himself, what from God’s gift
25_marg1782: Abominable: he calls the delight of the present life bread. For each one, when the prosperity of living well smiles on him, grows cheerful; and that very cheerfulness refreshes the mind like desirable food. But when he is struck by temptation, all joy is rejected by his mind, which before rejoiced as if filled with that same joy.
25_interl3200: that is, to the afflicted mind whatever before satisfied it pleasantly is turned to bitterness
25_interl3201: because through adversities the merits of virtues are laid open
25_marg1783: Shall be consumed away: as we are tempted by vices lest we be lifted up within, so outside we are worn by scourges lest, the world flattering us, we be led astray to seek anything outside.
25_marg1784: His flesh shall be consumed away: by the name of flesh the delight of the flesh is taken. So it is consumed away and the bones are laid bare, because when fleshly delight is thinned by the reproving scourges, the strong things of the virtues which lay hidden as it were under the flesh are laid open. For no one knows how much he has advanced except amid adversities.
25_interl3203: in adversities not only the vigour of strength is uncovered but also the weakness of humanity
25_marg1785: His soul hath drawn near to corruption, etc. The soul of the tempted just man is said to draw near to corruption, because he is not ignorant that, from his own strengths, he is close to ruin, so that he attributes it not to himself but to the Lord that he is far from ruin. So he draws near to the destroyers, because through weakness of the flesh he sees himself close to the death-bringing sins, from which by the divine gift he is made so much the farther as he finds himself close to them by his own merits. Yet God’s protection is believed less necessary if it is always had; it is usefully withdrawn sometimes, so that it may be shown that without it man is nothing.
25_interl3205: having shown the general plague in one, he brings in the general remedy
25_marg1786: If there shall be an angel for him: this angel is taken as Christ. He speaks for us to the Father, one of those like us. For while in all his workings he surpasses us by immense power, in one thing only, that is, in the truth of the form, he does not differ from us; who speaks to the Father for us by this, that he shows himself like us. For his speaking is to show himself man for us; apart from whom no just one would be found to intercede without sin for sinners.
25_marg1787: One among those like him: because truly man, but not born as others, not dead as others. For he rises of necessity, by himself, and on the third day.
25_marg1788: To declare man’s uprightness: the angel declared man’s uprightness. For, interceding for sinners, he showed himself a just man who would merit pardon for others.
25_marg1789: He shall have mercy on him: the Mediator has mercy on man in this, that he took the form of man.
25_marg1790: And shall say: Deliver him: his saying is to deliver man by taking on the nature of man and to show it free. For from that flesh which he took he showed this too to be free, which he redeemed.
25_marg1791: That he may not go down: of whom above: “His soul hath drawn near to corruption”; that is, because by knowing himself he is not ignorant that he is close to corruption, therefore let him not go down into corruption.
25_marg1792: I have found wherein I may be merciful to him: as if he openly said: because there was no man who could appear as a just intercessor before God for men, I made myself man to be merciful to men; and while I showed myself man, I found in what just man I might be merciful to men.
25_interl3207: by a wonderful dispensation God turns this into punishment for us, by which we committed fault
25_marg1793: His flesh is consumed: for in numbers the human race was pressed by the torments of vices and punishments; but when the Redeemer came, it returns to the days of its youth, that is, is renewed in the wholeness of its former life, so that it does not remain in that into which it fell, but, redeemed, returns to that for the receiving of which it was made.
25_interl3208: even man himself after the angel; otherwise man would never raise himself to seek eternal things
25_marg1794: He shall pray to God: because while our Redeemer intercedes with the Father for us, we too, the numbness of our former life shaken off, are kindled to the state of prayer; so it is aptly said: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him.” For he says first that the angel asks and afterwards man; who, unless the Lord himself first, interceding with the Father through his incarnation, asked for our life, our insensibility would never rouse itself to ask for the things that are eternal; but the prayer of his incarnation went before so that the awakening of our numbness might follow.
25_interl3209: this rightly after bitternesses, so that, sad at himself from terror of the judgment, and so with cleansed eyes, he may see the good things he seeks
25_marg1795: And he shall see his face: for after the contests of toils, after the waves of temptations, the soul is suspended in ecstasy, so as to contemplate the knowledge of the divine presence. And joy (jubilation) is called the unspeakable joy of the mind, which can neither be hidden nor opened in words; and yet it is betrayed by certain motions, though it is expressed by no proper terms.
25_interl3210: from the grace of contemplation follows the justice of working
25_interl3211: the justice of God is in giving, man’s in receiving
25_marg1796: And he will render to man his justice: not what he had from himself, but what he received when he was made, that he might have it; so that it may please him to cling to God, so that he may dread his threatening sentence.
25_interl3212: he would not know himself a sinner unless he had justice
25_marg1797: He shall look upon men, and shall say: I have sinned: Scripture never calls those men except those whom it distinguishes from the beasts by reason, that is, whom it shows not worn down by the beastly motion of passions. And the sense is: he looks on the examples of holy men, and weighing himself by their working together, he grasps that he is wicked.
25_interl3213: punishment questions whether man truly knows himself
25_marg1798: I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and … what I have deserved, etc. He who considers the examples of the wicked recognizes that he has been struck less than he deserved, because in their justice he sees how grave a fault it was that he erred.
25_marg1799: I have sinned, and indeed I have offended: indeed, not like one who confesses himself a sinner in words, and yet defends himself if he is accused; such a one wishes to seem humble, not to be.
25_interl3214: for the life of the good is a living reading, looking at which he will say
25_marg1800: He hath delivered his soul from going into, because when divine grace goes before in good working, our free choice follows; we are said to deliver ourselves, who consent to the Lord delivering us.
25_marg1801: That it may live and see the light: namely the light of truth, which one dead in heart cannot see; or he then, living, looks on the light who attends with the free eyes of the heart to the Lord in the form of Godhead at the judgment.
25_marg1802: Behold, all these things God worketh: of the tempted and scourged man it was said above: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. And below is joined: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him,” etc. In these sentences both above the grief of bitterness and below the gladness of security is set. And soon is added: “all these things God worketh three times within.” As if he said: what I have said of one is done three times in each one; that is, we find grief and gladness alternating in the mind of each elect man in three ways: in conversion, in testing, in death. In conversion there is heavy grief, when he wishes to throw off the heavy burden of temporal desires and carry the light yoke of the Lord in free service; but that familiar fleshly delight of his meets him. And what anxiety of heart is then in him, when on this side the spirit calls, on that the flesh calls back, so that it can be said of him: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. But because divine grace does not let him be long affected by this difficulty, it breaks the chains of sins and, consoling him, leads him to the freedom of a new way of life, and the following gladness refreshes the preceding sadness; because in the beginning God provided pleasant things, which no one should think the perfection; so that it can be said of him: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him,” etc. But after the first voice of grief and gladness, which each one comes to know through the effort of conversion, a second springs up, lest he be loosened by the negligence of security; as the enemies met them in the desert after the Egyptians were drowned: immediately bitter things, so as to test in the end the highest. For it often happens that vices rising up torture one already converted more than at the beginning, and now, now bend the mind of one resisting toward the fall of despair; so that it ought to be said of him: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. But because merciful God allows us to be tested by temptations, not reproved, consolation quickly comes, and calms the attacking motions of thoughts with inward peace, so that it ought to be said of this tempted and delivered man: “he shall see his face with joy.” After the infections of striking and after the hardship of testing, as he approaches the loosing of the flesh, sometimes even the just soul is troubled by terror of strict vengeance, fearing more the evils it does not understand; and even if it could taste anything calm in this life, it is shaken at the coming of the moment of death, so that it ought rightly to be said: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life.” But because the souls of the just are often purged from any foreign infections by the very dread of death, they receive eternal reward. And often by a certain contemplation of the inward reward they grow cheerful before they are stripped of the flesh, and it is rightly said: “he shall see his face with joy,” etc. But because the mind of each elect one is worn either by the toil of conversion, or by the temptation of testing, or by dread of the loosing, and, purged by that very wearing, is set free:
25_marg1803: There follows: “That he may withdraw their souls from corruption.” The light of the dying is that which we see with bodily eyes. And they are enlightened with the light of the living who, despising the temporal light, run back to the splendour of the inward brightness, so as to live there where they see the true light, where light is not one thing and life another.
25_interl3215: it is the property of the arrogant man to mix proud things with true
25_marg1804: Attend, Job, and hearken to me: Eliu, after he has set out many deep things of wisdom, shows by this speech what he is like within himself. For it is immense pride to demand reverence for oneself from an elder and to command silence on a better man.
25_marg1805: But if thou hast any thing to say, answer me: just preachers, while they rebuke, out of the grace of humility inquire whether perhaps they are mistaken in what they rebuke, and give leave to those rebuked to confess if they feel anything more just for themselves. The arrogant long to imitate this. For, putting haughtiness aside for a little in their words, they seek justice in those they rebuke, as if they might perhaps find it, not because they think so, but because they long to be adorned with the appearance of humility, lest they seem swollen, as they are.
25_interl3216: he did not say this from the heart, since, not waiting, he at once adds
25_marg1806: For I would have thee to appear just: because he did not utter this from the heart, he did not wait to hear what he had asked. For at once he added: “And if thou have not, hear me.” Eliu did not allow what he had asked to be said, but soon broke out with what he was carrying within.
25_interl3217: as if these things were poured down from heaven upon the unworthy
25_marg1807: And Eliu continued his discourse, and said: what is shown by the word of this pronouncing but the puffing up of haughtiness, so that words which came from the high root of pride might come forth with a certain loftiness, as it were, and strictness?
25_interl3218: he fears too much who thinks his words are not fittingly heard except by the wise
25_marg1808: Hear ye, wise men, my words: as if he said: as the ear does not know foods nor the throat words, so no fool understands the sentence of the wise. 25_interl3219: the ear: he does not seek to make men wise, but to show himself to the wise, so that, learned, he may be heard by the learned
25_marg1809: Judgment: whether he sought this judgment out of humility is weighed from what follows.
25_marg1810: For Job hath said: I am just, etc. That he said this not at all, the words of the sacred text, when searched, bear witness.
25_interl3221: see, he who sought judgment has brought forth judgment, from the fault which he invented, so that no sentence from Job might afterwards be waited for
25_interl3222: the arrogant man seeks more to scold than to cherish, so as to seem superior
25_marg1811: What man is there like Job: so that one understands: none. See, him whom the Lord told the devil was just beyond comparison, Eliu asserts a sinner beyond comparison; of whom he adds: “who drinketh up scorning like water,” etc. When water is drunk it is taken in so fluidly that it is not held back from being swallowed by any thickness of its own. 25_interl3223: from the company of the reprobate he judged him worthy of damnation
25_interl3224: because the proud man is a stranger to truth, he who exalts himself soon broke out into false things; what he rebukes in another he wickedly invents
25_marg1812: For he hath said: Man shall not please, etc. That he did not say this at all, anyone who reads blessed Job’s words recognizes.
25_marg1813: Therefore, ye men of understanding, hear me, etc. Again with the arrogance of pride he seeks those who, as worthy, may be able to understand him.
25_interl3225: it is not as Job says
25_marg1814: Far from God be wickedness: he said well, because there is no iniquity or wickedness in almighty God.
25_interl3226: which yet is not here, as he thinks
25_marg1815: For he will render to a man his work, etc. In this life this is by no means done. For he both freely forestalls many committing unlawful things and turns them to holy works, and chastens some devoted to right acts by the scourge coming between.
25_interl3227: at the last, even if here he afflicts without cause
25_marg1816: For in very deed God will not condemn without cause: he cannot condemn without cause by that condemnation by which at the last he punishes all that each one has wickedly committed here; nor does the Almighty overthrow judgment, because even if the things we suffer seem less than right, yet they are decreed right in the hidden examination.
25_marg1817: What other hath he appointed over the earth? 25_marg1818: If he turn … to him: his heart is crooked when it longs for the lowest things; it is made straight when it is lifted to the things above. 25_marg1821: Can he be healed that loveth not judgment? So because Eliu said that he who does not love judgment cannot be healed, accusing blessed Job of not loving judgment and of having condemned him who is just, he at once adds the justice of that same Just One, that is, the Lord, saying: “Who saith to the king: Thou art an apostate,” etc. A proud ruler slips into the fault of apostasy as often as he delights to preside over men and rejoices in the singularity of his honour, as if he were not one of those who preside, and not under the Lord; which is only from imitation of him who, despising the fellowship of the angels, said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the most High.”

Precepts ought neither to be forsaken from dread nor embraced from lust, lest either someone become worse proud, as if from humility, if he despises the order of the divine dispensation by fleeing it, or cast off the yoke of the ruler above by the very fact that private rule over others delights him.

25_marg1838: So that they caused the cry of the needy to come to him: for when these are proud, those who are oppressed by the proud cry to God; or because when these fall the poor, that is, the humble in spirit, are put in their place; which they are said to do because it happens by their fall; or when they sin the cry of the poor is heard, because while the Jews were proud against the Lord the prayers of the gentiles reached God. Or because these things can be taken of rulers: when they forsake the office of preaching for the cares of the world, they drive those under them to a cry, who murmur why a pretender holds the place. But because rulers have their own judge, it is a great caution for subjects not to judge rashly the life of those who rule. For not in vain did the Lord himself pour out the money of the changers and overturn the chairs of those who sold doves; surely signifying that through the masters he judges the life of the peoples, but through himself examines the deeds of the masters; though even the vices of subjects which are now either overlooked or cannot be judged by the masters are yet without doubt reserved for his judgment. Or by the swelling of the mighty the pride of the Jews, by the cry of the needy the desires of the gentiles, are figured. So while the Jews were proud, the prayers of the gentiles reached God; whose judgments he does not dare to discuss but reveres with wonder.
25_interl3258: “Yea, Father; for so hath it seemed good in thy sight”: what pleases God cannot be unjust
25_marg1839: For when he granteth peace: if you wonder that the gentiles were taken up: “when he granteth peace, who is there that can condemn?” If you are astonished that Judea was lost: “when he hideth his countenance, who is there that can behold him?” And because God judges the least things as the greatest, each as all, he adds: “whether it regard nations.” As if he openly warned: understand this judgment, which is described over one nation, as over all too, so that one is driven back, another chosen, hiddenly but none unjustly. So what we see done in the greatest things, let us fear warily in each of us too. He exercises this subtle judgment, that one is driven back, another chosen, both over the nations and over all men; because the Lord so attends to each as if he had leisure from all, and so attends to all at once as if he had leisure from each. And because he passed from the kind to the class, now from the class he turns to the kind and shows what Judea properly deserves.

25_marg1843: Saying: “Seeing then I have spoken. For he would not ask if he believed he had erred. For it is, as has been said, the proper fraud of the arrogant to be eager to ask about error at the moment when they know they have not erred; who in turn scorn to ask, or to be accused, whenever they truly know they have erred. 25_marg1864: Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth: as if the weak man is not strong in adversity because in prosperity he does not refrain from the gluttony of beasts nor from the flight of birds. The beasts of the earth are those who long for the lowest things by the habit of a fleshly life. The fowls of the air are those who pry into lofty things with the zeal of proud curiosity. So God teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and the fowls of the air, because while we recognize what we are, we neither sink beneath the lowest things by flowing down, nor are inflamed by lofty things through pride. Or by the beasts earthly men, by the birds the demons are designated. And it is understood: “this too he did not say.” Or the creeping things, which cling to the earth with their whole body, are those wholly earthly in thought; the animals which are lifted from the earth by the belly but are bent toward the earth are good things which are done for earthly ends.

Or he put foundation for depth, wishing to signify the abyss of hell, whose mouth is sin, through which one goes on to hell. Or sin has no bottom, in which the fallen soul is daily cast down to worse things, as in the well into which it has fallen it finds no bottom on which to fix itself.
25_interl3302: he wishes to console Job’s words with the reward of eternal things, as if he promised of himself freely what was due to him by right
25_marg1891: And the rest of thy table: the rest of the table is the refreshment of inward fullness, which is said to be full of fatness, because it is prepared by the delight of inward pleasure.
25_interl3303: the just will then judge all things the more powerfully, the more they have been judged here
25_marg1892: Thy cause hath been judged as that of the wicked: the cause of the good is justice; their cause is judged as that of the ungodly, because their justice is wearied here by the fatherly scourge.
25_marg1893: But they recover cause and judgment, because from that justice by which they now live, they will then shine forth at the height of judicial power. And Eliu promises these things as if new, which is the custom of the arrogant man; who, because he thinks he becomes cheap when he comes down to gentle things, soon rebukes so as to be feared.
25_interl3304: if anger overcomes correction, it oppresses before it corrects, and under the look of zeal for justice it is fury
25_marg1894: Therefore let not anger overcome thee: the arrogant, who wish to appear kind for the praise of men, reckon as a motion of anger whatever is done by the censure of discipline; and while for the praise of men they wish to appear kind, they reckon that those are oppressed by good rulers whom they see restrained from vices against their will.
25_interl3305: or: of places, which is in the older books; that is, because you are revered everywhere; if you read “of gifts,” it needs no exposition
25_marg1895: Neither let multitude of gifts turn thee aside: because you are revered everywhere, beware lest you be lifted up by the haughtiness of that same reverence. And he said “turn aside” (bend) because everyone who is lifted up in time is bent by the very fact that he is lifted up. These words fit the arrogant within the Church. As if it were said to holy Church: beware lest, if you are lifted up by the veneration of the whole world, you fall from inward intention.
25_marg1896: Lay down thy greatness: the arrogant, the martyrs having been taken away to the things above, mock the Church as if consoling her, saying: by no means trust that you have greatness, because, the former fathers having been taken away, you no longer have any in whose life you may glory.
25_marg1897: And all the mighty of strength: as if it were said: those clung to you as truly mighty who held in you by living what they spoke by teaching. But now those who preside over you are mighty in look, not in strength. For the greatness of the Church is in the mighty, who fought for the truth even to death; when these are taken away, the proud, who set themselves first as if they alone were left to the Church, mock the Church as if consoling her: as if you no longer have true mighty men who may be troubled, and in whom you may glory, but those who preside over you now are weak. For they do not know that when the strong are taken away, the weak are strengthened by God in their place. But those they once knew as weak they believe never grow strong. And because they see certain prelates propped up by earthly power, which is weakness, they despise all according to their reckoning of these, and scorn that these are put in the place of the ancient fathers.
25_marg1898: There is added: “Prolong not the night.” Peoples, as being numerous, are these weak ones who live everywhere at their pleasure. He says this truly but not humbly, and he strikes more by rebuking than he consoles. Whence he also adds: “Prolong not the night.” As if he said: do not act in the darkness of your ignorance so as to put the weak in the place of the strong. For to prolong the night so that peoples may come up in place of the mighty is if it is brought about through negligence that the unlearned and weak obtain the places of strong teachers.
25_marg1900: Let not anger overcome thee: let him who corrects others’ things first see that he is not overcome by anger, which would exceed the measure of punishment and oppress. And for anger to overcome the mind, the cause is the multitude of places, that is, of idle thoughts, in which the mind rests. For the mind, poured out over so many things and bent, does not give itself to justice. The mind of the just man strives always to cling to one thing; the wicked man’s varies, because apart from God nothing suffices, and so what he just now asked for he soon loathes. But when the mind is gathered, it adds: let it know that what it does is great, for otherwise it would not do it. For that very knowledge is the entrance of haughtiness; whence God allows it to be tempted, so that, weak, it may be humbled.
25_marg1901: Whence he says: “Lay down thy greatness.” For, struck by vice, it perceives what it is and ceases to be great, and lays down all the mighty fears of the mind without tribulation; because when humility advances through temptation, adversity itself is prosperous; yet this is not done without adversity, which makes for the mind a night of sadness. But this night ought not to be prolonged but quickly ended by consolation, because in it peoples come up in place of the mighty, that is, unworthy and manifold thoughts. For, troubled, now it thinks it has lost all, now what it had been, now what it is now, now whether it can rise again, now whether, conquered, it can remain. Eliu says such things rightly, if he knew to whom. For this does not fit Job, to whose insult too he adds: “Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity.” He follows iniquity after misery who, after the evils he bears through correction, inflames himself with a burning heart by the torches of impatience. Which Eliu believed blessed Job had done, because he heard him, set amid the scourges, speak out with free voices; not knowing that all he said he uttered not from the iniquity of impatience but from the virtue of truth, because by the sentence of the inward judge he did not err even when he justified himself.
25_marg1902: Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity: the proud call this the misery of the Church, that they are condemned while God waits.
25_marg1903: For this thou hast begun: he condemns uncertain and unknown things as certain and known. For he does not know whether Job said the things he heard from him from impatience or from virtue.
25_interl3308: even if some say he is John, Elias or Jeremias
25_marg1904: Behold, God is high, etc. Eliu, who above brought in many things morally, now lifts himself to the secrets of prophecy. Nor is it a wonder how an arrogant man could be filled with the prophetic spirit, since even Saul was in the number of the prophets, and an ass received reasonable words. So Eliu beholds the humble coming of the Redeemer, saying: “Behold, God is high,” etc. As if he said: he who will be seen humble in weakness remains high in strength.
25_interl3309: Moses, Josue, the prophets are lawgivers
25_marg1905: None is like him among the lawgivers: we can call lawgivers those whom we know admonished the people to right things from the law; but none of these is like him who alone is without sin, the Son without adoption.
25_interl3310: his judgments: that he chooses this one, rejects that one; Judea is rejected, the gentiles chosen
25_marg1906: Who can search out his ways? etc. As if he said: he whose action cannot be searched, how can he be rebuked? For no one judges well what he does not know. Whence he adds: “Remember that thou knowest not his work.” Men have sung of the Lord, because his power is made known to us either by the spirits above or by all perfect teachers; and even those who preach him revere his judgments as unpierced. And the sense is: he of whom all the strong have spoken, his judgments are hidden from the eyes of your mind.
25_interl3313: it is seen that he is God, but not his judgments
25_marg1907: All men see him: every man, by the very fact that he was made rational, ought to gather from reason that he who made him is God. And to behold him afar off is not yet to see him by sight, but still to weigh him only from wonder at his works.
25_interl3314: even the just man in this life; the wicked man even in the other
25_interl3315: then we know something as it were in part, when we perceive that we cannot know him worthily
25_marg1908: Behold, God is great, exceeding our knowledge: because God is present everywhere, when “behold” is said of him he is spoken of as present even to those who do not see; of the brightness of whose greatness whatever we know is beneath him.
25_interl3316: it signifies that it is long, but incomprehensible
25_marg1909: The number of his years is inestimable: he wished to speak of eternity somehow, and called that very length of eternity years. For when we wish to stretch out the shortness of time, we extend moments through hours, hours through days, days through months, and months through years. So because he wished to say something vast, but found nothing wider to say, he multiplied years without reckoning of number, saying: “the number of his years is inestimable”; so that, while it multiplies the things that are long with itself, human weakness may recognize that it cannot measure the length of eternity.
25_interl3318: lest they appear to the world
25_interl3320: even if abundant water stands in you, yet it fell drop by drop from the cloud; lest you set yourself before it
25_marg1910: He lifteth up the drops (stars) of rain, etc. The stars of rain are those who so shine by the merits of life that they also rain the word of preaching. Such were the prophets, in whose stead, when the Lord took them away, he sent the apostles. After the outward sacraments fell silent, there were those who rained like floods; or, the apostles having been led back to the things above, the Lord opened up divine knowledge with a larger outpouring through the tongues of the expositors who followed. Or the Lord withdrew the stars of rain and poured out showers like floods, because when he took the preaching apostles away from Judea, he watered the world with the grace of new teaching. “Stars of rain”: those are stars and not rain who live well but do not teach, as there are stars in the sky which rain does not follow. But others are rainy stars; and these are the two kinds of the just.
25_marg1911: Which flow from the clouds: because if the teaching of understanding did not begin from the holy apostles, it would by no means flow more largely through the mouths of the saints.
25_marg1912: That cover all above: when clouds cover the air, if we lift our eyes to heaven, we look not at heaven but at them; so our understanding is not allowed to pass to divine things unless it is first formed by the examples of the saints who went before, the prophets and apostles.
25_interl3321: see what he does in the world through the clouds
25_interl3322: clouds: men are a tent for God, who rests in them on the way, hidden
25_marg1913: If he will spread out clouds: the Lord spreads out the clouds when, opening the way of preaching to his ministers, he spreads them abroad on every side over the breadth of the world. These clouds are called his tent, which is usually set up on a journey, because, coming to us through grace, he is covered within the minds of his preachers.
25_interl3323: words do not suffice for believing without miracles
25_marg1914: And lighten with his light from above: through these clouds he lightens with his light, because through his preachers he lights up the darkness of our insensibility even with miracles.
25_marg1915: He shall cover also the ends of the sea: for when these clouds rain with words, and when they open by miracles the force of flashing preaching, they turn even the farthest bounds of the world to divine love.
25_marg1916: For by these he judgeth people: by the words of the preachers, that is, the drops of the clouds; by these lightnings of miracles God judges peoples, because he calls their hearts, terrified, to penance. If anyone says: what if God sees that some will act wickedly after baptism, and therefore, forestalled by death, they are not brought to baptism? If it is so, then the sins of some are punished before they are committed; which God does not do, who sets free even from those committed; but the judgments are hidden.
25_interl3324: that is, to the wicked and the tyrants
25_marg1917: And giveth food to many mortals: through the same clouds through which terror is struck, food is also given, because the dispensing belongs to the preachers, so that they know how to afflict minds in such a way that they also know how to nourish the afflicted with consolation. And he does not say to all but to many, for not all have faith.
25_marg1918: Whence it is openly added: “From the savage he hideth the light.” The savage are those who lift themselves up with haughty thoughts; to whom the knowledge of truth is denied.
25_marg1919: And commandeth it to come again: because the light of truth which is hidden from haughty and busied minds is revealed to the afflicted and humbled. Or the light was hidden from the savage, that is, the Jews, who dared to contradict the Redeemer for this reason, that among themselves they stood out as savage. But those who are to be received to faith at the end of the world, he commands it to come again to them; the wicked are blinded in their works; to which yet it is commanded to come again, because when they know themselves sinners they receive the light of grace.
25_interl3328: Christ alone ascends, because he is one with the body
25_marg1920: He sheweth his friend concerning it: he who strives to keep God’s will in his precepts is called his friend. So of this light of the eternal homeland God shows his friend that it is his possession, so that he may by no means despair through the frailty of his weakness, but may be strengthened by the example of the head to overcome, so that he may come up to it. So whose heart does not tremble at being lifted to so great a consideration?
25_marg1921: So there follows: “At this my heart trembleth.” Fear is put here for ecstasy, because as in ecstasy, so in fear the mind is taken out of itself. And the place of the human heart is the delight of the present life. So the sluggish heart, long given to earthly thoughts, when it is suddenly lifted through ecstasy to the highest things, has changed the place of its low thinking. But how this is done follows: “Hear ye attentively the terror of his voice.” Because the sinner, while he carries his heart weighed down in low thoughts, if he is touched by the breathing of divine grace, understands that all he does is punished by the strict judge’s punishment. It turns over in his mind how terribly the sentence will come from the judge’s mouth: “Depart from me.” So because the proud heart is first shaken by terror, so that, shaken, it may be made firm in love, it is rightly said: “he shall hear the hearing of his voice in terror.”
25_marg1922: And the sound that cometh out of his mouth: by the mouth of God the Only-begotten is designated; because as he is called his arm, since through him the Father works all things, so he is also called his mouth, through whom he speaks to us. And by the sound of the mouth the Spirit of the Lord can be designated, of whom it is written: “And suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” etc. By the terror of the voice too the force of dread can be understood, and by the sound of the mouth the sweetness of consolation; because the Spirit first terrifies those he fills away from earthly action, and afterwards consoles them with the hope of heavenly things.
25_interl3330: as if after the high he looks also on the lower; for the Church is now thought to be forsaken because she does not do miracles as the apostles did
25_marg1923: He beholdeth under all the heavens, etc. As if he said: he who rules the highest does not forsake the farthest. Because what is done spiritually is not seen by the fleshly. For there are those who reckon that God does not care for human affairs and that they happen by chance; whence he adds: “all the heavens.” Or he calls the preachers heavens. So the heavens having been lifted up, the Lord looks on the lower things, because even when the highest preachers have been taken away he ceaselessly cares for our weakness too.
25_marg1924: And his light is upon the ends of the earth: because after the lofty life of those who went before, he takes in even the ways of sinners with the illumination of his grace, or gathers the nations to faith. Or the ends of the earth are the ends of sinful men. For often, looked on by grace from above, they return to God at their last.
25_marg1925: So there follows: “After it a noise shall roar.” For him whom the Lord has filled by enlightening he turns his life into lament; and after it a noise will roar, because when he enters the mind it is plain that the groaning of penance follows.
25_marg1926: He shall thunder with the voice of his majesty: God thunders with the voice of his majesty when he makes known to us, already prepared through laments, how great he is in the things above. Set on earth, we hear the sound even from the higher things, when, thinking earthly things, we suddenly dread the sentence of terror from above.
25_interl3331: whence you hear his voice when you are pricked to compunction, “but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth”
25_marg1927: And shall not be found out, when … shall be heard: the voice of the Lord is heard when the breathing of his grace is conceived in the mind. But this voice of the Spirit coming upon it, which works itself into the ear of the heart, not even the mind enlightened by it searches out. For it cannot weigh by what passages the invisible power flows into it, in what ways it comes to it, in what it goes away.
25_marg1928: God shall thunder wonderfully with his voice: God thunders wonderfully with his voice because he pierces incomprehensibly into our hidden hearts; and the excess of that same driving takes place in the mind, while nothing sounds in the voice; and so, by the oldness of life, habit is changed.
25_interl3332: the completion of the work appears outside, but the manner of the working lies hidden within
25_marg1929: So it is added: “he that doth great and unsearchable things.” So that man, given to earthly uses, weighed down by wicked desires, suddenly glows toward new things and grows cold toward his accustomed ones.
25_marg1930: How this is done follows: “He commandeth the snow to go down.” Waters drawn up on high are packed together so as to become snow. But when that snow comes to the earth it is turned again into the liquid of waters. So the waters are the minds of preachers, which, while they raise themselves to contemplate things above, are made solid with higher understanding. So snows come from the heavens to earth when the lofty hearts of the saints, which are now fed by solid contemplation, come down for brotherly charity to the humble words of preaching. For water is drawn up from below, so as afterwards to be given back to the earth from above. So he who has been raised up from the earth looks back on what he was and comes down to the rest.
25_marg1931: So there follows: “and the winter rain, and the shower of his strength.” Winter is the present life, in which the cold numbness of our mortality binds us. This winter has rains, surely the preachings of rulers, which will cease in the eternal summer.
25_marg1932: And the shower of his strength: the shower of God’s strength is the preaching of the Godhead; for the shower of weakness is the preaching of the incarnation. And because, having heard the power of God, we soon return to ourselves, weighing what we have done ill or well, he adds: “He sealeth up the hand of all men.” For men scorn to weigh the evils they do; but, struck by preaching, they will wake up and recognize the weight of their wicked works. Or the Creator made man rational, so that he could not be ignorant of what he has done, and is compelled by the law of nature to know whether what he does is wicked or right. Because above he brought in the virtues of God’s clouds, he now brings it about that the attack of the adversary too against the life of the good may be made known. Or, after the wicked members, he adds about their head.
25_interl3333: “The firstling of an ass thou shalt change for a sheep,” that is, turn the beginnings of an unclean life to innocence
25_interl3334: lying in wait for those who go by
25_marg1933: For there follows: “Then the beast shall go into his covert.” This is that beast which the dying Lamb cast out of the hearts of many, which enters the hearts of the reprobate. And so the beast is taken as the ancient enemy, who first savagely attacked man and tore the wholeness of his life by evil persuasion. When, after the thunder of the clouds, at the end of the world he invades Antichrist, what else does he do but go into his covert, so as to abide in his own den? The hearts of the persecuting Jews too were before the den of this beast, who handed over to the gentiles to be struck him whom they could not lawfully kill themselves.
25_interl3335: that is, from the Lesser Bear
25_marg1934: So it is added: “Out of the inner parts shall a tempest come.” Scripture, when it mentions the inner parts over against Arcturus, designates the southern region opposite to the parts of the north. So by the name of the inner parts the Jewish people is expressed. For those who knew God were held in the warmth of faith, glowing as it were under the noonday sun. But the gentiles, because they had reached no knowledge of the understanding from above, remained cold, as without sun, under the north. So out of the inner parts a tempest comes and cold out of Arcturus, as if he said: from the Jews malice arises persecuting, from the gentiles power pressing down; while what Judea sought out of envy, the gentile judge carried out by Roman authority.
25_marg1935: So against this envy there is added: “When God bloweth there cometh frost.” Because the more the Holy Spirit breathed on the hearts of the faithful, the greater the miracles of virtues he bestowed, the more the numbness of heavier envy grew in the minds of the unbelieving. So water had been turned to frost while, the world going after the Lord, the envy of the Jews remained sluggish. But because the Lord loosed the hardness even of so great unbelief:
25_marg1936: There follows: “and again the waters are poured out abundantly.” Because after the Lord bore the savagery of the Jews even to death, he melted their hearts from the hardness of unbelief, and from hard persecutors they became great preachers, so that a so much richer harvest of the elect might rise up.
25_marg1937: So there follows: “Corn desireth clouds.” The elect are God’s corn, to be stored in the heavenly barns, who now in the threshing of the floor bear with the chaff; but this corn waits for the streams of the clouds so as to grow.
25_marg1938: And the clouds spread their light: for the clouds to spread their light is for the holy preachers to spread wide the examples of life both by speaking and by doing.
25_interl3336: as if: wherever he leads, and to what? Because as they cannot go where they will, so neither can they act as they will
25_marg1939: Which go round about: God’s clouds go round about everything, because by the light of preaching they light up the ends of the world; but because, subject to the divine nods, they cannot fulfil what they will, they cannot go except where the will of him that governs them leads them.
25_marg1940: To whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth: for often they long to act one way and are disposed another. For mostly they strive to correct gently, and yet their speech is led into harshness; mostly they long to cut some off harshly, and yet their vigour is reined in by the spirit of gentleness.
25_marg1941: Whether in one tribe, or in his own land: by one tribe Juda is understood, which in Scripture is mentioned as famous and many above the rest. And the whole of Juda together is called God’s land, which then brought forth to him the fruit of faith when the whole world strayed under the worship of idols. And the place of mercy is the gentiles themselves, who received reconciliation from mercy alone. So the Lord spoke of his clouds, whether in his land or in one tribe or in whatever place of his mercy, because he gave the preachers of the Old and New Testament sometimes to the tribe of Juda alone, and rejected almost the whole of Israel for the wicked government of its kings; sometimes he willed the clouds to shine in the place of his mercy, because he showed holy preachers to the gentiles too.
25_interl3338: as if weary of the weights of lofty things, he adds through boasting: “Hearken,” as if he said: you who are less than I
25_marg1942: Hearken to these things, Job: Stand, and consider the wondrous works of God: he saw him as it were lying down in comparison with himself, whom he warned by the words of such great preaching to stand. For there are those who consider God’s wonders lying down, because they wonder at the power of his working without following it.
25_interl3339: through words the light of the clouds appears; unless the rain falls, it is not known what is in the clouds
25_marg1943: Dost thou know when God commanded the rains? Eliu examines blessed Job about things to come and humbles him as it were for ignorance. And he calls the words of preachers the rains of the clouds, and the sense is: if you already see the preachers who are to come into the world, do you grasp when the Lord drives them to preach by the filling of the Spirit, or in what ways he makes the brightness of their life known to the world?
25_marg1944: Knowest thou the … paths of the clouds? For these clouds have very fine paths, namely the ways of holy preaching. So they bind those by paths who do not go out from the track of their intention by wandering through the broad desires of the world. Which paths are great, because the narrower they are in the present life for the very guarding of life, the more they are widened in the eternal reward.
25_interl3340: which is done only by the gift of the Holy Spirit
25_marg1945: And the perfect knowledges: perfect knowledge is both to do all things carefully and to know that of one’s own merits there is nothing.
25_interl3341: they are not humble within themselves
25_marg1946: Are not thy garments hot? This is said generally of the Church and specially of Job. By garments clinging to a living body the life of disciples joined to masters who live well is signified. For garments cannot be warm of themselves; but joined to the body of the living, while they cover the breathing pores of the limbs, they give out the warmth flowing from within; and from them the warmth returns to the body while the teachers are kindled the more for the good of those under them. And the sense is: in vain do you attribute to yourself those whom you see advance in virtues, reckoning that they grew warm through you; because unless the favour of the Holy Spirit touched them, they would remain cold in their insensibility. After he has said these things strongly, he adds through arrogance:
25_interl3343: which is not easily consumed by rust
25_marg1947: Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him: by the heavens the angelic spirits who were created in the heavenly places can be designated. The minds of the elect clinging to heavenly things are most strong, as if of molten brass, because they are consumed by no rust of changeableness away from the wholeness of the strength they began.
25_marg1948: Again he adds mockingly: “shew us what we may say to him.” You, who already enjoy the great light of understanding, ought to teach us, who are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance.
25_marg1949: Who shall tell him the things I speak? He says this despising him, as if he openly said: the things I, perceiving them sharply, speak unheard of his praises, who can tell them, or after he has heard them?
25_interl3344: he who swelled arrogantly now adds by way of teaching: “even if a man shall speak”
25_marg1950: Even if a man shall speak, he shall be swallowed up: everything that devours something, drawing it inward, hides it from sight, and snatches into the depth a thing that could be seen on the surface. So man, when he keeps silent about God, seems to be something by the reason in which he was made. But if he begins to speak of God, at once it is shown that he is nothing, because he is swallowed up by the immensity of his greatness. But he truly became known to men when he showed himself to them, having taken up humanity; which, because it had not yet been revealed:
25_marg1951: There follows: “But now they see not the light.” But how this same light is seen by men he suggests when he says: “the air on a sudden shall be thickened into clouds.” By the air the minds of worldly men are designated, which, given to the countless desires of this life, are scattered hither and thither, fluid like the air. But the air is thickened into clouds when loose minds are strengthened by the grace of the regard from above with firmness of virtue. For clouds are the firmer the denser they are. And all the apostles had been air; but suddenly the air was thickened into clouds, because through the regard of grace from above the loose hearts of fishermen were turned into the solidity of preachers; who, since, their ministry carried out, they run back to the secrets of heaven:
25_interl3346: but because they run with rain even to death, he adds what comes of it
25_marg1952: There follows: “and the wind shall pass and drive them away.” The passing wind is the present life; the passing wind drives the clouds away, because the course of temporal life takes the apostles away from the flesh, and hides them from the surface of the earth in secret rest, as in the pole of heaven. But what is done in holy Church from their labours he adds: “Gold out of the north.” By the north the gentiles, bound by the cold of sin, are signified; by the name of gold the souls of the faithful. So gold is said to come out of the north, because from the gentiles, long cold with the numbness of faithlessness, the life of the faithful, precious to God, is multiplied within holy Church.
25_interl3347: not glad only, because he fears for himself
25_marg1953: And to God praise with fear, etc. “To God” is said as if it were said by those who are on God’s side. So when gold came out of the north, a fearful praise came forth to God, because when the gentiles brought the brightness of their faith, the multitude of the Hebrews already faithful praised the divine judgments with dread; because surely Judea was justly driven back while the gentiles were devoutly called; and she feared the losses of her rejection when she saw the gains of another’s calling.
25_interl3348: even if we find him, not worthily
25_marg1954: We cannot find him worthily: because whatever we perceive in him is from faith, not yet from sight. Yet he adds what he considers he has now found.
25_interl3349: he cannot be perceived worthily, how much less spoken
25_marg1955: He is great in strength, and in judgment, and in justice: great in strength, because he overcomes the strong adversary. Great in judgment, because even if here he presses down his elect through adversities, at some time he lifts them up in the glory of eternal prosperity. Great in justice, because even if here he bears long with the reprobate, yet at some time he damns them without end.
25_interl3350: he says right things which yet he does not do, as a crooked bow shoots at itself
25_marg1956: Therefore men shall fear him: he calls men those who are strong for understanding.
25_interl3351: he who wishes to see the wisdom of God in passing, let him climb the sycamore tree, that is, humbly choose the foolishness of the world
25_marg1957: And all that seem to themselves to be wise shall not dare to behold him, etc. By these words he suggests the skilled indeed but arrogant, in which he touched himself. For those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate the wisdom of God, because they are as far from its light as they are not humble within themselves.
25_interl3352: sometimes God speaks gently, so as to be loved; sometimes terribly, so as to be feared
25_marg1958: Because he speaks to one who is scourged, he is said to have spoken out of a whirlwind. But whether he spoke to him through himself or through an angel is doubtful. For the stirrings of the air could have been made through an angel, and these words that follow conveyed through him. And again an angel could have shaken the air outwardly into a whirlwind, and yet the Lord inwardly, through himself, have sounded the force of the sentence into his heart without words.
25_interl3353: as if: what he says I know, but who says it I know not
25_interl3354: because by strictness he presses him down so that he may not be lifted up
25_marg1959: The first reproach is such a question: “Who is this?” And we do not say this except of one we do not know. And for God not to know is to reprove; he surely does not know the arrogant, that is, does not approve their life. And in saying “sentences” and not adding what kind, we take good ones, which the unskilled man put forth wrapped in words, because they had been uttered with words of boasting. For the fault of unskilfulness is to understand the right not rightly, that is, to bend the heavenly gift to the appetite for earthly praise. So, this being despised, the words are turned to teaching Job.
25_marg1960: Gird up thy loins like a man: to gird the loins is to rein in lust either in deed or in thought. But since we know that Job was endowed with chastity, why is it said to him: “Gird up thy loins like a strong man,” that is, restrain lust, unless because there is one lust of the flesh and another of the heart, by which we glory in our chastity and virtues? So it is said to him that he who had first overcome the lust of corruption should now restrain the lust of pride.
25_interl3355: while I stir you to lofty things which you cannot grasp, answer, that is, see yourself humble
25_marg1961: I will ask thee, and answer thou me: our Creator is wont to question us in three ways. Either when he strikes us with the strictness of the scourge, and shows how much patience is in us or lacking to us. Or he commands certain things we do not want, and lays open to us our obedience or disobedience. Or he opens some hidden things to us and hides others, and makes known to us the measure of our humility. So blessed Job, after the questioning of the blows, is examined by the questioning of speech, so that he may consider what the things above are, and, while he hardly grasps them, may return to himself, so as to know how near to nothing he is in comparison with things above. For he who, laid low with sores, stood so firm in virtues had to be humbled. So he sends a medicine ahead of one who is to overcome and to be restored to prosperity. “Where wast thou when I laid up the foundations of the earth?” In Scripture we take foundations to be the preachers, whom the Lord set first in the whole Church, and on them the structure of the building that followed rose up. So lest Job be lifted up in mastery over the power of his virtues, in the first part of the speech he is examined by the remembrance of the holy preachers, so that the more wonderful he saw them come, the more cheaply he might value himself in comparison with them. And the sense is: consider the virtue of the strong, and weigh me, their author before the ages; and when you look up to them whom I made in time as wonderful, weigh how much you ought to be subject to me, whom you know to be the author of wonders without time.
25_interl3356: even if this was future in deed, it was already done in predestination
25_interl3357: among which are all the elect
25_marg1962: Or who hath stretched the line upon it? No one is ignorant that God stretches these lines, but this is said to Job so that he may recall what he could know and pass over, weighing more sharply that the ordering of man is not in human strength but in the hand of God. Lines of measurement are stretched in the dividing of lands. And the Lord, coming to the Church in the flesh, measured the measures of the earth with lines, because he marked off the bounds of the Church with the fineness of hidden judgment. The hidden lines or measures of this earth were stretched when the preachers, by the working of the Holy Spirit, were called into some parts of the world to go, and kept back from others so as not to approach them.
25_marg1963: We take the bases of this earth to be the teachers of holy Church, who bear up the whole weight of the Church by the fixed seriousness of their ways.
25_interl3361: because he joined both the two peoples to each other and both the corners
25_marg1964: Morally. As the mind of the wicked is dust, so that of the just is earth, whose foundation is faith. So “Where wast thou,” that is, you, a sinner justified by me: call to mind where I found you, and you will be humble. And because man is proud even of good things, God sets a measure on those who advance, so that through what is lacking what is present may be kept humbly. Whence he adds: “tell me if thou hast understanding: who hath laid the measures?” Who but God, who gave this to one and that to another, so that out of many there may be one body. The line is stretched over the soul of the just man when the examples of the fathers are shown to it, so that it may keep its measure and go neither short nor beyond; upon which are the bases, that is, the soul’s intentions, on which the whole rests; whence: “If thy eye be evil.” These are grounded on the foundation, that is, Christ, because we are made firm on the foundation more strongly when we follow the words of God from the inner precepts and weigh them by understanding in the inmost sense.
25_marg1965: He adds: “who laid the corner stone thereof?” Morally. The corner stone is a twofold understanding: that in God’s precepts we do outward things, or by contemplating perceive inward ones. To which our mind would never rise unless the Creator had taken up our nature, who showed in himself the examples of both lives. And so he is the corner: in the cities he teaches and heals; on the mountains he prays; so that neither contemplation be forsaken for care of neighbours, nor care of them for contemplation. The mystery of whose incarnation even the angels wonder at. “Or who laid the corner stone thereof?” Him who, receiving in himself here the Jewish people, there the gentile people, joins as it were two walls in the one building of the Church. Since this can be said not of the founding of the world but of the Church, it is plain that what goes before too ought not to be said of the origin of the world. And when he had said much of the building of the Church, he added how even hostile nations were joined to it.
25_interl3362: with the evening stars, that is, elect men
25_marg1966: When the morning stars praised me together, etc. For even the elect angels wondered at the mystery of Christ’s incarnation; who, because they were created first in time, are not unfittingly called morning stars. Or because, often sent to exhort men, while they announce the coming morning they chase the darkness of the present life from human hearts. These morning stars praise the Redeemer’s power along with the evening ones, because together with the men redeemed at the end of the world they glorify the bounty of grace from above.
25_marg1967: And all the sons of God made a joyful melody: it is called jubilation when the gladness of the heart is not fulfilled by the power of the mouth. So the angels praise, who already see the breadth of such great brightness on high. But men make jubilee, who still bear the narrowness of their mouth below. And because the Lord knew these things as future, he tells them as done. But because when the good make jubilee, envy inflames the wicked, whom yet God moderates:
25_interl3363: what God did to the sea he adds
25_marg1968: Of whom there is at once added: “Who shut up the sea with doors,” etc. The sea is the world; and by the name of the womb is designated the hidden and malicious thinking of the fleshly. Through this womb the wicked conceive, when they think evil. Through it they bring forth, when they carry out the evil they have thought. So the sea broke forth as issuing out of the womb when the waves of worldly threats, conceived from the wickedness of fleshly thinking, raged for the ruin of holy Church. But by God’s doing this sea was shut up with doors, because holy men were set against the swellings of the persecutors as a kind of doors, so that by their miracles the wrath of the persecutors might be broken and the Church stand.
25_interl3364: so that it might not see what it does
25_marg1969: Of which sea there follows: “When I made a cloud the garment thereof.” The raging sea is clothed with a cloud, because the cruelty of persecutors is clothed with the veil of its own folly, and is not able to see the light of truth. And because it is held in by the ordering from above, lest it be let loose against the saints as far as it wills, there follows: “and wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands.” By swaddling bands the feet and arms are bound, lest they be tossed hither and thither with loosened freedom; because the persecutors of the Church, by the unsteadiness of a restless heart, indeed think childish things, but, held in by hidden ordering, do not stretch out their arms where they will; and even if they lightly desire to commit every evil, they are by no means allowed to carry it out.
25_marg1970: Because he moderates the wrath of the persecutors by the ordering of his judgments.
25_interl3366: the glory of Christ and the reverence of the preachers
25_marg1971: And made it bars and doors: the holy teachers, open by preaching to those who follow, shut by their authority to those who resist, are called doors, because they both open the entrance to the faithful and again set themselves against the faithless lest they enter. And by the bar, by whose setting the doors are made firm, the incarnate Lord is designated, because he set these doors the stronger against the onrush of the raging sea the more he strengthened them by his keeping.
25_marg1972: And doors: he repeated “doors” for confirmation. But if you take the sea generally as the world, the Lord set doors against the world, reining it in first by the law, afterwards by the Gospel; and this “out of the womb,” that is, when the world was growing up near its origin. And then he clothed it with a cloud, because then not openly the light …; he set bounds around its immoderate wanderings, that is, the limit of the precepts. And because he checked the movements of men by sending the Mediator, he adds: “I made it bars”: Christ, who made firm the doors, that is, the precepts, by doing them, and the sea goes no further. Whence he adds: “The sea saw and fled.”
