25_marg1973: And here thou shalt break: a broken wave sinks back into itself when wickedness, overcome, is accused by the very one who did it. “Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further.” Because surely there is a hidden measure of judgment both of when the storm of persecution leaps forth and when it rests, lest either, not stirred up, it should not exercise the elect, or, unmoderated, should sink them in the deep. “And here thou shalt break thy swelling waves.” When the knowledge of the faith is stretched even to the persecutors, the swelling of the troubled sea is calmed, and there the sea breaks its waves, because coming to the knowledge of the truth it blushes at all it did wickedly. But because this is said to blessed Job so that the glory of his heart from so many virtues might be pressed down, let these things also be discussed morally.
25_marg1974: Who shut up the sea with doors: morally. The sea is our heart, troubled with fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with pride. “When it broke forth as issuing out of the womb.” The womb of wicked thinking is youth, of which it is said: “The imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth.” And the Lord alone shuts up the sea with doors, because he sets the bars of inspired fear against the wicked movements of the heart.
25_marg1975: When I made a cloud the garment thereof: our heart, tumultuous with thoughts, is clothed with a cloud, because it is darkened by the confusion of its restlessness so as not to behold eternal rest purely. “And wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands,” because it is still bound back from contemplating the highest things by the tender senses of its weakness. “I set my bounds around it.” The Lord sets his bounds around this sea, because he humbles our heart, still troubled by the vexation and care of its corruption, under a measure of contemplation, so that though it longs for more, it yet does not climb beyond what is granted it. Or because he looks on the unlawful movements of the heart, and in some he forbids them consent, in some he holds them back even from delight. Surely he sets bounds on the raging sea, so that it by no means goes out into deed, but the wave dashes itself, murmuring, within the bosom of the mind in temptations. “He made it bars and doors.” By the doors we take the virtues, by the bar the strength of charity. For the raging sea scatters these doors, namely the virtues, unless charity, set against it from the hidden part of the mind, binds them fast. “Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further,” because while each of the elect is both tempted by vices and yet strives against doing what is wickedly suggested, the sea is as it were held shut. Which, even if within it presses the mind with the tumultuous waves of thoughts, yet does not pass the shores of good living that have been set.
25_interl3368: through the incarnation he enlightens the elect
25_marg1976: Didst thou since thy birth command the morning? Allegorically. Understand: as I did. The rising of Christ’s Godhead has no before and after, but the rising of his humanity has. Through this rising the dawn knew its place, because the morning knew him. Or the dawn is turned from darkness into the light of morning. Or by the name of the dawn the Church is designated. Or because the dawn announces that the night has passed, yet does not show the full brightness of day; because we already do some things that belong to the light, and yet in some things we are not yet without the remnants of darkness.
25_interl3369: the future, in which there will be perfection
25_marg1977: And shew the dawning of the day its place: the place of the dawn is the perfect brightness of inward vision. The dawn considers its place when holy Church burns to contemplate the beauty of the Creator. And he well declares that after his birth he showed the dawn its own place, because before he himself became known through the body, he held the blessedness of the future reward in the minds of a few.
25_marg1978: And didst thou hold the extremities of the earth shaking them? The Lord held the extremities of the earth, because at the end of the ages he came to the Synagogue, already forsaken and subject to foreign kings. And he shook the ungodly out of it, because those who refused the preaching of faith he drove back even from the glory of fleshly sacrifice. Or he held the extremities of the earth because, forsaking the teachers of the law and shaking them out, that is, strongly condemning them, he took fishermen. And rightly he shook the extremities of the earth and held them, because when he terrified the weak hearts of the humble with holy fear, he by no means forsook them in strict judgment; and because he held the extremities of Judea in the apostles, he shakes the ungodly out of it, because he rejected the scribes and Pharisees as the desert of their ungodliness demanded.
25_interl3371: he had made a seal out of clay; now, the other way round, the seal shall be restored as clay
25_marg1979: Whence there follows further: “The seal shall be restored as clay.” The Lord found the people of Israel clay, whom he found given over to the service of the gentiles, slaving at bricks in Egypt; and when he filled them with the knowledge of himself, when he held shut in prophecy whatever the Truth revealed of himself at the end, what else did he make but a seal for keeping the mystery? But when, after the divine secrets, it loved the earth more than the truth, it returned to the clay of Egypt. It showed itself clay after the seal in the eyes of the Truth when through the malice of ungodliness it lost the mysteries of the word it had received, and chose to savour earthly things.
25_marg1980: And shall stand as a garment: coarser garments, when they have been put on, because they do not cling well fitted to the limbs of the wearer, are said to stand. So Judea stood about the knowledge of the truth, because it showed that it served the Lord, but would not cling to him through the understanding of charity.
25_marg1981: Where it is openly added: “From the wicked their light shall be taken away.” Because while they refuse to believe the truth, they lose the knowledge of the law for ever. For it is written: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy.”
25_marg1982: And because they lifted themselves up by the works of the law, there is added: “and the high arm shall be broken.” The high arm is broken when, the grace of faith having been preached, the proud working of the law is rejected. All these things can also be said otherwise, as follows: “shaking the extremities,” etc. Allegorically. A thing shaken is driven hither and thither; so was Judea, some saying “he is good,” others “no, but he seduceth the people.” Or the earth is the Church, whose extremities the Lord shakes under Antichrist, and yet, holding them, does not forsake them; from which the ungodly will then fall, who are within in appearance only; and those who are a seal while they seem faithful return to the clay that they were before. “And shall stand,” that is, persist in evil, “as a garment,” that is, for a short time, because they soon grow old. Or it is said to stand as a garment so that it may be shown that it cannot stand, because a garment that is put on is seen stretched over the body, and taken off it is folded up; so he who stands in the Church, stripped, lies cast away. And these obscure things he now opens when he says: “their light shall be taken away,” etc., that is, the feigned or true faith which they had held while living ill; and then his arm, that is, Antichrist himself, shall be broken. Or he shakes men with fear at least at their last, and holds them converted, and shakes ungodly movements out of them; and death, the punishment of guilt, goes with it, in which man, who was a seal and the image of God, becomes clay. And this clay will last until the resurrection, like a garment taken off and empty of the spirit. This is a special punishment of pride; but because it is common, what is proper to it is added: the light is taken away, that is, the glory of life, and the loftiness of the heart is broken; but in death the just have light.
25_interl3373: as I did, into hell, to draw man back
25_marg1983: Hast thou entered? As if he said: as I did, who not only sought the sea, that is, the world, through the flesh and soul I took up, but also, through that same soul laid down willingly in death, came down to the very bottom of hell as to the depth of the sea.
25_interl3374: these are the depths of the sea
25_interl3375: to each of the places of the elect
25_marg1984: And walked in the lowest parts of the deep: as the deep of the waters is grasped by none of our sight, so the hidden things of hell are pierced by no sense of knowledge of ours. So for the Lord to walk in the lowest parts of the deep is to find, in the place of his condemnation, nothing that holds him back. For to walk about belongs not to one bound but to one free.
25_marg1985: Have the gates of death been opened to thee? The gates of death are the opposing powers, which the Lord, coming down, opened, because by dying he overcame their strength; which by another name are called darksome doors, because, while they are not seen through the darkness of their hiding, they open the way of death to deceived minds. These darksome doors the Lord sees, because he both looks on and presses down the deceitful malice of the unclean spirits, and makes us see it so that we may beware. Or the Lord sees the darksome doors when, piercing the bars of hell, he struck down the cruel spirits.
25_marg1986: Or into the depth, that is, into the hearts of the wicked, even the most despairing, God enters and pricks them, and treads down the vices like waves; whence confession is born; and the gates, that is, wicked thoughts, are opened to the Lord, and so he enters; and the doors, that is, hidden evils, being destroyed, virtue widens those that were narrow before; which is to be considered as lying hidden, because, pressed by adversities, it lies hidden, but God sees it. Or consider how wide the just are, and stop glorying in yourself. But let us return to what was said above in another sense, and say that this is added because after his death and resurrection the Church grew.
25_marg1987: Whence he says: “Hast thou considered the breadth of the earth?” For while the Lord sought the narrows of death, he widened his faith among the gentiles. As if he said: weigh what I bore and consider what I bought. Do not complain of the blow while you do not know what rewards await you in the repaying.
25_marg1988: Tell me if thou knowest: justice is designated by the name of light, iniquity by darkness. And the sense is: if you suppose you have full knowledge, say whose mind it fills by coming.
25_marg1989: That is, the iniquity in which the blind man endures.
25_marg1990: That is, that you may judge whether he who is now seen as wicked will end his life in wickedness, or he who is seen as just will close the end of his life under the protection of justice.
25_marg1991: That is, that you may discern to whom persevering good action will give an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom his action, holding him fast to his end, will damn to eternal punishment. For “house” is put for dwelling, “path” for the action that leads to the house. And about so weighty a question he is asked, which is wholly unknown to the enemies, so that, being unable to know the end of others, he may feel the same about his own.
25_interl3376: he ought not to be lifted up who knows not how he came here, nor how or when he will go out
25_marg1992: Didst thou know then that thou shouldst be born? As if he said openly: what wonder if you do not understand the end, who do not grasp even the beginning? Or “didst thou know,” that is, as I did, who knew I was to be born, because I was before as God; but because man begins to be only when he comes to be born, he did not know he was to be born. Why then does man complain of scourges, if he who foreknew it was born to them?
25_interl3377: out of the wicked are made snow, that is, the white, and hail that strikes the enemy; and so put yourself before no one
25_marg1993: Hast thou entered? In the snow or hail, cold and hard, are to be understood the hearts of the wicked, which the Lord has prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war, so that when our adversary the devil strives to tempt, he may use their ways against us as his own weapons. Or because the Lord knows many elect laid up within the life of the wicked, because he makes saints out of such. He declares that he has treasures in the snow or hail. As if he said: put yourself before no one for your works, because you do not know how many workers of justice and defenders of right faith I am going to make out of those you see still cold through guilt; which, because it is done through the coming of the Mediator:
25_interl3381: so that through them he may assail us and purge us
25_marg1994: There follows: “By what way is the light spread?” He himself is the way, for he says: “I am the way.” By this way the light is spread, because by his presence the gentile world is enlightened. And he said “spread,” because the light of preaching shone forth not narrowed but shining wide.
25_marg1995: And heat divided upon the earth: the light being spread, the heat is divided, while each receives unequally the gifts of the Spirit by which they are kindled. Or, after the light is said to be spread, heat is divided upon the earth, because when the light of preaching shone out, soon the heat of persecution blazed up from the hearts of the faithless, spread everywhere. Or justice is the light; what is spread is not continuous; so in this life is the light, while we know these things and do not know those. But say by what way, that is, in what order I pour justice into hearts, when I fill now with this virtue, now with that: “Thou knowest not whence the Spirit cometh, or whither he goeth.” Against the light soon the heat of temptation rises, which is divided, because one is tempted by this vice, another by that which is near him.
25_interl3383: the more persecution grows, the more preaching too
25_interl3384: most violent is that which makes all things here be scorned and eternal things loved
25_marg1996: Who gave a course to violent showers? The heat being divided, to have given a course to the most violent shower is to have strengthened the onrush of preaching amid the straits of persecution. This shower is sometimes, but has no course, because the preaching comes to the ears but, inward grace ceasing, does not pass through to the hearts of the hearers.
25_interl3385: so that it may prick the heart
25_marg1997: Or a way for noisy thunder: by the thunder the preaching of terror from above is taken, at the perceiving of which human hearts are shaken. Christ too is called thunder, who was brought forth to us out of the agreeing prophecy of the fathers as by the clashing of clouds, who sounded terribly; whence the apostles too were called sons of thunder.
25_interl3387: as the shower and thunder do
25_marg1998: That it should rain on the earth: the heat being divided, the earth deserted without man is rained on, because, the persecution of the faithful having been scattered in the regions of Judea, the gentile world, long forsaken and as it were a stranger to the pouring-in of reason, is bedewed with the drops of preaching. In which, because there was no lawgiver, and no one who sought God reasonably, it was as if there was no man. It was called desolate either for lack of counsel or of the fruit of good work. He gave a course to the most violent shower, and a way to the noisy thunder, so that it should rain in the desert and fill the trackless and desolate land and bring forth green grass; that is, he joined inward inspiration to outward preaching, so that the withering hearts of the gentiles might grow green, the shut be opened, the empty filled, the barren sprout. Or each one who receives the word of God with the ear, not the heart, is a deserted land which has no man, that is, the sense of reason; or if it is there sometimes, it does not dwell there; but God pricks such too and fills them, and they yield fruit. And in this place we take the green grass to be the knowledge of holy doctrine or fitting works.
25_interl3389: the gentile world was trackless, to which the way to God was not open by the Word
25_interl3390: God’s grace is commended still more highly
25_interl3391: who pours into us in the darkness of this life
25_marg1999: Who is the father of rain? etc. The Lord is called the father of rain, because preaching from above is begotten not of our merit but of his grace. The drops are the preachers; for when they temper their preaching for the weak, they sprinkle as it were tender dew; but when they speak the things they perceive of things above with the strength in which they excel, they pour out as it were rain flowing abundantly.
25_marg2000: Out of whose womb came the ice? Having said by what grace the gentile world was called, he adds by what strictness Judea was driven back; because if there is mercy, there is also judgment. For in the frost and ice we take the hearts of the Jews, bound by the numbness of faithlessness, who at the Lord’s coming lost the heat of faith and charity, and, cast out of the hidden bosom of grace, went out as it were as ice from the Creator’s womb.
25_marg2001: And the frost from heaven who …: because the Jews, whom he created naturally good, he by just judgment allowed to go out from him cold through their own malice. The heaven was the ancient fathers, from whose offspring these cold ones came forth, whom God is said to have begotten, because, though he had made them good, he justly allowed them to go out from him for their malice. Or the ice and frost is Satan, who went out by malice from the warmth of God’s secrets frozen; he is the frost made from heaven, who, made in the heavenly places, fell from the highest to the lowest, to bind the hearts of his followers with cold; who hardens the water, that is, the apostates, into his own likeness, he who is stone; whose deceitful counsels cannot be known by the deceived; and this is “the surface”: one thing appears outside, another lies hidden within; the appearance of his persuasion is good, like solid ice on top, while deep malice is underneath.
25_interl3392: while the gentiles soften, the Jews harden, which is done by hidden judgment; whence the Apostle: “O the depth”
25_marg2002: The waters are hardened like a stone: we take the waters as the peoples, by the name of stone the gentiles. And the sense is: those soft hearts of the Jews, open to faith, are turned into the insensibility of the gentiles. But because these things are done by the hidden judgment of God, there follows: “and the surface of the deep is congealed,” because, a kind of veil of our ignorance being laid over it, the incomprehensibility of divine judgment is in no way pierced by the eye of the human mind. “Out of whose womb.” Morally. God conceives the mind of man when he forms it in his fear; he begets it when he brings it on to open virtues; but if they are lifted up, he leaves them, and they go out cold from the womb, that is, from the bowels of mercy. This going out is in judgment, because for now he bears with them in the bosom of the Church; whence Job ought to be humbled. Heaven is the word of God, the knowledge of which God often gives; but he who grows proud of it is blinded in that very word, and, hardened, rushes down to the lowest, and binds others; these God begets, not that he makes the guilt but because he does not free them from it; but because, the true image of virtue being forsaken, it is held for the praise of men, the water is hardened like a stone.
25_marg2003: And the surface of the deep is congealed: water hardens on the surface through ice but is fluid within; so their hearts, loose, show themselves strong through hypocrisy, imitators of the strong. Or the earth, rained upon, lest the seed of lust …, in the grass out of the womb, that is, the hidden place, brings forth frost, that is, temptations, so that the more slowly the fruit rises through humility, the more richly; and though the mind is in heaven, intent on eternal things alone, it is reined in by the frost of human weakness. If yet it presses down these temptations, and sets itself in a certain strictness of living, so that even if loose thoughts within provoke it, they do not draw it to consent in deed, they are pressed down by a certain hardness, and the strictness drawn over it presses down the heaving deep of the heart. Or the ice and frost is the adversity of the present life which presses the saints, so that they may be stronger in the eternal summer; and because prosperity alone loosens, adversity makes solid. The waters are hardened like a stone, that is, the weak man imitates the passion of Christ through endurance; and because, pressed outwardly, he guards the inward things better, the surface of the deep is congealed; that is, the mind is fortified by adversities to keep its deep gifts, as Paul, lest he should melt away amid praises, covered his secrets by bearing adversity.
25_marg2004: Shalt thou be able to join together the shining …? It is plain that no man can do this, but yet Job is questioned about these things so that he may take refuge humbly in God, who alone is shown to be able to do it. The Pleiades are named from their plurality; they are both near one another and divided. Through them, which are seven, he means all the saints, who amid the darkness of the present life enlighten us with the light of the Spirit of sevenfold grace; who, sent at various times from the world’s beginning to its end, are as it were separated, and joined through the intention of their mind while they preach one thing. As if he said: shalt thou be able to join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, as I do, who, being one, fill all things, and join the minds of the elect with the sense of unity?
25_marg2005: Or canst thou stop the turning about of Arcturus? In Arcturus, which by its circling lights the spaces of night without setting, not the life of the saints brought forth piece by piece but the whole Church together is designated, which suffers weariness and yet is not bent down to the failing of its own state. It bears the circling of labours, but does not hasten to setting with the times; but while it stands the night of the world is ended. This circling the Lord at some time breaks up, because he changes the labours of the Church to rest; then he joins the Pleiades more fully, because then all the saints will be coupled to one another by the very sight of vision, when at the end the Church is freed from the labours she now bears. We have something further to think about the stars of the Pleiades and Arcturus. For the Pleiades rise from the east, but Arcturus from the region of the north. And wherever Arcturus turns in its circling, it shows the Pleiades; and when the light of day draws near, the order of its stars is drawn out. So by Arcturus, which is born from the region of cold, the law can be designated; and by the Pleiades, which rise from the east, the grace of the New Testament. For the law came as it were from the north, which held its subjects with such harshness of rigour. For while it commanded some to be overwhelmed with stones for their faults, others to be punished with death by the sword, as a numb region, a stranger as it were to the sun of charity, it pressed the seeds of its precepts more with cold than it fed them with warmth. Nor is it any wonder that by the seven stars of Arcturus the Old Testament is expressed, because in the veneration of the law the seventh day stood out as worthy of reverence, and the vows of the appointed sacrifice were stretched over a whole week. But the Pleiades, which, as was said above, are seven, show the grace of the New Testament the more openly, the more clearly we all see that through it the Holy Spirit enlightens his faithful with the light of his sevenfold gift. So wherever Arcturus turns, it always shows the Pleiades, because through everything the Old Testament speaks the works of the New Testament are announced; for under the text of the letter it covers the mystery of prophecy. And our Redeemer, coming in the flesh, joined the Pleiades, because he had in himself together all the workings of the sevenfold Spirit, abiding. For no man had all the workings of the Holy Spirit together, except only the “mediator of God and men,” whose own is the same Spirit who proceeded from the Father before the ages. And while he joins the Pleiades, he breaks up the turning of Arcturus, because while he made known that he himself, made man, had all the workings of the Holy Spirit, he loosed the labour of the letter in the Old Testament, so that each one may now faithfully understand it with the freedom of the spirit, who before served in fear amid so many dangers. So let blessed Job hear: “Shalt thou be able to join together,” etc. As if it were said openly: you can indeed have the lights of certain virtues, but you are never able to exercise all the workings of the Holy Spirit together. “Or canst thou stop the turning about of Arcturus?” As if it were said: even if you already perceive what is right, do you by your own strength destroy the labour of coarser understanding in other hearts too? So consider me, who choose the foolish things of the fleshly while I show myself through the foolishness of the flesh, so that you may humble these things which you think the strong points of your virtues, the more as you do not grasp even the footprints of my weakness.
25_marg2006: Canst thou bring forth the day star in its time? The Father brought forth the day star in its time, because “when the fulness of the time was come, he sent his Son, made of a woman,” who appeared like the day star amid the darkness of our night, because, the obscurity of sin being chased away, he announced to us the eternal morning. Morally: daily the day star rises for the elect, and the evening for the reprobate, because the word of God is light to believers, darkness to the envious.
25_marg2007: And make the evening star to rise upon the children of the earth: the Lord makes the evening star rise upon the children of the earth, because he allows Antichrist to rule over the unbelieving hearts of the Jews, as their desert demands; who are therefore justly made subject to this evening star by the Lord, because of their own will they wish to be children of the earth, seeking earthly and not heavenly things, and were blinded to the brightness of our day star which they should have beheld. Which, because it is done by hidden judgments that cannot be grasped by men in this life, there follows: “Dost thou know the order of heaven?” To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of the dispositions above. To set down its reason on the earth is to open the causes of such secrets before human hearts. And the sense is: all that you suffer you ought to bear the more patiently, the more, being ignorant of heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer these things.
25_interl3395: namely as I; do not then wonder at your suffering
25_marg2008: Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds? The Lord lifts up his voice in the cloud when through the tongues of his preachers he shapes exhortation to the darkened hearts of unbelievers. And the onrush of waters covers him when the savagery of the crowd of resisting peoples presses his well-doing members. Through himself he lifted up his voice in the cloud when he preached many things to his persecutors veiled in figures of riddles. At this lifting up of his voice the onrush covered him, because the crowd soon rose up raging against him. Whence: “A cloud filled the house of the Lord,” that is, obscurity, and so the priests cannot carry out the due of the mystery.
25_interl3396: after the voice he adds miracles
25_marg2009: Canst thou send lightnings, and will they go? Lightnings come out of the clouds; so wonderful works are shown forth from the holy preachers. The lightnings go when the preachers flash with miracles and pierce the hearts of the hearers with reverence from above; whence: “Unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again,” because the saints go out from the sight of God for our sake, but soon run back to contemplation. Otherwise the preaching would dry up, because there they take what they pour out. And returning they say “Here we are” when they attribute whatever they know they have done strongly not to themselves but to the powers of God. Or they are sent and go when they go out from the secret of contemplation to the public of action. They return and say to God “Here we are,” because after outward works they run back to contemplation.
25_interl3398: in the senses, so that he may live as it sounds
25_marg2010: Who hath put wisdom in the heart of man? The cocks are the preachers, who amid the darkness of this present life are eager to announce the coming light by preaching as by crowing. As if he said: who pours the grace of wisdom from above into the heart of a man humanly wise? Or who but I gave understanding to the holy preachers themselves, so that they may know when and to whom they should announce the coming morning?
25_interl3400: who sends forth sound and judges and rebukes the hours of the night, that is, the deserts of sinners, and who first rouses himself with his wings
25_marg2011: Who can declare the order of the heavens? As God is the author of understanding, so also of speech, which ceased when he showed himself in his beauty. Or he now declares the order of the heavens when he makes known heavenly secrets to the elect.
25_marg2012: Or who can make the harmony of heaven to sleep? That is, he hides the hymns and joys of the angels from the reprobate; which yet became more widely known when Christ, appearing, took up even the unworthy and shut out those who seemed worthy. Whence, when the dust, that is, sinners, were made firm on the earth, that is, the Church; and the clods, that is, united in charity by the pouring-in of the Spirit. Or the clods according to diverse merits, such as virgins, the married, etc. And this Church, the Jews being scorned, seizes the gentiles, not by her own strength but by God’s. “Who can declare the order of the heavens?” Morally. The Lord then declares the order of the heavens when he makes known to us how he rules over the elect spirits. Then he declares the order of the heavens when, the darkness of our mind being wiped away, he shows himself in clear vision; and then the harmony of heaven sleeps, because when the rewarder of works appears in judgment, the words of exhortation will now cease. For by the harmony of heaven the agreeing speech of the preachers is signified; whence also the very time of the resurrection is openly joined to it.
25_marg2013: When was the dust poured on the earth? He speaks of things still to come as if past; for he has done the things that are to come. So the dust is then poured on the earth when through the resurrection it is brought back into solid limbs.
25_marg2014: And the clods fastened together: because surely firm bodies, gathered out of dust, rise again.
25_marg2015: Wilt thou take the prey for the lioness? etc. The lioness is the Church, who seized the gentiles and turned them into her own body. For her the Lord seizes prey so as to satisfy the appetite of her whelps, because for her increase he snatched countless ones out of the gentile world, and through the gain of souls satisfied the hungry longings of the apostles. For these whelps, through tenderness of mind and weakness of fear, after the Lord had suffered, sat with the doors shut for fear of the Jews, as is written of them: “When the doors were shut,” etc.
25_interl3402: that is, they are hidden in their thoughts until the opportunity comes; and others, when taken, hunger with great hunger
25_marg2016: When they couch in the dens and lie in wait in holes? etc. With the doors shut, the whelps who were to seize the world lay as it were hidden in certain holes, when the apostles, not yet made firm by the Spirit, did not preach with firm authority. But against their adversaries they lay in wait as in dens, so as afterwards, growing bold, to snatch the prey of souls. So others too after them lie down, waiting for the time of teaching.
25_marg2017: Who provideth food for the raven? By the name of the raven the gentile world, black with sins, is designated. This raven was food, when the Church sought it; but now it receives food, because it itself seeks out others for conversion. Whose young ones, that is, the preachers brought forth from it, do not presume on themselves but on the strength of their Redeemer.
25_interl3403: because charity divides one heart toward many
25_marg2018: Whence it is well said: “when her young ones cry to God.” For they can do nothing by their own strength.
25_marg2019: Wandering about, because they have no meat, etc. In this wandering nothing else is signified than the longings of the eager preachers, who, while they strive to receive peoples into the bosom of the Church, kindled with great ardour, send their desire now to gather these, now those. By the raven can be designated the Jewish people, black through the desert of unbelief, for whom food is prepared when its young ones cry, because while the apostles pray, the people long faithless is led to the knowledge of faith, and is satisfied by the preaching of its sons as by the voice of the young ones. And also when the young ones wander, the raven finds food from it, because while the Jewish people looks on the gentile world converted through the labour of the preachers, at the last it will at some time blush at the folly of its unbelief.
25_marg2020: Morally. The raven is the preacher, who cries with a loud voice the memory of sins, bearing the blackness of his weakness. He does not fully feed his disciples on the lofty secrets until they show the blackness of humility and the beauty of their flight to be lofty to him; first he lets them be afflicted with want, so that they cry to God and, wandering in the nest, wait for food with open mouth. For this discretion a larger plenty is given to the raven himself by God; for he receives greater things not only for himself but also for those he feeds.
25_marg2021: Knowest thou the time when the wild goats bring forth? etc. He calls ibexes small four-footed beasts which live and give birth among the rocks, and when they fall catch themselves unhurt on their horns. In them the person of spiritual masters is signified, who like ibexes give birth among the rocks, because in the teaching of the fathers, who are called rocks for their solidity, they beget souls to conversion; they themselves, like ibexes, feel the harm of no fall while they are caught on their horns, because whatever ruin of temporal adversity comes upon them, they catch themselves on the testaments of holy Scripture, and are saved as by the catching of their horns. They are themselves the hinds, who live with their vices slain as if serpents were killed, and from that very killing of vices burn more keenly for the fountain of life. And Job is well examined about the time of the bearing of the ibexes and the hinds. As if it were said to him: you believe you have done something lofty because you do not yet foresee the time when spiritual masters, sent into the world, beget sons through the teaching of the ancient fathers. For if you looked on their fruit, as on the bearing of the ibexes and the hinds, you would think very humbly of your own virtue. The southern region gives the name ibexes to birds which live by the streams of the Nile; the east and west to small four-footed beasts; so by these can be marked the hearers who bring forth everything through the examples of the strong fathers. He says “time,” because first the seed of God is conceived in the heart, afterwards formed, at last comes out in birth; and when this happens God, who does it, knows. Whence he says: “Knowest thou,” as I do? Many bring forth miscarriages before their time. “Hast thou observed,” as if carefully: it belongs to few to weigh what labour, what pain there is, and also what caution.
25_interl3407: the time, because the saints do not at once bring forth what they have within, but at the fitting time what God works in their minds
25_marg2022: Whence he also adds: “Hast thou numbered the months of their conceiving?” By the months, which are days heaped together, multiplied virtues are understood; which, because the preachers first heap them up in themselves, minds of virtues are made as it were in the conceiving of holy preaching. These months the Lord alone numbers, because he who gave them weighs the same good things in their hearts. And because the effect of fruits now follows according to the measure of the virtues, there is rightly added: “and knowest thou the time when they bring forth?” Understand: as I do; because surely, while I behold the hidden things of the heart, I weigh within, in the weight of the thought, the effect of the work to come outwardly.
25_interl3408: whence: “Bow down thy heavens and so come down”
25_interl3410: so as to draw us back from eternal groaning and pain
25_marg2023: They bow themselves to bring forth young, and etc. The holy preachers are now as it were hinds in the pain of bearing, because now with roaring they sow in tears; who bow themselves so as to bring forth, because unless they came down from the immensity of inward contemplation to our weakness, they would never beget sons.
25_marg2024: Because those who are born by the preaching of the fathers sometimes go before their teachers by suffering.
25_marg2025: Because, going out of their bodies, they find those pastures of inward greenness. And having gone forth they do not return, because, escaping the straits of the present life, they no longer seek to receive the preaching of life from their teachers.
25_marg2026: Who hath sent out the wild ass free? Now the words are turned to the life of those who seek the secrets of a withdrawn way of life, whom the wild ass, which lives in solitude, signifies; who is fittingly called free, because great is the slavery of worldly business, by which the mind is sorely worn while prosperity is sought and adversity dreaded. So he is sent out free who, having trodden earthly desires underfoot, is unburdened of the craving for temporal things. Or the wild ass is an animal of the field, because the Lord, taking an animal body, profited the gentile world more than Judea, as if he came not into the house but rather into the field; who is said to be sent out free, because he became a sharer of our nature, not of our guilt. Or the wild ass is Christ, of whose incarnation it is added, through whom the power of the preaching spoken of was given.
25_marg2027: And who hath loosed his bonds? His bonds were loosed then, when the weaknesses of his passion were changed for him into the glory of the resurrection. To hunger, to thirst and the like were the bond of our mortality. The bonds of each one too are loosed by divine help, when the inner reins of fleshly desires are undone. And because after his resurrection he called the gentile world to faith, there follows: “To whom I have given a house in the wilderness.” The Lord gives the wild ass a house in the wilderness, when the saints, withdrawn from fleshly desires, dwell in the silence of the mind. The same applies to the gentile world, in which there was hardly a man who used reason to understand God.
25_interl3413: they are houses when God dwells in them, tents when he comes to them
25_interl3414: saltness is wont to kindle thirst
25_marg2028: And his dwellings in the barren land: the land of saltness is this same wilderness, which, before it knew the true wisdom of God, had brought forth saltness; which, bringing forth no greenness of good understanding, savoured perverse things. Because holy men too, as long as they live in the tents of this life and are kindled by the daily heats of their desire for the heavenly fatherland, are said to have their tent in the land of saltness.
25_interl3415: but will enter with few through the narrow gate
25_marg2029: He scorneth the multitude of the city: to scorn the multitude of the city is to shun the wicked pursuits of human life, so that it no longer pleases him to imitate the lost ways of earthly men, who are many through the abundance of iniquity. Or, that is, he despises the ways of human life. Or certainly he forsook the many wandering through the broad way, and chose the few walking through the narrow.
25_interl3417: of the devil, or of the belly, which is spoken of especially, because it destroys the walls, that is, the virtues of the soul; when the near one is overcome, the outward enemy is more easily overcome
25_marg2030: He heareth not the cry of the driver, etc. The driver is understood as the devil, who once gave man the coin of evil persuasion, and daily demands from him the guilt of this debt. Or he calls the belly the driver, which demands a kind of debt from us, because even by nature it seeks that the daily fruit of human labour be spent on it. So abstinent men, who in this place are figured by the word wild ass, while they hold back the desires of gluttony by force, scorn as it were the words of the driver crying out, but hear him when he asks rightly. The driver can be taken as the devil, who brought in guilt by persuading and demands punishment by raging. His speech is, before death, the crafty persuasion of man; his cry is the violence, now plunder, after death.
25_interl3419: because from there he is fortified on every side
25_interl3420: when these are tamed, higher things are seen better
25_marg2031: He looketh round about the mountains of his pasture: he calls mountains the lofty of this world, on whom the Lord is said to look, that is, to change them from their iniquity for the better. These mountains are his pasture, because surely he is satisfied by the conversion of the straying and the humility of the proud. And it is to be noted that he says “looketh round about,” not “looketh into.” For he was made flesh in Judea, which was in the midst of the gentiles; he looks round about the mountains, because he gathered the lofty of this world, set round about on every side, out of the whole of the gentile world.
25_marg2032: The mountains of pasture are the high contemplations of inward refreshment, or the high sentences of holy Scripture.
25_marg2033: And seeketh for every green thing: for this wild ass to seek green things is for the holy man, having despised passing things, to desire those that will last for ever. For all things that were made in time are dry, which at the coming end are dried up from the pleasantness of the present life as by the summer sun; but those are called green which wither by no temporality. Or the green things are the hearts that cling to that inheritance which Peter calls unfading. So whoever desires to be sought out by the Lord, longing for the eternal fatherland, let him grow green in the inward planting of the heart.
25_interl3421: the rhinoceros: in the male, a horn in the nose; in the nature, folly; in the horn, pride
25_marg2034: Shall the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee? The rhinoceros is of an untameable nature, which, if it is caught and held, dies at once. And it designates the powerful of this world. And the sense is: shall the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee? Understand: as it serves me through those whom I send. For it is brought to blessed Job’s knowledge, for the humbling of his virtue, how wonderful are the things sometimes done through the apostles, who subject the world to God, and bend to him the tamed pride of the powerful of this world; so that blessed Job may value himself the less, the more he sees such difficult souls gathered to God through others.
25_interl3422: in figure of the Church; but what is impossible to man is easy to God; let him see then through whom it can be done
25_marg2035: Or will he stay at thy crib? The crib is not unfittingly taken as sacred Scripture, in which the holy animals are satisfied with the fodder of the word. And God tied the rhinoceros to his crib, so that, well shut in, he might receive the fodder of life who before wandered through the field of pleasure. For now princes gladly hear the Lord’s preaching and read it steadily. But because, after receiving the fodder of preaching, this rhinoceros ought to show the fruit of good work:
25_marg2036: There follows: “Canst thou bind the rhinoceros with thy thong to plough?” For princes, while they fear God in their acts, what else are they but bound with thongs? And when they do not cease to preach, by laws put forth, that faith which they long attacked by persecuting, they sweat as it were with the labours of the plough.
25_interl3425: as he that is subject to you is after me
25_marg2037: Or will he break, etc. The clods lying on top of tilled land are wont to press down the seeds cast in and choke what springs up. By these are signified those who by their hardness neither receive the seeds themselves nor let others bear the fruit of the seeds received. And after the almighty subdued the prince to himself, he converted or crushed the hard hearts of unbelieving persecutors, or of the false in the Church whom power presses down, when the simplicity of the Church was laughed at; so that, as broken clods, they no longer pressed down, but, loosened, sprouted at the seeds of the word they had received; so that princes not only remain believers, but also, in zeal, break the hardness of another’s heart. And by the name of valleys he means the soft hearts of the poor, which the clods, that is, certain hard men laid over them, hinder.
25_interl3426: he adds still more lofty things about the powers of the world, so that Job may think humbly of his virtues
25_marg2038: Wilt thou have confidence? etc. The Lord declares that he has confidence in the strength of the rhinoceros, because he bent the strength he gave in time to the earthly prince to the service of his worship. For because he is feared by his subjects, he persuades the more easily, the more he also points out with power the one who is truly to be feared.
25_marg2039: And leave thy labours to him: the Lord leaves his labours to this rhinoceros, because to the converted earthly prince he entrusted the Church which he bought by his death; because he committed into his hand with how much care the peace of the faith is to be guarded. And the sense is: I see the strength of earthly princes about to serve my worship. So I value the things you now do the less, the more I already foresee that I will bend even the greater powers of this world to myself.
25_marg2040: Wilt thou trust him? etc. The seed is taken as the word of preaching, the barnfloor as the Church. Who then would believe that this rhinoceros would render the seed to the Lord, that is, repay with works the word of preaching it had received? Which of the weak could believe that it would gather the Lord’s barnfloor? Behold, afterwards he puts forth laws for the Church who long raged against her with various torments. So let Job hear what princes do, lest he be lifted up by his own power, and let him by no means lift himself up within himself for the glory of so great a virtue. But because princes lay themselves down in great humility, the wicked, who long raged against the Church in open hostility, now turn to other devices of fraud.
25_interl3428: pressed by fear of these, the wicked feign religion and do harm within
25_marg2041: Whence there follows: “The wing of the ostrich,” etc. The heron and the hawk surpass the other birds in swiftness. But the ostrich has the likeness of their feathers, but has not the speed of their flight. For it cannot be raised from the earth; it lifts its wings as if for flight, in appearance only, but yet never holds itself up from the earth by flying. So hypocrites stretch out wings through the figures of holiness, but, weighed down by the weight of worldly cares, are in no way lifted from the earth.
25_marg2042: Of the ostrich: whose huge body has thin feathers, unlike the heron and the hawk. For so the hypocrite, if he does any things that lift him, more weigh him down; but in true preachers there is much virtue, little guilt, and their virtues are solid, so that they press down the winds of favour; those of the hypocrite are thin, which the breeze passes through.
25_interl3431: after the appearance he speaks of the works by which they are known
25_marg2043: When she leaveth her eggs, etc. Earthly offspring, namely, which is to be cherished long until it becomes a living flying thing; but the hypocrite begets by speaking, does not cherish by living. The good teacher too, lest he grow insolent, because God warms the abandoned eggs even without him; and if this is not checked in him, he returns to the folly of the ostrich, as below. But to have left the eggs on the earth is to give the sons no example of heavenly life; but because care from above does not forsake them:
25_marg2044: As if he said: as I, who warm them in the dust; because I kindle with the fire of my love the souls of the little ones set in the midst of sinners.
25_marg2045: By the foot the passage of action is understood. So the ostrich, deserting its bones, forgets that the foot may tread on them, because hypocrites forsake those whom they beget as sons, and do not care at all lest, left without the care of exhortation or the guard of discipline, the examples of wicked works pervert them.
25_marg2046: Or that the beasts of the field, etc. The field is the world. The beast: the ancient enemy, who, lying in wait for the plunder of this world, is daily satisfied with human death. And the sense is: if the devil, raging in this world, snatches away the sons brought forth in a good way of life, the hypocrite does not care at all.
25_interl3432: because his mind is scattered through outward things; but the good man’s mind, gathered, has the strength of living for itself and for those it loves; but the hypocrite, intent outwardly, has laboured in vain
25_marg2047: She is hardened against her young ones, etc. For he whom the grace of charity does not fill looks on his neighbour as a stranger, even if he himself begot him to God. The Synagogue too looks on those as not its own whom it finds living otherwise than it taught, and with hardening savagery exercises itself in their torments.
25_interl3433: but labours about their outward things
25_marg2048: She hath laboured in vain, no fear constraining her. Hypocrites are numb toward heavenly things, burn with earthly anxieties. So they trembled there where there was no fear. Who often burst into palaces, knock at the doors of the powerful, say that they fear God, and that therefore they sweat with such zeal in defending the patrimonies of others.
25_interl3434: for God not to give is to deprive; as if: he did not unjustly take away, but justly did not give
25_marg2049: He repeated this by adding “hath not given,” which, because he promised it, he deprived her of.
25_interl3435: this indeed is covered in peace, but in temptation it is laid open that he was a wolf under the appearance of a sheep
25_marg2050: He calls wings the pressed-down thoughts of the hypocrite, which, when time shall be, he lifts on high, because when he has found the opportunity, he shows them by growing proud. But now, because he feigns himself holy, because he draws in on himself what he thinks, he folds his wings as it were to his body through humility.
25_marg2051: She scorneth the horse and his rider, etc. To every holy soul its body is a horse, which it knows both how to restrain from unlawful things with the bridle of continence and to let go by the impulse of charity in the exercise of good work. By the name of the horseman he expresses the soul of the holy man. So the hypocrite scorns, because when he has broken out into open iniquity he despises the holiness of the elect. And the rider of the horseman is the Lord, who, possessing the soul of the just, rules it. And to scorn the rider of the horseman is to leap forth even to injury of the Creator. But now let the strength of the rhinoceros and the folly of the ostrich be set out otherwise. So by the rhinoceros, that is, the unicorn, that people can be understood which, while it took pride among all men from the law it had received, bore as it were a single horn among the other beasts.
25_marg2052: Of which it is said: “Shall the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee?” As if it were said: that people which you see grow proud with its foolish pride in the slaughter of the faithful, do you bend it under the right of your preaching in figure of holy Church? Understand: as I do. Which was done in Paul, who also stayed at God’s crib, because he did not disdain to chew over the words of the Gospel. And by God’s thongs he is not only held back from fighting the truth, but also bound to plough, so that, now serving the refreshment of men, he draws the plough of preaching; who broke the clods in the valley after the Lord, because in the humble minds of certain of the faithful, into whom the Lord had already entered while yet they by no means drew back from their former observance, Paul crushed the hardness of the law by refuting it, so that the grains of seed which the furrow of the heart, cut by the plough of faith, received should not perish, pressed down by the keeping of the letter.
25_marg2053: In the strength of this rhinoceros God had confidence, because the more cruelly he bore him inflicting hard things on him, the more steadfastly he foreknew him bearing adversity for him; to whom he also left the labours he had borne in the flesh, because he drew him, converted, even to the imitation of his own passion; who also rendered the seed to God, and gathered the barnfloor, the Church. And what we have said of Paul let us believe was done in many others too. But because we have heard what the Lord did with the elect, now let us hear about the reprobate; therefore there follows: “The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron,” etc. By the name of the ostrich the Synagogue is signified, which had the wings of the law, but, creeping in heart on the lowest things, never lifted itself from the earth. And by the heron and the hawk the ancient fathers, who, as far as they could perceive things to be understood, were able also to fly through them by living. So the wing of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron, because the voice of the Synagogue held the teaching of the earlier ones in speaking, but knew it not in living. “When she leaveth her eggs on the earth.” In eggs, one thing is what is seen, another what is hoped for. So by the ostrich’s eggs the apostles, born of the Synagogue according to the flesh, are designated. Who, while they show themselves despised in the world, teach to hope for glory above. For, cast away among the proud, they lay on the earth like eggs, but in them lay hidden that whereby they might live, and, lifted up on the wings of hope, fly to heavenly things. Which eggs the ostrich left on the earth, because the Synagogue, scorning to hear the apostles, abandoned them to the gentiles to be called. These the Lord warmed in the dust, because he raised up the living young of the apostles in that long-cast-away gentile world, whom the Synagogue, even though it begot them, did not lift from the earth. “She forgetteth that the foot.” Then the foot treads on the egg and the beast breaks it, when they are abandoned on the earth; because human hearts, while they always desire to think and always to do what is wicked, lay themselves down to be broken by the beast of the field, that is, the devil. “She is hardened against her young ones.” The Synagogue too looks on those as not its own whom it finds living otherwise than it taught, and with hardening savagery exercises itself in their torments. “She hath laboured in vain, no fear constraining her.” For in her labour it was not fear but cruelty that drove her to pant after persecutions. Or “God hath deprived her,” etc., because, knowingly, she lost humility; unknowingly she also lost the understanding of the truth. “When time shall be, on high,” etc. The ostrich sets up her wings on high when the Synagogue contradicts her Creator, not dreading as before, but now openly fighting, at the coming of Antichrist. “She scorneth the horse and his rider.” One comes from evils to graver ones: first he shows that he is not good, then he despises the good, at last he leaps forth to injury of God.
25_marg2054: Wilt thou give strength to the horse? But because the good are now mixed with the wicked, he begins about them, so that, having heard what you should shun and remove, you may hear also what you should love by imitating. For in this place by the name of the horse the holy preacher is taken; to him the Lord declares that he gives first strength and afterwards neighing. For the preacher first receives strength by quenching vices in himself, then comes to the voice of preaching for the teaching of others. And it is to be noted why the horse’s neighing is said to be put round its neck, because the voice of preaching flows from within but surrounds outside. For by what he stirs others to live well, by that he binds the works of the preacher to doing well, lest his action pass outside his speech. So neighing is put round the horse’s neck, because the life of the preacher too is besieged by his own words, lest it go forth into wicked works.
25_marg2055: Or clothe his neck, etc. As if it goes outwardly round about while inwardly it is drawn through the neck; it binds that from which it comes forth, because the preacher’s life is held by his own words, lest he act otherwise; and it is a collar on the neck, the sign of virtue in one who acts strongly.
25_marg2056: Wilt thou lift him up like the locusts? In the locusts the perfection of preachers is expressed; which, whenever they try to lift themselves into the air, first raise themselves pushing with their legs and afterwards fly with their wings. So the saints first rest on the good works of the active life, and then at last hold themselves up in the leap of contemplation, in which they do not last long, but take themselves back again to cares. Otherwise: locusts in the morning hours hardly lift themselves from the earth, but when the heat has blazed up they fly higher. So the preacher, while he sees quiet times for the faith, is taken as humble and despised. But if the heat of persecution grows hot, he shows of how great loftiness he is. And the sense is: wilt thou lift him up like the locusts? Understand: as I do. Who lift him up to be roused to higher things by this, that I allow him to be tormented by the heavier heat of persecution.
25_marg2057: The glory of his nostrils is terror: in this place foreknowledge is designated by the nostrils. For through the nostrils we sometimes know beforehand by use; whence in this place too by the nostrils of this horse the foreknowledge and expectation of the holy preacher are designated. The glory of his nostrils is terror, because the vision of the strict judge, which the unjust man dreads to come, the just man eagerly awaits; and whence the just man glories, awaiting his reward, thence the unjust is crushed, shuddering at the judgment. But the just man, what do we …?
25_interl3436: “They went from the presence of the council rejoicing, that they were accounted worthy”
25_marg2058: He breaketh up the earth with his hoof: in the horse’s hoof the strength of labour is shown. The horse breaks up the earth with his hoof when the preacher casts earthly thoughts out of the hearts of his hearers by the example of his works; when with strong searching he examines the earthly thoughts in himself, and, digging a well in himself, always draws out the earth. “He pranceth boldly,” because he is not broken by adversities.
25_interl3437: even when he is not sought
25_marg2059: Because he sets himself against the wicked and evildoers in defence of justice.
25_marg2060: In fear, punishment to come is dreaded. In the sword, punishment is already felt from the present blow. So because he does not dread adversities to come, he despises fear. And because he is not overcome even by the blow that comes upon him, he by no means turns his back to the sword. But what is done by the adversaries follows.
25_marg2061: Above him shall the quiver rattle, etc. By the name of the quiver the scheming of the wicked is designated. For the wicked, when they rejoice in the snares they think out against the good with secret schemes, prepare as it were arrows in a quiver. So the quiver gives out a sound against the horse, when the scheming of the wicked against the preacher more deceitfully makes known the plan which it deceitfully covers; because they set up the same snares which ought to profit the good, and send them secretly, so that, with threats sent before, they may terrify as by the sound of the quiver. But when they are not at all terrified by threats, soon the cruelty of the persecutors is brought to open punishments.
25_marg2062: Whence there follows: “the spear … shall glitter.” Against the preacher, after the sound of the quiver, the spear is brandished, when, after terrors shown, open punishment is brought forth, now striking from close by. But sometimes it happens that those who rage in persecution do not so much grieve that they do not soften the preacher as that through his words they lose others too; so because they do not overcome him by striking, lest perhaps others too who hear him forsake them, they soon prepare a shield of answer against the speaker’s words. Whence there follows: “and shield.” For against God’s horse, because the counsels of the wicked make a din, the quiver sounds. Because open punishment is sought, the spear is brandished; and because he is resisted also by disputation, the shield is carried in front. But he is not checked in his fervour by these things.
25_interl3439: which announces the danger of war
25_marg2063: Whence there is added: “Chafing and raging he swalloweth the ground,” etc. To sinning man it was said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go.” The trumpets blare when the powers of this world terribly forbid the saints to speak. So because the preacher, inflamed with zeal for the faith, does not cease to draw any sinners to himself, glowing he without doubt swallows the ground. And because he does not at all dread the threats of the persecutors, he makes no account of the trumpet’s noise sounding. And not only does he persevere in labours, but, what is greater, he exults in labours.
25_interl3440: here it is plain that he is not dealing with an irrational horse
25_marg2064: Whence there follows: “When he heareth,” etc. “Vah” is a word of exultation. So the horse, hearing the trumpet, says “Ha,” because the strong preacher, when he sees the contest of suffering draw near him, exults at the exercise of virtue. But he would by no means come unshaken to this war of suffering unless he reached that same suffering beforehand by intent meditation.
25_interl3441: preparing himself meanwhile by the exercise of lesser things
25_marg2065: Whence there follows: “he smelleth … afar off,” etc. As if he said: he therefore overcomes any contest, because he prepares his mind for the contest before the contest. For to smell the battle afar off is to know beforehand by thinking all adversities still placed far off, lest perhaps, unforeseen, they be able to overcome.
25_marg2066: The encouraging of the captains, etc. The captains of the opposing side are the authors of error. It is to be noted that he says the captains encourage but the army shouts, because those who preside among the unbelieving and heretics persuade as if by reason the wicked things they command to be held. But the crowd subject to them, because it follows their voices without judgment, while it makes a din through the madness of confusion, is said to howl with a beastly mind. “Wilt thou give strength to the horse?”
25_marg2067: Another moral reading. Under the figure of the horse he speaks of the preacher who is strong in war, a captain of the faith, or of any soldier, how he advances from his first way of life. Every one over whom God presides is a horse, to whom God first of all gives the strength of faith, to which neighing is joined, while what he believes with the heart he confesses with the mouth. He is lifted up like a locust at the beginning, because if in some acts he clings to the earth, in some he is raised up. For the beginnings of conversion are mixed with the new life through intention and with the old through habit; nor does that old one harm so much, which always assails; these weaknesses God bears with mercifully. His nostril is the foreseeing of the future judgment, where there is glory for the good things, but also terror for the evils still mixed in. So the judgment is to him both glory and terror; but counting fear slavish, as a son he begins to love his father. And because fear was on account of fleshly action, before all things he masters the flesh; because when with the hoof, that is, strong abstinence, he breaks up the earth, the flesh being pressed down, he rejoices more securely in heavenly hope. And this is: “He pranceth boldly.” Boldly, because he strongly holds the body down. He exults in the hope of eternal things. And glad, the body, the enemies’ helper, being pressed down, he sees more keenly their frauds, which to foresee from afar and to resist is to go forward to meet armed men, that is, the evil spirits, who are girded against us with frauds, covering evils under the appearance of good, as if they are covered with arms so as not to be seen naked. Against which he strives in vain who does not first overcome himself. But he goes forward to meet them who by exhorting forestalls their snares in another’s heart. Whence the enemies tempt such a victor more sharply about himself, so that his care may turn back from others to guarding himself and those forsaken may perish. But he, relying on the grace of God, both cares for his own weakness and does not forsake others. And this is: “He despiseth fear, he turneth not his back to the sword.” He despises, because he is frightened by no temptation into keeping silent. Nor does he turn his back to the sword, because even if violent temptation strikes him, yet he is not driven back from care of his neighbour, like Paul, who, though heavily struck, yet does not keep silent. The horse is struck and not stopped from his course; whence the enemy, despised, seeks out sharper darts, so that, the captain turned to flight, the horses he ruled may be scattered. So he multiplies various things from the quiver: through snares he hurls; the spear he brandishes openly; because some vices he covers with the hope of virtues, others he puts forward as they are, openly, when he sees him grow weak. He does not seek frauds except when he seeks to deceive the strong. If not even so does he succeed, he puts up the shield, that is, certain difficulties against his efforts, and so cannot conquer. Or he resists and closes the road of one advancing. But against these things God’s horse, chafing and raging, swallows the ground, that is, consumes earthly things in himself, nor makes account of the trumpet’s noise. The noise of the trumpet sounds when, amid things well done, some fault from close by tempts terribly. But he neither forsakes good things and turns aside from the vice that is born of good. For he would make account of its sounding if, on account of the evil that springs up, he feared to act rightly. And lest, while he prospers in virtues, he be lifted up, he rejoices to be beaten by temptations. And this is: “When he heareth,” etc.; the shaking of temptations betrays the weak; the recognition of weakness is the guard of virtues. And he overcomes temptation because it is not unforeseen. “He smelleth the battle afar off,” that is, from the causes going before he recognizes what vices follow after: as from learning, arrogance; from justice, cruelty; from zeal, anger. He sees also what crowd of evils rushes in if he admits even a few. And this is: “the encouraging of the captains,” etc. For some are the captains, and others are those which soon follow. The queen is pride, which hands over the one it captures to the seven principal vices, as to its captains; which captains many vices follow: “Pride is the beginning of all sin.” Her first daughters are vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, lust; against which seven the sevenfold Spirit is given. From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, incontinence, obstinacy, discord, presumptions of novelties. From envy: hatreds, whispering, detraction, exultation at a neighbour’s adversities, affliction at his prosperity. From anger: quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, clamour, indignation, blasphemy. From sadness: malice, rancour, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness about the precepts, wandering of the mind toward unlawful things. From avarice: treachery, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, violence, hardenings of heart against mercy. From gluttony: foolish mirth, buffoonery, uncleanness, much speaking, dullness of sense about understanding. From lust: blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, love of self, hatred of God, affection for the present world, horror or despair of the future. Of these seven, five are spiritual, two fleshly; but they are so akin that one is brought forth from another, because vainglory begets envy, envy anger. From anger the troubled mind is saddened. Sadness, having nothing in itself to be glad of, seeks outside and makes one avaricious. Among the fleshly, lust is born of gluttony. These seven bring themselves into the deceived mind as if under a kind of reason, and therefore they are said to encourage; their followers, while they drag it into every madness, confound it with a beastly clamour. For vainglory suggests that one should be over others so as to profit more. Envy shows as if by reason that others are not to be higher than him or equal. Anger urges that injuries done should not be borne, lest they become wont to be done. Sadness as it were proves that he has nothing to rejoice in, when all his neighbours are so bitter to him. Avarice says it is right to gather, lest he be in want, and he spends better what others keep. Gluttony says that all things were made by God for eating, that the gifts of God ought not to be refused. Lust, since time is short and we do not know what follows, says that we should not lose the time we live. For if God disapproved of intercourse, he would not have made male and female.
25_interl3444: anyone is renewed, or the gentile especially
25_interl3445: the hawk does this by nature
25_marg2068: Doth the hawk wax feathered by thy wisdom? etc. Having said under the figure of the horse how great, how strong the saint is against contests, he begins under the figure of birds to tell how far he flies in contemplation. For every year the hawk casts off its old feather as a new one grows. What then is it for the hawk to grow feathers in the south, except that each of the saints, touched by the Holy Spirit, grows warm, and, casting off the habit of his old way of life, takes the form of the new man? And the sense is: did you give to any of the elect understanding, which you yourself do not have of yourself, so that when the Holy Spirit breathes he spreads the wings of his thoughts, opens them by confessing, so as to cast off the weights of the old way of life and take the feathers of virtues for the use of flight? The hawk lays down its old feathers at the time of the south wind.
25_interl3446: as at mine, who breathe in what I command
25_interl3447: places his counsel in things above
25_marg2069: Will the eagle mount up at thy command? etc. In this place by the name of the eagle the keen understanding of the saints and their lofty contemplation are figured. The eagle is lifted up at God’s command when the life of the faithful, obeying the divine commands, is held up on high. It makes its nest on high, because it does not set the dwelling of its mind in an abject and lowly way of life.
25_marg2070: She abideth among the rocks: in sacred speech, when a rock is named in the singular number, Christ is understood; when in the plural, holy men are expressed. Whence Peter: “Be you also as living stones.” So the eagle is said to abide among the rocks, because they are placed, by the standing of their mind, in the sayings of the ancient and strong fathers. The rocks can also be understood as the heavenly powers, because like rocks set on high they are strangers to every movement of changeableness, as trees are not. So the holy man waits for the everlasting glory of the angels, and, a guest in this world, longing for those things he beholds, is already fixed on high.
25_marg2071: What are the cragged flints but those strongest choirs of angels? For they are broken off, because part of them fell, part remained; who stand whole indeed in the quality of their merit, but broken off in the quantity of their number. By the same he means the inaccessible crags. For the charity of the angels is very inaccessible to the heart of sinful men. But whoever is so caught up in contemplation that he already sets his intention among the choirs of angels, it is not enough for him unless he can see also him who is above the angels.
25_marg2072: There follows: “From thence she looketh for the prey.” The same stretches the eye of the mind out of those angelic choirs to the glory of the majesty above, because he hungers for it while not yet seen, by which at last, seen, he is satisfied. But because, weighed down by the flesh, we cannot see God as he is, there follows: “and her eyes behold afar off.” As if he said: the saints stretch the sharpness of their intention strongly, but do not behold God from nearer, the greatness of whose brightness they cannot pierce. But the preachers themselves, when they see that their hearers cannot take in the word of the Godhead, turn to the words of the Lord’s incarnation alone.
25_interl3448: but neither does it open to the young what it sees from on high
25_marg2074: Whence there follows: “Her young ones shall suck up blood.” As if it were said: she herself indeed is fed on the contemplation of the Godhead, but because her hearers can by no means perceive the secrets of the Godhead, they are satisfied by knowing the blood of the crucified Lord. To lick blood is to venerate the weak things of the Lord’s passion. But because the preacher’s soul, freed from the flesh, is soon led to him who of his own will fell into death for us:
25_interl3449: the conversion of sinners is the refreshment of the just; or Christ now sitting in heaven
25_marg2075: There follows: “And wheresoever the carcass shall be, she is immediately there.” As in that saying: “Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered together.” Otherwise: every one who has fallen by the death of sin can be called a carcass. And the holy preacher, where he sees sinners to be, flies there anxiously, so as to show the light of quickening to those lying in the death of sin. So, having heard of so many virtues of the saints, blessed Job is understood to have been astounded and to have fallen silent in the terror of wonder.
25_marg2076: For there follows: “And the Lord went on, and said to Job.” The holy man did not think that by this strictness of the scourge his merits were being increased, but that vices were being cut away; and because he knew none in himself, he believed himself struck unjustly; and to reprove the one striking is to murmur at the blow. But the Lord, considering that the things he uttered he had gathered not from swelling but from the quality of his life, rebukes him tenderly, saying: “Shall he that contendeth with God be so easily silenced? surely he that reproveth God,” etc. As if he said more openly: you who spoke such great things about your own action, why have you fallen silent on hearing the life of the saints? It was to reprove me, to doubt about my striking whether it was just. And you said true things about yourself indeed, but you did not know where the scourges were tending; because if there is nothing to correct, there is something to make grow. I have told of others; even if you knew their merits, you did not know their loftiness. So, having heard their virtues, answer if you can about your own. But every just man, attending to the good things of others, is not proud as if of being singular.

25_interl3451: as you see some equal, others less, and that the punishment is an increase of merit

25_marg2077: As if he said: I would defend my speech if I had uttered it with the weight of reason. Or, after the tongue is convicted of having used lightness, what remains but that it be reined in by silence?
25_marg2078: Answer: he is reproved for silence as before for speech; if he does not know why he was struck, let him yet in silence revere it, because it is from a just one.
25_interl3454: work will cover speech; this he says of himself, and in figure of the Church, which covers with the merits of life the faults of the tongue, which no one can tame
25_marg2079: I will lay my hand upon my mouth, etc. That is, that in which I see that I have displeased the strict judge by my speech, I hide before his eyes under the veil of right work.
25_marg2080: One thing I have spoken: for us to speak to men is to open a hidden meaning. But for us to speak to the divine ears is to show the movement of the mind even by the expression of action. And blessed Job confesses that by his speaking he had sinned twice. For to speak one thing unlawfully is to do things worthy of the scourge. And to speak another is even to murmur about the scourge. And the sense is: I believed myself right among men, but now that you speak, I have found myself wicked both before the scourges and stiff after the scourges.
25_interl3456: because, with you teaching, I have learned that man has no justice
25_interl3457: that I doubted about the scourges, as if less patient
25_marg2081: To which I will add no more: because now, the more finely I understand while you speak, the more humbly I search into myself. For a man nearer the light feels what he was before, and loves the more what he now tastes, and judges what lies beneath, and the worthier he is, the more unworthy he seems to himself, and the nearer he is, the farther away.
